In an article lamenting the woeful state of science education (a column in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction), Asimov remarked that a chemistry professor would be ashamed to admit that he only read comic books, even if it were true, whereas an English professor would boast of his ignorance of calculus.

3. Context. The remark supports the discussion's answer to Robin Dunbar's question of whether humanities professionals are as scientifically literate as scientists are culturally literate: the answer is no.

4. Significance. Ignorance of this sort feeds the belief that science is static, a 17th century discovery with fixed methods, rather than "a dynamic, knowledge-generating process that continues to evolve." Asimov's contrast shows why understanding science matters even for people who will never do science.

U1-P11Person

Identify Theodosius Dobzhansky and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 9 epigraph, p. 125

1. Who. Theodosius Dobzhansky, the evolutionary geneticist, supplies the epigraph of Derry's Chapter 9, "Ultimate Questions: Science and Religion" (quoted from Mary Midgley's Evolution as a Religion).

2. Quotation. "Science and religion deal with different aspects of existence. If one dares to overschematize for the sake of clarity, one may say that these are the aspect of fact and the aspect of meaning" (Derry, p. 125).

3. Meaning. Derry builds the chapter on this division: "Science attempts to bring coherence to our experiences, whereas religion attempts to infuse our experiences with meaning" (Derry, p. 125). Scientific statements concern sensory information and public discourse; religious ones concern the transcendent.

4. Significance. Because science and religion deal with the aspects of fact and of meaning, with different purposes and methods, Derry sees no inherent conflict; conflicts arise when one invades the realm of discourse proper to the other. Telling a question of fact from a question of meaning keeps a scientific argument within what the evidence can warrant.

U1-P12Person

Identify A. D. White and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 9, p. 127

1. Who. A. D. White (Andrew Dickson White, first president of Cornell University) wrote The Warfare of Science with Theology, originally published in 1895 (Derry ch. 9, For Further Reading).

2. Contribution. White "spent about 800 pages documenting in detail this dismal record of religious interference with science (and that was only through 1895)" (Derry, p. 127). The record includes the banning of Copernicus's work, Galileo's trial by the Inquisition, the burning of Giordano Bruno, lightning rods denounced as impious, and Anglican attacks on Darwin.

3. Derry's reading. All of the cases White documented, from Christian Western Europe, involve religious authorities making statements about nature that have no particular spiritual content and contradict the evidence of the senses.

4. Significance. Derry sees no inherent conflict between science and religion, since their purposes and methods differ; conflicts happen when one invades the realm of discourse proper to the other. He adds the less discussed reverse case, scientists who pass off religious statements as scientific deductions.

U1-P13Person

Identify Michael Polanyi and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 9, p. 128

1. Who. Michael Polanyi is "the chemist/philosopher" Derry cites in Chapter 9; his Science, Faith, and Society is in the chapter's reading list (Derry ch. 9).

2. Idea. Science is skeptical about any individual result, claim or theory, but to do science at all, scientists need an underlying faith that nature is "in some sense lawful, rational, and orderly." Polanyi emphasized that scientists "must also have an implicit faith that the overall premises and methodologies of science are valid" (Derry, p. 128).

3. Meaning. The simple contrast of religion based on faith and science based on experience is wrong: both faith and experience are intrinsic to both religion and science, but in very different ways.

4. Significance. Scientific reasoning rests on presuppositions that no single experiment proves, so a scientist's skepticism about results sits alongside trust in the premises and methods of science. Polanyi's epigraph to Derry's Chapter 1 (Unit 2) makes a related point about discovery.

U1-P14Person

Identify Laplace and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 9, p. 131

1. Who. Laplace (Pierre-Simon Laplace) was a French mathematician and astronomer, the author of Celestial Mechanics (Derry, p. 131).

2. Story. When Napoleon asked Laplace why he left God out of Celestial Mechanics, Laplace replied "I had no need of that hypothesis" (Derry, p. 131).

3. Derry's reading. "Laplace was correct, of course, but that doesn't tell us anything about God. It only tells us something about celestial mechanics." Science can get along quite well without religion, but this does not mean that science has invalidated religion or that the two are incompatible.

4. Significance. That science does not require nonmaterial entities does not logically exclude their existence, so it is impossible to prove on scientific grounds either that God exists or that God doesn't exist. A method that works without an assumption tells us about the method's domain, not about whether the assumption is true.

U1-P15Person

Identify Francis Bacon and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 10, pp. 133-136

1. Who. Francis Bacon, the English philosopher and statesman, "eloquently expressed the idea that science would contribute many practical benefits to society in general" and hoped society would devote resources to science in return (Derry, p. 133).

2. Work. "The prophet of public funding for science was Francis Bacon." In his fictional work New Atlantis, written in 1624, Bacon envisioned a utopian society that supported systematic scientific research to unlock the secrets of nature and systematic applications of that knowledge to produce practical benefits (Derry, p. 135).

3. Context. Bacon's work may have influenced the founding of the Royal Society, but the King gave only his good name, not money. For the next three centuries research was done on low budgets, until World War II (Derry, p. 135).

4. Significance. Derry judges that "Bacon's vision has come to pass": governments now fund science mainly for practical returns such as economic prosperity, military security and better health. Public funding ties science to society, which through public policy decides how research resources are allocated and how technology is used.

U1-P16Person

Identify Vannevar Bush and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 10, pp. 133, 136

1. Who. Vannevar Bush was "the head of the scientific war effort" in the United States during World War II (Derry, p. 136). His words open Derry's Chapter 10.

2. Report. Franklin Roosevelt asked Bush to write a report on the role of government in postwar science. Derry says the influential report, "entitled Endless Horizons, recommended large scale funding of scientific research by the government and led to the creation of the National Science Foundation" (Derry, p. 136). Since then the federal government has dominated the funding of science.

3. Epigraph. "Science, by itself, provides no panacea for individual, social, and economic ills. It can be effective in the national welfare only as a member of a team" (Derry, p. 133).

4. Significance. Bush's report turned Bacon's vision of publicly funded science into policy. Scientists may be moved by curiosity, but society funds science for practical reasons, so funding decisions shape which questions are investigated. Note that the 1945 report is usually cited as Science, the Endless Frontier; Endless Horizons (1946) is the Bush book Derry quotes in the epigraph.

Unit 2

Can Science Be Defined

Readings Discussions 2.1 and 2.2; Derry Prologue, pp. 1-8, and Chapter 1, pp. 11-25.

Official study guide questions4

U2-SG01Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the similarities and differences between research in the sciences and in the humanities.

Source Discussions 1.2, 2.1, 3.2; Derry Prologue

Research in the sciences and research in the humanities are often treated as two separate cultures, but the readings show that they share much of their reasoning while differing in what they study and in how a conclusion is checked.

The first similarity is that both begin with questions. Discussion 3.2 describes science as a question-and-answer process: a good question, asked in context, generates conjectures that others then criticize. A historian asking why a revolution broke out, or a literary scholar asking what a poem means, works in the same way. Both also depend on imagination and judgment. Derry's Prologue says that a picture of science as nothing but testing statements against the world is "impoverished", because imagination, logic, creativity, judgment and metaphor are all part of science. These are exactly the tools of humanistic interpretation. Both fields build models. Derry, sitting on a jury, asked what model of the accident was consistent with the photographs of the damage, which is the same reasoning a historian uses to reconstruct an event from surviving documents. Finally, both are public and critical. A scientific paper and a work of history are each published so that others can examine the evidence and challenge the argument, and in both fields the conclusions are relatively, not absolutely, true (Discussion 2.1).

The differences lie in the object of study and in the standard of evidence. The sciences study natural phenomena that can be observed, measured and, in many cases, reproduced. When Derry wanted to know whether copper bowls work by making egg whites more acidic, a simple acidity measurement settled the question, and a light-absorption experiment confirmed the alternative. The humanities study human meanings, values, texts and unique historical events. The French Revolution cannot be rerun with a control group, and there is no instrument that measures what Hamlet means. As a result, the sciences lean heavily on correspondence with the facts, tested by prediction and experiment, while the humanities lean more on coherence, meaning how well an interpretation fits the whole text, its context and other accepted knowledge. The sciences also aim at general laws and causal explanations that hold for every case of a kind, while the humanities often aim to understand one particular work or person in depth. For that reason several rival interpretations can stand together in the humanities, while a scientific community usually works toward a single accepted theory, as chemists eventually did with Kekulé's benzene ring.

These differences are matters of degree, not a wall. Discussion 1.2 notes that modern science began during two of the greatest periods of literature and art, ancient Greece and the Scientific Revolution, and Robin Dunbar argues that the average scientist is as culturally literate as the average humanities graduate. Both kinds of research are disciplined, public attempts to understand. The sciences test their understanding mainly against nature, and the humanities test theirs mainly against the record of human thought and expression.

U2-SG02Study guide

Write out summary definitions of science from the readings presented in this Study Guide and in the textbooks. Then, comparing your summaries, write a definition of science that is consistent with all of them.

Source Unit 2 Overview; Discussions 1.1, 2.1, 2.2, 4.1; Derry Prologue

Summary definitions from the readings

1. American Heritage Dictionary (Unit 2 Overview). Science is "the observation, identification, description, experimental investigation, and theoretical explanation of natural phenomena." This definition stresses activities and a subject: nature.

2. Unit 2 Overview. The sciences cannot be unified by subject matter or by one method. "The" scientific method is a bundle of discipline-dependent methods. What all sciences share is the goal of understanding and the basic inductive attitude and point of view.

3. Discussion 2.1. Science is the most accurate method known for gaining knowledge of the world. It assumes that there is a material world and that knowledge of it can be gained, communicated to others and verified. It generates relative knowledge by methods that do not give certainty but yield bodies of theory accepted as relatively true in the context of currently available methods.

4. Discussion 2.2. Science is a human activity: the systematic questioning of nature. Its reasoning recognizes a problem, proposes hypotheses, criticizes them, seeks a theory that explains them, and, to be fully scientific, tests them empirically.

5. Derry, Prologue. Cassirer sees science as an abstract method that brings constancy and regularity to the world; Mumford sees it as a driver of technology. A colleague's definition, that scientific statements must be tested against the behaviour of the outside world, is true but impoverished, because it leaves out imagination, logic, creativity, judgment, metaphor and instrumentation. Science is neither only textbook content nor only method: "the results of science are inseparably intertwined with its thought processes." The meringue example adds that science is about real things, seeks coherent understanding, places observations in a general framework, uses pictorial models and instruments, and makes predictions that test its interpretations.

6. Derry, Chapter 1. There is no single recipe for discovery. Science proceeds by many routes: serendipity, intuition, idealized models and calculation, exploration and observation, and the hypothetico-deductive method.

7. Discussion 1.1 and Derry ch. 9 (Unit 1). Science adopts the scientific point of view and Pólya's inductive attitude, adapting belief to experience with intellectual courage, honesty and wise restraint. It is a public discourse that seeks coherence, and its results are tentative.

Comparing the summaries. The dictionary and the Prologue's colleague emphasize empirical testing; the Overview and Chapter 1 deny that there is one method but insist on a common goal and attitude; Discussion 2.1 adds that the knowledge produced is relative, not certain; Derry adds that content and process cannot be separated and that imagination and models matter. None of them conflict, because each picks out a different part of the same enterprise.

My consistent definition. Science is a public, human enterprise whose goal is a coherent understanding of the natural world. Guided by the inductive attitude, it uses a family of methods that differ by discipline (observation and measurement with instruments, imagination and models, logical and mathematical reasoning, and the testing of predictions against experience) to produce a body of knowledge that is never certain but is accepted as relatively true and remains open to criticism and revision.

Reasoning: each part of the definition comes from at least one reading (goal and attitude from the Overview; public and tentative from Discussion 2.1 and Derry ch. 9; empirical test from the dictionary and the Prologue; plural methods from Chapter 1), and nothing in it is contradicted by any of them.

U2-SG03Study guide

Robin Dunbar, an animal behaviourist and primatologist, had claimed that science is nothing other than learning. On this basis, he has argued that every creature with any capacity to learn, however limited, is engaging in a form of science. Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing whether or not this claim is consistent with the definitions of science that you have encountered in this unit.

Source Discussion 2.2; Unit 2 Overview; Derry Prologue and ch. 1

Robin Dunbar's claim that science is nothing other than learning, so that every creature able to learn does a form of science, contains a real insight, but it is not consistent with the definitions of science in this unit. Learning is necessary for science, but it is not sufficient.

Dunbar is right about the roots of science. Pólya's inductive attitude, discussed in Unit 1, is the effort to adapt our beliefs to our experience, and any animal that learns does this in a simple way. A rat that learns which lever delivers food has, in effect, formed an expectation and revised it by trial and error. Discussion 2.2 admits that apes and other primates experiment when they face a problem. Discussion 2.2 also argues that science must have grown out of some more basic human characteristic, and learning from experience is an obvious candidate. In this sense, Dunbar shows a continuity between ordinary learning and science.

However, every definition in the unit asks for more than learning. The dictionary definition in the Overview describes science as the observation, identification, description, experimental investigation and theoretical explanation of natural phenomena. A learning animal observes and remembers, but it does not describe, deliberately experiment or explain in theory. Discussion 2.2 calls science the systematic questioning of nature and says that no other species is known to do it. Derry's meringue example shows the extra features: science seeks a coherent understanding, places specific observations in a general framework, uses models and instruments, and makes predictions that test its interpretation. When Derry rejected the acidity explanation, he did so by measuring acidity, not by rewarding or punishing himself. Discussion 2.1 adds that scientific knowledge must be communicated and verified by others. A bird that learns to avoid a bitter insect keeps that knowledge private and cannot put it up for criticism, which Derry (ch. 9) treats as essential to science as a public discourse.

Dunbar's claim also fails a test of evidence that Discussion 2.2 sets for a similar argument. When a skeptic suggests that whales and dolphins may have elaborate scientific theories, the response is that there is no empirical evidence for it. Calling every act of learning science avoids that test by stretching the definition until it covers everything. As the alchemy example in Discussion 2.1 shows, the answer depends on what we take the purpose of the activity to be. If science is defined as any learning, Dunbar is trivially right, but the word loses the power to distinguish science from habit, trial and error or rumour.

The most consistent position, then, is that science is a specialized, systematic and public extension of the learning that many animals share. Learning supplies the raw adaptation of belief to experience; science adds deliberate questioning, theory, testing and criticism. Dunbar's claim describes the foundation of science, not the building.

NoteSource note: Dunbar makes this argument in The Trouble with Science, cited in the Unit 2 study questions and in Discussion 1.2. The essay assesses the claim as the study guide states it.

U2-SG04Study guide

Choose one of the examples of a scientific discovery given in Chapter 1 of What Science Is, by Gregory N. Derry, and list the ways in which this example fits with the definition of science that you developed in study Question 2, above.

Source Derry ch. 1 §5, pp. 21-25 (Jenner)

I choose Jenner's discovery of the smallpox vaccine (Derry ch. 1 §5). It fits each part of my definition from Question 2.

1. A human enterprise with the goal of understanding. Jenner set out to understand why some people who had cowpox were protected from smallpox and others were not, rather than simply accept or reject the milkmaid's legend. He was driven by the dream of a world free from smallpox, which shows science as a human activity with human motives.

2. About the natural world. His subject was real disease in real cows and people in the dairy country of Gloucestershire, where cowpox could be observed directly.

3. The inductive attitude. He showed intellectual courage by taking a folk belief seriously when local doctors dismissed it, wise restraint by refusing to accept it on anecdotes alone, and intellectual honesty by changing his hypothesis twice when the evidence required it.

4. Observation and measurement. For several years he observed every case in the dairies, interviewed former patients and kept careful notes. Derry says his careful, accurate and honest observations were always the foundation of his conclusions.

5. Imagination and models. His key ideas were imaginative reorganizations of the data: first that "cowpox" was really several distinct diseases, then, while looking at two cows at different stages, that the strength of the matter in the pustules rises and falls.

6. Testing predictions. His final hypothesis predicted that matter taken at its strongest stage would protect. In May 1796 he took matter from Sarah Nelmes and infected James Phipps, then inoculated him with smallpox in July. The boy showed no symptoms, so the prediction was confirmed.

7. Tentative, relatively true knowledge. Each version of the hypothesis was held only until evidence contradicted it. The outbreak of true cowpox followed by smallpox shattered his first hypothesis and forced a revision.

8. Public and self-correcting. He had to persuade the medical community and the public, and when careless imitators gave vaccination a bad reputation, he corrected the problems. Vaccination was eventually accepted because others could repeat it.

Reasoning: Derry presents this case as the best example of the hypothetico-deductive method, and every element of my definition (goal, attitude, observation, imagination, testing, tentative knowledge, public character) appears in it.

Learning objective drills3

U2-OBJ01Objective

Formulate a general, if incomplete, definition of science.

Source Unit 2 Overview objective 1

1. A working definition. Science is a public, human enterprise that aims at a coherent understanding of the natural world. Guided by the inductive attitude, it uses many discipline-dependent methods (observation, instruments, imagination, models, mathematics and the testing of predictions) to produce knowledge that is accepted as relatively true but is always open to revision.

2. Goal. Understanding is the common goal of all the sciences, since they share neither a subject matter nor one method (Unit 2 Overview).

3. Attitude. The inductive attitude adapts belief to experience and prefers matters of fact (Overview; Pólya in Discussion 1.1).

4. Empirical constraint. Scientific statements must ultimately be tested against the behaviour of the outside world (Derry, Prologue; the dictionary definition).

5. More than testing. Imagination, logic, creativity, judgment, metaphor and instrumentation are also part of science, and its results cannot be separated from its thought processes (Derry, Prologue).

6. Relative knowledge. Science gives not certainty but bodies of theory accepted as relatively true in the context of currently available methods (Discussion 2.1).

7. Why it is incomplete. The definition leaves open questions that later units take up, such as how to draw the line between science and pseudoscience and what exactly counts as testing. That is why the objective calls it general and incomplete.

U2-OBJ02Objective

Describe, briefly, the history of several cases of scientific discovery: Roentgen's discovery of X-rays, Kekulé's discovery of the structure of benzene, the discovery of energy bands in solids, Humboldt's biogeographical studies and Jenner's discovery of the smallpox vaccine.

Source Unit 2 Overview objective 2

1. Roentgen and x-rays (1895). While testing whether a little of the cathode rays escaped through the glass of his tube, Roentgen covered it with black cardboard. When he switched on the voltage, he noticed a faint glimmer from a phosphor screen several feet away, more than thirty times as far as cathode rays can travel in air. He then systematically studied the new rays: they passed through a thousand-page book and a thick board, were stopped by lead and platinum, were not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, and showed the bones of his hand. He published, others quickly replicated his results, and he won the first Nobel Prize in physics.

2. Kekulé and benzene (1865). Faraday had shown in 1825 that benzene is six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms, but no structure fitted Kekulé's rule that carbon makes four bonds and hydrogen one, or explained why benzene would not take up extra hydrogen. After long work, Kekulé dozed by the fire and saw a snake of atoms seize its own tail. He spent the night working out the consequences of a ring structure. The ring explained known reactions and predicted new ones, won a debate against rival structures, and was later refined by quantum theory.

3. Energy bands in solids (1928-1931). Calculations suggested electrons in a metal should collide with an ion after passing one or two, but resistance measurements showed they passed hundreds. Felix Bloch modelled electrons as quantum waves moving through a perfectly periodic lattice and found they move freely, with resistance caused by vibrations and imperfections. Rudolf Peierls varied the electron-ion forces and found ranges of forbidden energies, band gaps. Alan Wilson (1931) explained why not all solids are metals: a full band makes an insulator, a partly empty band a metal, and a full band with a small gap a semiconductor.

4. Humboldt and biogeography (1799-1804). On his expedition to South America and Mexico, Humboldt measured latitude, air pressure and the earth's magnetic field, analysed volcanic gases and brought back thirty cases of geological and botanical specimens. Climbing in the Andes, he saw vegetation change with altitude, from palms and bananas at the base through coffee and grains to shrubs and finally alpine grasses and lichens, in the same sequence seen when travelling from the tropics toward the poles. He concluded that temperature, soil, sunlight, rainfall and topography together determine the life of a region: the theory of biogeography.

5. Jenner and smallpox vaccine (1796). A milkmaid told Jenner that having cowpox protects against smallpox. Because some people who had cowpox still caught smallpox, local doctors dismissed the idea. Jenner studied cases for years and concluded that several different diseases were called cowpox, and only the true cowpox protected. When milkers with true cowpox still caught smallpox, he hypothesized that the cowpox matter protects only at its strongest stage. In 1796 he infected James Phipps with peak-stage matter from Sarah Nelmes and later exposed him to smallpox; the boy stayed healthy.

U2-OBJ03Objective

Show how each of these cases of scientific discovery exemplifies some aspect of your definition of science.

Source Unit 2 Overview objective 3

My definition: science is a public, human enterprise aiming at a coherent understanding of nature, guided by the inductive attitude, using many methods and producing relatively true, revisable knowledge.

1. Roentgen: the inductive attitude and the empirical constraint. He took an unexpected glimmer seriously instead of dismissing it as stray light, then let the evidence decide what the rays could do. His prepared mind and methodical follow-up show that luck becomes science only through systematic observation.

2. Kekulé: imagination and testing. The snake image shows the role of imagination in science, which Derry says a narrow testing-only definition leaves out. The ring was accepted only after its consequences matched known reactions, so imagination generated the hypothesis and evidence judged it. The later quantum correction shows that knowledge is relatively, not absolutely, true.

3. Band structure: models, mathematics and coherence. An idealized model of electron waves in a periodic lattice, worked out by calculation, gave a single coherent explanation of metals, insulators and semiconductors. This shows the goal of understanding, met by deduction from a model rather than by a new experiment.

4. Humboldt: observation, instruments and the general framework. Careful measurements with instruments over a huge range of places allowed him to place particular observations about plants into a general framework of biogeography. This shows that there is more than one scientific method, since his work was exploratory rather than experimental.

5. Jenner: the hypothetico-deductive method and self-correction. Observation, hypothesis, testing, revision, prediction and a deliberate experiment show the empirical, self-correcting side of science, and his struggle to convince others shows its public character.

6. Conclusion. Together, the five cases show the claim in the Overview: they share the goal of understanding and the inductive attitude, while their methods differ.

Lists and concept recall4

U2-R01Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Derry's five discovery cases (ch. 1) and the dominant element in each. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Derry's five discovery cases (ch. 1) and the dominant element in each

Derry (ch. 1) tells five discovery stories, each chosen to show one dominant element, while admitting that other factors were also at work.

1. Roentgen's x-rays: serendipity and methodical work. A lucky, unexpected glimmer was noticed by a well-prepared mind and followed by painstaking study of the new rays.

2. Kekulé's benzene ring: detailed background and a dreamlike vision. After long immersion in the problem, the answer came in a flash of visual intuition (a snake seizing its tail), which was then tested against known reactions.

3. Band structure in solids: idealized models and mathematical calculations. Bloch, Peierls and Wilson calculated the consequences of electron waves in a periodic lattice, and band gaps emerged unexpectedly from the mathematics.

4. Humboldt's biogeography: exploration and observation. Extensive field measurements across Latin America revealed that vegetation changes with altitude much as it does with latitude.

5. Jenner's smallpox vaccine: the hypothetico-deductive method. Observation, hypothesis, testing, revision and a designed experiment led to vaccination.

6. Significance. The cases support Derry's opening claim, backed by Polanyi's epigraph, that there is no single recipe for discovery. Scientific reasoning takes many routes, so a definition of science cannot be a list of fixed steps.

U2-R02Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: The hypothetico-deductive method. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source The hypothetico-deductive method (Derry, p. 24)

1. Definition. In the hypothetico-deductive method, we make observations, organize them into a hypothesis, test the hypothesis against further observations and modify it as needed, then make predictions from the modified hypothesis and design experiments to test them (Derry, p. 24).

2. The logic. The hypothesis is the "hypothetico" part; deducing what should happen if it is true is the "deductive" part. A failed prediction counts against the hypothesis, and a successful one supports it without proving it.

3. Example: Jenner. Observations of cowpox cases led to the hypothesis that only true cowpox protects; a new outbreak contradicted it; the revised hypothesis said only peak-stage matter protects; it predicted that peak matter would protect Phipps; the 1796 experiment confirmed it.

4. Significance. Derry calls it highly successful and notes that elementary textbooks often present it as "the scientific method". Its strength is that it exposes ideas to tests that could fail.

5. Limits. It is only one route to discovery. Roentgen's luck, Kekulé's vision, the band calculations and Humboldt's exploration show that hypotheses can come from many sources, and the method itself does not say where good hypotheses come from.

U2-R03Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Themes of the meringue example. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Themes of the meringue example (Derry Prologue, pp. 4-6)

Derry's Prologue uses the copper-bowl meringue to show several themes of science (pp. 5-6).

1. Science is about real things that happen in the world: egg whites beaten in copper bowls really are creamier and harder to overbeat.

2. Science tries to provide a coherent understanding: the copper effect is explained by the same protein chemistry that explains why foam forms at all.

3. Specific observations are placed in a more general framework: the bowl effect is understood through the general behaviour of proteins unfolding and bonding.

4. Interpretations are often based on pictorial models: protein chains are pictured as coiled chains that unfold and form a network around air bubbles.

5. Instruments and measurements augment observation: an acidity measurement ruled out the first guess, and light-absorption measurements detected conalbumen-copper complexes.

6. A coherent picture leads to predictions that test it: if copper complexes are present, the meringue should absorb certain colours, and it does; the same fact also explains the yellow colour.

Significance: the example shows that even an everyday question is answered by the same reasoning that drives large discoveries, and that a first plausible guess can be wrong.

U2-R04Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: The four dichotomies behind this course's view of science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source The four dichotomies behind this course's view of science (Discussion 2.1)

Discussion 2.1 says the course's view of science depends on distinctions that it lists as four items. Three are explicit pairs, and the fourth combines them into a view of science.

1. Absolute versus relative knowledge. Absolute knowledge would be complete and certain; relative knowledge is knowledge held relative to the evidence and methods currently available.

2. Absolute (certain) versus relative truth. A statement can be claimed as true without qualification, or as true within the context of current methods, so that it may later be revised.

3. Coherence versus correspondence as criteria of truth. Coherence asks whether a claim fits consistently with the rest of what we accept; correspondence asks whether it matches the facts of the world.

4. Certainty versus methods that yield relatively true theory. The course views science as an enterprise that generates relative knowledge by methods that do not give certainty but do yield bodies of theory that can be accepted as relatively true in the context of currently available methods.

5. Example. Kekulé's ring with alternating double bonds was accepted because it was coherent with bonding rules and corresponded with the known reactions of benzene, yet quantum theory later showed all six bonds are identical. It was relatively true, not absolutely true.

6. Significance. The dichotomies let the course claim that science is possible and the most accurate method known without claiming certainty, so the course can proceed "without chasing the wild goose of perfection too far."

Key term questions7

U2-T01Term

Define or distinguish Serendipity. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Serendipity is discovering something you are not looking for (Derry ch. 1 §1).

2. Prepared mind. It is not mere luck. Pasteur's maxim is that "chance favors only the prepared mind": the discoverer must have the knowledge to recognize what the accident means.

3. Role in this unit. It is the dominant element of Roentgen's discovery. While testing his cardboard cover, he noticed a faint glimmer from a distant phosphor and, knowing how far cathode rays could travel, realized it meant a new kind of ray.

4. Follow-up. The discovery became science only through his painstaking study of the rays' properties, publication and replication by others.

5. Another example. Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mould on a contaminated culture plate had killed the bacteria around it, which led to penicillin.

6. Distinction. Serendipity differs from Kekulé's flash of intuition, which answered a problem he was actively trying to solve; serendipity answers a question no one had yet asked.

U2-T02Term

Define or distinguish Hypothetico-deductive method. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. A pathway to discovery in which we make observations, organize them into a hypothesis, test the hypothesis against further observations and modify it, then deduce predictions and design experiments to test them (Derry, p. 24).

2. Role in this unit. It is the dominant element in Derry's account of Jenner, and it is the route most often taught as "the scientific method".

3. Example. Jenner's hypothesis that peak-stage cowpox matter protects predicted that James Phipps, infected with such matter, would resist smallpox; the 1796 experiment confirmed it.

4. Logic. A failed prediction refutes or forces revision of the hypothesis; a successful one supports it without making it certain.

5. Distinction. It is one of several routes. Band gaps emerged from calculation and Humboldt's theory from exploration, so the method is not a compulsory recipe.

U2-T03Term

Define or distinguish Band gap. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. A band gap is a range of energies in a solid in which no electron states can exist, lying between bands of allowed energies (Derry ch. 1 §3).

2. Discovery. Rudolf Peierls found band gaps unexpectedly while calculating with Bloch's model of electron waves in a periodic lattice. No one had predicted them.

3. Role in this unit. Alan Wilson (1931) used the gap to explain why some solids conduct. To carry a current, an electron must gain energy and move to an empty state; in a full band the next empty states lie above the gap, so the solid is an insulator. A partly empty band makes a metal.

4. Example. Silicon is a semiconductor: its band is full but its gap is small (about 1.1 eV), so heat lifts some electrons across it, and it conducts better as the temperature rises, unlike a metal. Quartz has a large gap and is an insulator.

5. Significance. The case shows idealized models and mathematics as a route to discovery, and the concept became the basis of the microelectronics revolution.

U2-T04Term

Define or distinguish Biogeography. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Biogeography is the study of how the physical conditions of an area (temperature, soil, sunlight, rainfall and topography) together determine the plant and animal life found there (Derry ch. 1 §4).

2. Origin. Alexander von Humboldt developed it from his 1799-1804 expedition to Latin America.

3. Key observation. In the Andes, vegetation changed with altitude, from palms and bananas to coffee and grains, then shrubs, then alpine grasses and lichens, in the same order seen when moving from the tropics toward the poles.

4. Role in this unit. It shows exploration and observation as a route to discovery: a theory that gave meaning to countless descriptions and classifications.

5. Example. Southern Saskatchewan's dry, hot summers support grassland, while the cooler, wetter north supports boreal forest; the same latitude effect appears on a mountain as a tree line.

U2-T05Term

Define or distinguish Vaccination. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Vaccination is deliberately infecting a person with material from a mild, related disease (in Jenner's case cowpox) to give immunity against a dangerous one. The word comes from the Latin for cow (Derry ch. 1 §5).

2. Distinction from inoculation. The older practice of inoculation used matter from real smallpox pustules. It could cause severe cases or death and could spread smallpox to others; vaccination avoided both risks.

3. Role in this unit. It is the result of Derry's example of the hypothetico-deductive method: observation, hypothesis, revision and a designed test.

4. Example. In 1796 Jenner vaccinated James Phipps with matter from Sarah Nelmes's cowpox and later exposed him to smallpox; the boy showed no symptoms.

5. Significance. The method spread despite early resistance and botched copies, and it eventually led to the global eradication of smallpox, declared by the World Health Organization in 1980.

U2-T06Term

Define or distinguish Relative knowledge / relative truth. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Absolute knowledge and truth. Absolute knowledge would be complete and certain, and an absolute truth would hold without qualification for all time (Discussion 2.1).

2. Relative knowledge and truth. Relative knowledge is knowledge held relative to the evidence and methods available. A relative truth is a claim accepted as true in the context of currently available methods for exploring the world, and it may be revised when better methods appear.

3. Role in this unit. The course views science as generating relative knowledge by methods that do not provide certainty but do yield theories that can be accepted as relatively true. This answers the question "Is science possible?" without requiring certainty.

4. Example. Kekulé's ring with alternating single and double bonds explained benzene's reactions and was accepted, but quantum theory later showed that all six bonds are identical. The earlier structure was relatively true.

5. Distinction. Relative truth is not "anything goes": a relatively true theory is the best-supported account available, not just one opinion among equals.

U2-T07Term

Define or distinguish Coherence and correspondence. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Coherence. A claim is judged true if it fits consistently with the rest of an accepted body of knowledge or theory (Discussion 2.1).

2. Correspondence. A claim is judged true if it matches, or corresponds to, the facts of the world, as checked by observation and experiment.

3. Role in this unit. They are the two criteria of truth the course uses. Science needs both: Discussion 3.2 asks whether a conjecture is consistent with accepted theory (coherence) and whether it corresponds to the facts (correspondence).

4. Example. The copper-bowl explanation coheres with known protein chemistry, since conalbumen binds metal ions and copper stabilizes its coil, and it corresponds with measurement, since light absorption shows conalbumen-copper complexes in the meringue.

5. Distinction. Coherence alone could accept a beautiful but false system, and correspondence alone gives isolated facts without understanding. The acidity hypothesis was coherent with the cream of tartar case but failed correspondence when acidity was measured.

Applied cases and reasoning12

U2-A01Applied5 marks

State a provisional definition of science that includes its goal, attitude, empirical constraints and public character. Explain why a list of scientific subjects is insufficient.

Source Unit 2 Overview and Derry Prologue

1. Provisional definition. Science is a public, human enterprise whose goal is a coherent understanding of the natural world; guided by the inductive attitude, it tests its ideas against observation and produces knowledge that is relatively true and open to revision.

2. Goal and attitude. Understanding, together with the inductive attitude of adapting belief to experience, is the one thing all sciences share (Unit 2 Overview).

3. Empirical constraints and public character. Its statements must be checked against the behaviour of the outside world (Derry, Prologue) and stated in terms others can examine, repeat and criticize, as Roentgen's results were quickly replicated.

4. Why a list of subjects fails. The Overview notes that the sciences range from physics to library science, and that the unifying principle "cannot be found in their subject matter." A list says what is studied, not how or why.

5. Reasoning. The same subject can be studied unscientifically: astrology and astronomy both study the stars, and alchemists studied metals for 2000 years (Discussion 2.1). A list also cannot handle new fields, such as band theory, which arose when semiconductors were a mere curiosity. Only a definition in terms of goal, attitude and method can sort cases.

U2-A02Applied10 marks

Reconstruct the copper-bowl meringue investigation. Identify the observation, an initial explanation, a test that rejected it, and the alternative explanation supported by further evidence.

Source Derry Prologue

Derry's Prologue reconstructs the investigation in steps (pp. 4-6).

1. Observation. A cooking tradition dating back at least to the eighteenth century says egg whites whipped in a copper bowl make a creamier meringue that is less prone to overbeating, and slightly yellow.

2. Question. How and why does the copper bowl have this effect?

3. Background: why foam forms. Egg white is water plus proteins (ovalbumen, conalbumen and others) whose long chains are folded compactly. Whipping, mainly through contact with the air in the bubbles, unfolds the chains, which bond to each other into a network that holds water and reinforces the bubble walls.

4. Background: overbeating. If beaten too long, the network becomes too tightly bonded, holds too little water, and the meringue curdles into lumps in a watery liquid.

5. Related fact. Cream of tartar prevents this. It is slightly acidic, and its extra hydrogen ions interfere with the cross-chain bonding.

6. Initial explanation. By analogy with cream of tartar, one might guess that copper makes the egg white more acidic.

7. Test that rejected it. A simple measurement of acidity shows no such increase, so the idea is wrong (and it would have been hard to explain anyway).

8. Alternative explanation. Conalbumen binds metal ions. Copper ions scraped from the bowl enter the conalbumen and stabilize its coiled structure so it does not unfold and cannot join the network too strongly. Standard laboratory chemistry had shown this decades earlier.

9. Further evidence. Conalbumen-copper complexes absorb specific colours of light. Light-absorption experiments on meringues beaten in copper bowls do reveal stable conalbumen-copper complexes.

10. Bonus confirmation. The same light absorption gives the complex a yellow colour, explaining the yellowish meringue, an observation the explanation was not designed for.

Reasoning: the case shows a hypothesis generated by analogy, rejected by measurement, and replaced by one that fits known chemistry and passes a new test.

U2-A03Applied5 marks

Why was noticing an unexpected glow only the beginning of Roentgen's discovery of X-rays? Explain the roles of preparation and systematic follow-up.

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. The glow alone meant nothing. Roentgen first thought the glimmer was reflected stray light. A less prepared observer might have stopped there, and the unexpected glow would have been lost.

2. Preparation let him see its importance. He knew from Lenard's work that cathode rays travel only about an inch in air, so a glow from a phosphor more than thirty times that distance away could not be cathode rays. Pasteur's maxim applies: "chance favors only the prepared mind."

3. His experimental skill set the stage. The accident happened because he had designed a careful test, covering the tube with black cardboard to look for faint escaping rays.

4. Systematic follow-up made it a discovery. He tested the new rays' penetration (through a thousand-page book, a thick board and metal plates, but blocked by lead and platinum), showed they were not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, and recorded the bones of his hand on photographic film.

5. Publication and replication. Only after this methodical work did he publish, and others quickly replicated the results. Derry calls the discovery "a marvelous combination of luck and skill."

U2-A04Applied5 marks

Kekule's image of a snake suggested a structure for benzene. Explain why the image could generate a hypothesis but could not establish that hypothesis by itself.

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. What the image did. Kekulé's vision of a snake seizing its tail suggested that benzene's chain of six carbon atoms closes into a ring, which satisfies four bonds per carbon and one per hydrogen and leaves no room for extra hydrogen.

2. Why it could generate a hypothesis. He had spent years immersed in organic chemistry and benzene's reactions, and his thinking was strongly visual. The image organized that knowledge into a new possibility.

3. Why it could not establish it. A dream is private and says nothing about whether molecules actually behave that way. Rival structures were also proposed, and any image can suggest a false idea as easily as a true one.

4. What established it. Kekulé spent the night "working out the consequences of the hypothesis." Derry says the question then became purely empirical: does the ring explain all known reactions and predict new ones accurately? It did, and it won a debate of several years against rivals.

5. Even then it was tentative. Problems remained (energies and the arbitrary placing of double bonds) until quantum theory showed all six bonds are identical. Imagination proposes; evidence and reasoning decide.

U2-A05Applied5 marks

Explain how idealization made the energy-band problem tractable in Derry's account. What would be required to judge whether the idealized model was useful?

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. The problem. Electrons moving among massive positive ions should collide almost at once, yet resistance measurements showed they passed hundreds of ions. A real metal, with its vibrating and imperfect ions, was too complex to calculate.

2. The idealization. Bloch treated the electrons as quantum-mechanical waves and the ions as a perfectly periodic, fixed lattice, leaving out vibrations, impurities and imperfections. Peierls kept this model and simply varied the strength of the electron-ion forces.

3. Why it made the problem tractable. The simplified model could be solved mathematically. It showed that waves move freely through a perfect lattice, and the left-out features then explained resistance (vibrations and imperfections). The calculation also revealed allowed bands and forbidden gaps.

4. Judging its usefulness: agreement with experiment. Bloch's results agreed well with measured resistance, and Wilson's interpretation explained why metals conduct and insulators do not.

5. Judging its usefulness: new explanations and predictions. A useful model should also explain facts it was not built for. Band theory explained why semiconductors conduct better at higher temperatures, and decades later it guided the microelectronics revolution.

U2-A06Applied10 marks

Compare Humboldt's field observations with Wilson's theoretical work. Identify what makes both scientific despite their different procedures.

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. Humboldt's procedure: exploration and field observation. From 1799 to 1804 he travelled through South America and Mexico, measuring latitude, air pressure and the earth's magnetic field, analysing volcanic gases and bringing back thirty cases of geological and botanical specimens.

2. His result was inductive. From the altitude zones of the Andes and their likeness to latitude zones, he generalized a theory of biogeography: temperature, soil, sunlight, rainfall and topography together determine life in a region.

3. Wilson's procedure: theory and interpretation. In 1931 he worked at a desk with the band calculations of Bloch and Peierls, asking why, if electrons move easily through any lattice, every solid is not a metal.

4. His result was deductive. He reasoned that in a full band an electron cannot gain energy without entering the gap, so full bands mean insulators, partly empty bands mean metals, and full bands with small gaps mean semiconductors.

5. The difference. Humboldt started from masses of new observations and found the pattern; Wilson started from a model and existing facts and found the right interpretation. One used instruments in the field, the other mathematics.

6. Shared goal: understanding. Both sought a coherent explanation rather than more facts. Humboldt's theory "gave meaning and context" to his classifications; Wilson's gave a unified account of metals, insulators and semiconductors. The Overview says this goal is common to all sciences.

7. Shared empirical constraint. Both answered to the natural world: Humboldt's theory rests on precise measurements, and Wilson's explained measured facts, including the puzzling temperature behaviour of semiconductors.

8. Shared general framework. Each placed specific observations into a general framework, a theme of the meringue example.

9. Shared public, tentative character. Both were published and built on by others, and both were open to revision: details of Humboldt's Cosmos are now obsolete, and semiconductor behaviour was still debated in 1931.

10. Conclusion. What makes both scientific is not one procedure but the shared goal of understanding, the inductive attitude and accountability to evidence. As the Overview puts it, "the" scientific method is a bundle of discipline-dependent methods.

U2-A07Applied5 marks

In Jenner's investigation, some apparent counterexamples challenged the initial cowpox hypothesis. Explain how a revised hypothesis could account for them and produce a further test.

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. The initial hypothesis and its counterexamples. The legend said cowpox protects against smallpox, but some people who had cowpox still caught smallpox, so local doctors dismissed it.

2. First revision. Jenner's records showed different symptoms in different cases, in both people and cows. He concluded that "cowpox" was several distinct diseases and only the true cowpox protects. This explained the first counterexamples.

3. A new counterexample. Milkers who had true cowpox in a dairy outbreak caught smallpox the following year.

4. Second revision. Watching two cows at different stages, he hypothesized that the matter in the pustules rises and falls in strength, and protects only at its strongest. The puzzling milkers had caught cowpox in its earliest stages, so the revision fits the facts.

5. The further test. The revision is not just an excuse, because it makes a new prediction: matter taken at its peak should protect. In May 1796 Jenner infected James Phipps with peak-stage matter from Sarah Nelmes, then exposed him to smallpox in July. The boy showed no symptoms, confirming the prediction.

U2-A08Applied5 marks

Apply the hypothetico-deductive method to a hypothetical observation that seedlings near a window grow faster. Specify a hypothesis, a prediction, a comparison and a possible result that would require revision.

Source Derry Chapter 1

1. Hypothesis. The seedlings by the window grow faster because they receive more light for photosynthesis.

2. Prediction. If light is the cause, then giving seedlings more light should make them grow faster even away from the window, and shading window seedlings should slow them down.

3. Comparison. Plant identical seedlings of one species in the same soil and pots, with the same water. Put both groups in the same spot near the window, and shade one group so it gets less light. Then measure height or dry mass after two weeks. Using many seedlings per group and assigning them at random reduces chance effects.

4. Result that supports it. The unshaded group grows clearly faster, so the hypothesis survives the test but is not proved.

5. Result requiring revision. If the two groups grow at the same rate, light is not the explanation. Something else about the window, such as warmth from the sun or air movement, could be the cause. A new hypothesis (for example, temperature) would then lead to a new prediction and a new comparison, as in Jenner's revisions.

U2-A09Applied10 marks

Assess the claim that every instance of learning by an animal is science. State what depends on the definition of science and what evidence would be relevant.

Source Discussion 2.2 and Unit 2 Study Question 3

1. The claim. Robin Dunbar argues that science is nothing other than learning, so any creature that can learn does a form of science (Unit 2 Study Question 3).

2. What depends on the definition. Whether the claim is true depends on what we take science to be, just as Discussion 2.1 shows that whether alchemy is possible depends on its assumed purpose. If science means any adaptation of behaviour to experience, the claim is trivially true. If science has stricter conditions, it is false.

3. The unit's definitions are stricter. The dictionary definition requires observation, description, experimental investigation and theoretical explanation; Discussion 2.2 speaks of systematic questioning of nature; Derry asks for coherent understanding, general frameworks, models, instruments and tested predictions.

4. Public character. Scientific knowledge must be communicated and checked by others (Discussion 2.1; Derry ch. 9). A pigeon that learns which button gives food cannot submit its conclusion for criticism.

5. What is right in the claim. Learning is the root of the inductive attitude, adapting belief to experience (Pólya). Apes and other primates experiment when facing a problem (Discussion 2.2), and Discussion 2.2 holds that science grew out of more basic human traits.

6. Relevant evidence: deliberate testing. We would need evidence that animals do more than trial and error, for example that they vary one condition while holding others constant to choose between explanations.

7. Relevant evidence: general explanation. We would need evidence that animals form general models of why things happen and use them to predict new cases, not just repeat what was rewarded.

8. Relevant evidence: communication and cumulation. We would need evidence that animals share, criticize and build on one another's findings over generations, as Roentgen's results were replicated and built on.

9. Burden of evidence. Discussion 2.2 answers the suggestion that dolphins have science by noting that there is no empirical evidence for it. The same standard applies here: until such evidence appears, the stronger claim is unsupported.

10. Assessment. Under the definitions in this unit, learning is necessary but not sufficient for science. The claim is best restated as: science is a systematic, public extension of the learning many animals share.

U2-A10Applied5 marks

Explain why the existence of people who call themselves alchemists does not by itself establish that the purpose they claim is achievable. Apply the same distinction to defining science.

Source Discussion 2.1

1. Existence is not achievement. For over 2000 years many intelligent, educated people, even Isaac Newton, called themselves alchemists (Discussion 2.1). That shows people did alchemy, not that alchemy could reach its goal.

2. It depends on the purpose. If the goal was to turn lead into gold by supernatural means, alchemy seems impossible and its practitioners deluded. If the goal was inner transformation (Jung) or spiritual illumination (Burkhardt), alchemy may have been possible.

3. Applying it to science. That people called scientists do things called science does not by itself prove that science can achieve its goal. Our answer depends on what we take that goal to be.

4. The goal matters. If science aims at absolute, certain knowledge, it may be impossible. If it aims at relative knowledge, theories accepted as relatively true by current methods, it is clearly possible and has been very successful.

5. Assumptions matter too. Science also assumes there is a material world and that knowledge of it can be gained, communicated and verified. A good definition of science must therefore state its purpose and assumptions, not just point to the people who practise it.

U2-A11Applied10 marks

Compare scientific inquiry with interpretation in the humanities. Identify shared reasoning activities and explain a relevant difference in questions or standards of evidence.

Source Derry Prologue and Unit 2 Study Question 1

1. Shared activity: asking questions. Both begin with a good question set in context, then propose answers and criticize them (Discussion 3.2).

2. Shared activity: imagination and judgment. Derry says imagination, creativity, judgment and metaphor are part of science (Prologue). The humanities use them to interpret texts, art and history.

3. Shared activity: building models. Derry, on a jury, asked what model of the accident was consistent with the photographs. A historian reconstructs an event from documents in the same way.

4. Shared activity: argument from evidence. Both must support conclusions with evidence and logical reasoning, not authority.

5. Shared activity: public criticism. Both publish so that others can examine and challenge the work, and both produce relatively true, revisable conclusions (Discussion 2.1).

6. Difference in questions. Science asks about natural phenomena and general causes: why does a copper bowl stop overbeating? The humanities ask about human meaning and value: what does a poem mean, and why did people act as they did?

7. Difference in evidence. Science can often measure, repeat and control. An acidity test settled one meringue hypothesis. Humanistic evidence is usually a unique text or event that cannot be rerun.

8. Difference in criteria. Science leans on correspondence, tested by prediction; the humanities lean more on coherence, meaning how well an interpretation fits the whole work and its context.

9. Difference in outcome. Science works toward one accepted theory, as with Kekulé's ring, while several rival interpretations of a novel can stand together.

10. Conclusion. The difference is one of degree. Discussion 1.2 notes that modern science arose alongside great periods of art and literature, and Dunbar argues scientists are as culturally literate as humanists. Both are disciplined searches for understanding with different objects and tests.

U2-A12Applied10 marks

A student presents observation, hypothesis, experiment and conclusion as a compulsory sequence followed by every scientist. Use two Chapter 1 cases to evaluate this description.

Source Derry Chapter 1 and Unit 2 Overview

1. The claim. The student says every scientist follows a compulsory sequence: observation, hypothesis, experiment, conclusion.

2. What is right about it. Derry calls this pattern the hypothetico-deductive method, highly successful and often taught as "the scientific method". Jenner's work broadly follows it.

3. Jenner shows it is not a straight line. He observed, hypothesized, was refuted by the true-cowpox outbreak, revised, observed for several more years, revised again and only then experimented. The steps loop.

4. Roentgen reverses the order. He began with a hypothesis (some cathode rays escape the glass) and an experiment to test it. The key observation, the distant glimmer, came by accident in the middle of the experiment, and it answered a question he had not asked.

5. What followed Roentgen's observation. He did not form one hypothesis and run one experiment; he explored the rays' properties in many directions before concluding.

6. Kekulé's hypothesis came from a vision. The ring was not drawn from a fresh observation but from years of immersion and a dreamlike image. The sequence says nothing about where hypotheses come from.

7. Kekulé's test was not a new experiment. He first deduced the consequences of the ring and checked them against known reactions and syntheses.

8. Further cases. Band gaps emerged unexpectedly from calculations on an idealized model, with no experiment first, and Humboldt's biogeography came from exploration rather than a controlled experiment.

9. Support from the readings. Derry says no simple methodology is available in a recipe book, and Polanyi's epigraph says natural laws are not found by applying an explicit operation. The Unit 2 Overview calls "the" scientific method a bundle of discipline-dependent methods.

10. Evaluation. The sequence is a useful simplified summary of how claims are checked, but not a compulsory recipe for how discoveries are made. What all the cases share is the goal of understanding and accountability to evidence, not a fixed order of steps.

Multiple choice practice15

U2-MC01Multiple choice2 marks

Which dominant element does Derry use Roentgen's discovery of x-rays to illustrate?

  1. A. The hypothetico-deductive method
  2. B. Serendipity combined with methodical work
  3. C. Idealized mathematical models
  4. D. Exploration and observation

B. Serendipity combined with methodical work. A lucky glimmer was noticed by a well-prepared mind and followed by systematic study of the rays (Derry ch. 1 §1).

U2-MC02Multiple choice2 marks

Kekulé's ring structure of benzene was suggested by:

  1. A. a calculation using quantum mechanics
  2. B. a dreamlike vision of a snake seizing its own tail
  3. C. an X-ray photograph
  4. D. Faraday's determination of its composition

B. A dreamlike vision of a snake seizing its own tail. It came after long immersion in the problem, and he then tested the ring against known reactions. Faraday only found benzene's composition, and quantum theory came decades later.

U2-MC03Multiple choice2 marks

In the energy-band explanation in Chapter 1, why does a large gap above a filled occupied band impede conduction?

  1. A. Electrons cannot exist in a solid.
  2. B. All solids have identical conductivity.
  3. C. Electrons lack nearby available energy states into which to move.
  4. D. The gap makes the solid a superconductor.

C. Electrons lack nearby available energy states into which to move. To carry a current, electrons must gain a little energy; in a full band the next empty states lie above the gap, so small energy inputs cannot move them (Wilson).

U2-MC04Multiple choice2 marks

Humboldt's key observation in the Andes was that:

  1. A. vegetation changes with altitude much as it changes with latitude
  2. B. volcanoes produce oxygen
  3. C. all mountains have the same plants
  4. D. the earth's magnetic field is constant

A. Vegetation changes with altitude much as it changes with latitude. This led him to the theory of biogeography (Derry ch. 1 §4).

U2-MC05Multiple choice2 marks

Jenner's final hypothesis was that cowpox protects against smallpox only when:

  1. A. the patient is a child
  2. B. the cowpox matter is taken at the disease's strongest stage
  3. C. it is mixed with smallpox matter
  4. D. it comes from a milkmaid's left hand

B. The cowpox matter is taken at the disease's strongest stage. This explained why milkers who caught true cowpox in its earliest stages still got smallpox.

U2-MC06Multiple choice2 marks

Derry presents Jenner's work mainly as an example of:

  1. A. serendipity
  2. B. the hypothetico-deductive method
  3. C. a flash of intuition
  4. D. pattern recognition

B. The hypothetico-deductive method. Derry says the case mainly illustrates observe, hypothesize, test and modify, predict, and experiment, although luck and inspiration also played a part.

U2-MC07Multiple choice2 marks

According to the Unit 2 Overview, what do all the sciences share?

  1. A. The same subject matter
  2. B. One identical scientific method
  3. C. The goal of understanding and the inductive attitude and point of view
  4. D. The use of laboratories

C. The goal of understanding and the inductive attitude and point of view. The Overview says subject matter differs and "the" scientific method is really a bundle of discipline-dependent methods.

U2-MC08Multiple choice2 marks

Discussion 2.1 uses alchemy to show that whether an activity is "possible" depends on:

  1. A. the laws of chemistry only
  2. B. our point of view and what we take its purpose to be
  3. C. whether Newton practised it
  4. D. government approval

B. Our point of view and what we take its purpose to be. Turning lead into gold, psychological growth (Jung) and spiritual illumination (Burkhardt) are different purposes with different answers.

U2-MC09Multiple choice2 marks

In Discussion 2.2, what is missing from the argument that science is uniquely human, which places it in the "borderlands of science"?

  1. A. A clear question
  2. B. Hypotheses
  3. C. Empirical testing
  4. D. Criticism by a skeptic

C. Empirical testing. The argument has a question, hypotheses and skeptical criticism, but it is hard to imagine how the hypothesis could be tested, so it sits in the borderlands of science.

U2-MC10Multiple choice2 marks

Which statement best reflects Derry's Prologue?

  1. A. Science is only the facts in textbooks.
  2. B. Science is only its methods of investigation.
  3. C. The results of science are inseparably intertwined with its thought processes.
  4. D. Science needs no imagination.

C. The results of science are inseparably intertwined with its thought processes. Derry says content without method is lifeless and method without content is meaningless; he also stresses imagination, ruling out D.

U2-MC11Multiple choice2 marks

"Chance favors only the prepared mind" is a maxim of:

  1. A. Roentgen
  2. B. Pasteur
  3. C. Kekulé
  4. D. Humboldt

B. Pasteur. Derry quotes Pasteur's maxim to explain why Roentgen, with his well-prepared mind, recognized the unexpected glimmer.

U2-MC12Multiple choice2 marks

The meringue example in Derry's Prologue shows that copper bowls prevent overbeating because:

  1. A. copper makes egg whites more acidic
  2. B. copper ions bind to conalbumen and stabilize its coiled structure
  3. C. copper keeps the bowl cold
  4. D. copper adds air bubbles

B. Copper ions bind to conalbumen and stabilize its coiled structure. An acidity measurement ruled out A, and light absorption by conalbumen-copper complexes confirmed B (and explains the yellow colour).

U2-MC13Multiple choice2 marks

An imaginative picture suggests a molecular structure. What is needed before accepting it scientifically?

  1. A. A vivid image alone
  2. B. An appeal to the dreamer's authority
  3. C. Consequences that can be checked against evidence
  4. D. A guarantee that no rival can be imagined

C. Consequences that can be checked against evidence. An image can generate an idea, as Kekulé's did, but only deduced consequences tested against reactions can evaluate it.

U2-MC14Multiple choice2 marks

Which pair most clearly illustrates different routes within science?

  1. A. A published claim and an unpublished rumor
  2. B. Humboldt's field exploration and Wilson's theoretical modelling
  3. C. A repeated ritual and an unfalsifiable prophecy
  4. D. A definition and a slogan

B. Humboldt's field exploration and Wilson's theoretical modelling. Both are science yet use very different methods while sharing the goal of understanding and accountability to evidence; the other pairs include non-science.

U2-MC15Multiple choice2 marks

A proposed explanation fits existing observations. What is the most useful next step in hypothetico-deductive inquiry?

  1. A. Identify a further testable consequence
  2. B. Declare it permanently proved
  3. C. Replace testing with a testimonial
  4. D. Reject all previously accepted knowledge

A. Identify a further testable consequence. A new prediction gives an independent check, as Jenner's peak-stage hypothesis led to the Phipps experiment; fitting existing data never proves a hypothesis permanently.

People and attributions8

U2-P01Person

Identify Ernst Cassirer and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry Prologue, p. 3

1. Who. Ernst Cassirer is one of the "two noted philosophers" whose opening quotations begin Derry's Prologue, "What Is Science?" The quotation comes from his An Essay on Man (Derry Prologue).

2. Quotation. "Science is the last step in man's mental development and it may be regarded as the highest and most characteristic attainment of human culture" (Derry, p. 3).

3. Meaning. Derry reads Cassirer as "discussing science as an abstract method to bring constancy and regularity to the world," in contrast with Lewis Mumford, who treats science as a driver of technology (Derry, p. 3).

4. Significance. "Both of these viewpoints contain an element of truth; neither is comprehensive." The two quotations show that people who use the word science may not mean the same thing, so science cannot be defined by one slogan: imagination, logic, creativity, judgment, metaphor and instrumentation are all part of what science is.

U2-P02Person

Identify Lewis Mumford and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry Prologue, p. 3

1. Who. Lewis Mumford is the second of the "two noted philosophers" quoted at the start of Derry's Prologue. The quotation comes from his The Pentagon of Power (Derry Prologue).

2. Quotation. "The belief that science developed solely out of a pursuit of knowledge for its own sake is at best only a half truth, and at worst, mere self-flattery or self-deception on the part of the scientists" (Derry, p. 3).

3. Meaning. Science did not develop solely from a pursuit of knowledge for its own sake. Derry says Mumford "is considering science as a driver of technology, a method to bring about practical changes in life," whereas Cassirer sees an abstract method that brings constancy and regularity to the world (Derry, p. 3).

4. Significance. Each view holds part of the truth and neither is comprehensive. Science seeks understanding, but it also grows out of, and feeds, practical and technological needs, so an adequate account of what science is has to include both its methods and its uses.

U2-P03Person

Identify J. B. S. Haldane (1892-1964) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 2.1 epigraph

1. Who. J. B. S. Haldane (1892-1964) was a British biologist. His words, from Possible Worlds and Other Essays, are the epigraph of Discussion 2.1, "Is Science Possible?"

2. Quotation. "Now, my suspicion is that the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we can suppose. ... I suspect that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamed of in any philosophy" (Discussion 2.1).

3. Meaning. Nature may exceed not only our present theories but our capacity to imagine it, so no philosophy or theory can claim to have captured all of it.

4. Significance. Discussion 2.1 asks whether science is possible. Science is the most accurate method known for gaining knowledge of the world, but it assumes answers to questions it does not justify (Is there a material world? What is knowledge?). It yields relative knowledge, not certainty: bodies of theory accepted as relatively true for the methods now available. Haldane's remark is a reason to hold scientific theories open to revision.

U2-P04Person

Identify Carl Jung (1875-1961) and Titus Burkhardt and the ideas or contributions the assigned readings attribute to them. Explain their significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 2.1

1. Who. Discussion 2.1 cites the psychologist Carl Jung (1875-1961), author of Psychology and Alchemy, and the historian Titus Burkhardt, author of Alchemy: Science of the Cosmos, Science of the Soul.

2. Jung. Jung suggested that alchemy's goal was a psychological transformation in the practitioner, "changing the dross of the lower self into the gold of personal growth and individuation" (Discussion 2.1).

3. Burkhardt. Burkhardt claimed that the actual goal of alchemy "was neither material wealth nor psychological integration, but spiritual illumination" (Discussion 2.1).

4. Significance. If alchemy's goal was to change lead into gold by supernatural means, it seems impossible and its practitioners deluded; on Jung's or Burkhardt's reading it may be possible after all. Whether it is possible "depends on our point of view, and what we take as its purpose." In the same way, our view of whether science is possible depends on what we take its goals to be and on whether we accept its basic metaphysical assumptions.

U2-P05Person

Identify Maxine Singer and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 2.2 epigraph

1. Who. Maxine Singer was an American molecular biologist. Her words are the epigraph of Discussion 2.2, "Is Science Uniquely Human?" (quoted in Shirley Jones's collection The Mind of God and Other Musings).

2. Quotation. "Science is not an inhuman or superhuman activity. It's something that humans invented, and it speaks to one of our great needs," the need "to understand the world around us" (Discussion 2.2).

3. Meaning. Science is something humans invented to meet our need to understand the world. No other known species engages in the systematic questioning of nature, so the discussion looks for the roots of science "in that which is fundamentally human": since science was not practised 10,000 years ago and is now, it must have evolved out of some more basic human characteristic.

4. Significance. The discussion's own argument is an example of scientific thinking: a question is recognized, hypotheses are proposed, a skeptic criticizes them, and a theory is needed to justify them. It lacks only empirical testing, which places it in "the borderlands of science."

U2-P06Person

Identify Michael Polanyi and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 1 epigraph, p. 11

1. Who. Michael Polanyi, the chemist and philosopher, supplies the epigraph of Derry's Chapter 1, "A Bird's Eye View: The Many Routes to Scientific Discovery," from his Science, Faith, and Society (Derry ch. 1).

2. Quotation. "Now, I am not suggesting that it is impossible to find natural laws; but only that this is not done, and cannot be done, by applying some explicitly known operation" (Derry, p. 11).

3. Meaning. There is no recipe for discovery. Science is "too wide-ranging, multifaceted, and far too interesting for any single answer to suffice," and "No simple methodology of discovery is available for looking up in a recipe book" (Derry, p. 11).

4. Significance. Derry's five cases show different routes to discovery: accident (Roentgen's x-rays), a flash of intuition (Kekule and benzene), calculation (band structure in solids), voyages of exploration (biogeography) and the hypothetico-deductive method (Jenner's smallpox vaccine). Scientific reasoning includes judgment, skill and imagination, not only an explicit procedure such as a single "scientific method."

U2-P07Person

Identify Louis Pasteur and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 1, pp. 13-14

1. Who. Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist. Derry quotes his famous maxim in the account of Roentgen's discovery of x-rays (Derry ch. 1).
