2. Quotation. Discovering something you aren't looking for, often called serendipity, is not uncommon in the sciences, but Pasteur's maxim is that "chance favors only the prepared mind" (Derry, p. 13).

3. Example. Roentgen's discovery was "a marvelous combination of luck and skill." His mind was prepared by his skill in experimental techniques and his thorough knowledge of previous work on cathode ray phenomena, and he recognized the importance of "the faint glimmer he did not expect to see" (Derry, pp. 13-14).

4. Significance. Luck supplies the opportunity, but only preparation lets a scientist notice an unexpected result, and only "painstaking detailed investigation" afterwards turns it into a discovery (Derry, p. 14). Serendipity is a route to discovery, not a substitute for method.

U2-P08Person

Identify John Hunter and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Derry ch. 1, p. 21

1. Who. John Hunter was "the highly regarded surgeon" in London under whom Edward Jenner trained after going there in 1770 (Derry, p. 21).

2. Contribution. Medicine was still using "many traditional methods of doubtful efficacy," but Hunter "was a pioneer in the application of scientific thinking to medical practice, and he taught Jenner to do the same" (Derry, p. 21).

3. Context. Against his teacher's wishes (Hunter wanted Jenner to stay in London and make a reputation), Jenner moved back to Gloucestershire, where he could follow up the local legend that having cowpox protects against smallpox.

4. Significance. Derry tells Jenner's story as the hypothetico-deductive method. The scientific habits Hunter taught showed in Jenner's careful observations and records, his study of the cases where cowpox failed to protect, and his conclusion that "cowpox" was several different diseases, only one of which conferred immunity. That is how a folk belief became a tested medical discovery, the smallpox vaccine.

Unit 3

How Does Science Proceed

Readings Discussions 3.1 to 3.4; Derry Chapters 2 to 5, pp. 26-65.

Official study guide questions10

U3-SG01Study guide

What are the two sorts of error Giambattista Vico says can be made in thinking about the past? Can you identify times when you have made these errors? Do you find that you tend to make one kind rather than the other, or that you make one kind in some areas of your life and the other in other areas?

Source Discussion 3.1 and its footnote 40

Giambattista Vico (Discussion 3.1) names two opposite mistakes people make when they look at the past.

1. The conceit of nations. This is looking back to a golden age populated by individuals of incomparable intellectual and moral genius. Vico had in mind the deification of "founding fathers." Footnote 40 compares it to young children who regard their parents as the source of all wisdom and truth.

2. The conceit of scholars. This is the opposite mistake: viewing people of the past as ignorant and primitive, with nothing to teach the present. Footnote 40 compares it to adolescents who assume their parents are hopelessly out of touch, as in Mark Twain's remark that as a youth he found his father ignorant, but when he was older he was amazed at how much the old man had learned.

3. Why the errors matter for science. The conceit of scholars tempts us to ask why Tycho rejected the Copernican theory, or why geologists rejected continental drift for over 40 years, as if they were foolish. In fact Tycho had a very good reason (no stellar parallax could be observed with the instruments of his time), and drift had no credible mechanism. The conceit of nations makes past heroes infallible and hides how their good ideas were mixed with bad ones: Kepler's laws came wrapped in number mysticism, and Galileo kept his circles. Discussion 3.1 says the remedy is to recognize the historical continuity of humanity, including its social and cultural dimensions. Past science is the foundation of present science: the Greek search for the elementary components of matter survives in modern atomic theory, and Galileo could study motion only because medieval mathematicians had clarified velocity and acceleration.

Times I have made these errors

4. Conceit of scholars, at work. Part of my job in the Saskatchewan government is maintaining computer applications that other people built years ago. When I first open old code, it is easy to think the original programmers simply did not know better. Usually that is unfair: they worked with the tools, hardware and budgets of their time, and an odd-looking design often turns out to protect a business rule or a limit that still matters. The same thing happens when I remember the systems I supported at the Taiwanese manufacturing company and the bank in Vietnam in the early 2000s; by today's standards they look primitive, but they solved the problems of their day.

5. Conceit of nations, in my personal history. After I moved from Vietnam to Canada in 2007 and started over as a kitchen helper at McDonald's in Regina, it was tempting to remember my earlier life in Ho Chi Minh City, my computer science studies and the colleagues who trained me, as a kind of golden age, better and wiser than it really was. Nostalgia for a homeland is very close to what Vico literally called the conceit of nations.

6. Which error I tend to make. I make different errors in different areas, as Vico's footnote suggests (the same person can make the first error as a child and the second as an adolescent). In technology, which has changed quickly over my career from bank hardware to Android and iOS apps, I lean toward the conceit of scholars, because older usually looks obsolete. In personal and cultural matters I lean toward the conceit of nations. The correction is the same in both cases, and it is the one Discussion 3.1 recommends for the history of science: ask what the people of the past knew, what tools they had and what problems they faced, before judging them.

NotePoints 4 to 6 are built from the facts in My background.txt (your work history and your move to Canada in 2007). The particular situations are illustrative; replace them with episodes that really happened to you.

NoteDiscussion 3.1 asks why "Isaac Newton (1546-1601)" rejected the Copernican theory. Those are Tycho Brahe's dates, and Discussion 3.3 confirms that it was Tycho who rejected it.

U3-SG02Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) linking the sense of wonder as a motive for science, the search for understanding and the goal of generality.

Source Discussion 3.1; Discussion 3.2; Derry ch. 2 epigraph (Poincaré)

Discussion 3.1 suggests that the psychological roots of science are the capacity to wonder, the desire to understand and the desire for truth. They form a chain: out of wonder we ask questions, to understand we seek answers, and to know the truth we test those answers. The goal of generality links the chain, because understanding in science means seeing particular facts as cases of a general order.

Wonder is the starting point. Aristotle wrote that it is owing to their wonder that people began to philosophize, pursuing science "in order to know, and not for any utilitarian end." Newton's Opticks is a string of wondering questions: why do the planets all move the same way in concentric orbits while comets move every which way, and what keeps the fixed stars from falling on one another? Poincaré says the scientist studies nature not because it is useful but because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful. Wonder alone, however, produces only questions.

Understanding is what wonder seeks. Carl Sagan calls understanding "a kind of ecstasy," and Discussion 3.1 says the motive of science is wonder together with "the satisfaction that comes with understanding." As Poincaré writes in the epigraph to Derry's Chapter 2, merely to observe is not enough, "we must generalize," and "a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house." To understand a fact is to place it within a pattern that covers many facts.

That is why generality is the goal. Mendeleev knew thousands of facts about individual elements, but his achievement was a periodic law that tied them together, and its generality let him predict the properties of gallium and germanium. Kepler's three laws summarized Tycho's measurements for every planet, and Newton then showed that his laws of motion and universal gravitation explained Kepler's laws and, in Derry's words, "any motion due to any kind of force." Each step brought more phenomena under fewer principles, and the more general an understanding is, the more questions it answers at once.

Generality also disciplines wonder. A general claim says something about cases not yet examined, so it can be tested against experience, for internal consistency and against the scrutiny of other scientists. Discussion 3.1 notes that once individuals become scientists their desire to understand "must be disciplined," because they contribute to a shared cultural worldview rather than a private one. Kepler's wonder at cosmic harmony led him first to the Platonic solids, which he abandoned when the numbers were not quite right, and later to ellipses, which survived because they fit Tycho's precise data.

The three ideas therefore form a cycle. Wonder raises questions, the search for understanding answers them by finding general patterns, and each general answer opens new things to wonder about, as Newton's mechanics later led to the puzzle of Uranus's orbit and the discovery of Neptune.

U3-SG03Study guide

What are the four characteristics of a good question?

Source Discussion 3.2

Discussion 3.2 says the most important test of a good question is that it grabs a scientist's imagination and demands an answer; it is something to lie awake at night wondering about. Such a question has four characteristics.

1. Depth. It goes to the heart of a situation.

2. Tantalizing. It seems to hold out the possibility of an answer.

3. Suggestive. It almost tells one how to look for an answer.

4. Fruitful. The answer, when obtained, will have significant meaning for several areas of science.

Example. Kamerlingh Onnes asked what happens to the electrical resistance of a metal as its temperature becomes very low (Derry ch. 3). It had depth, because it went to the heart of how metals conduct electricity. It was tantalizing, because his laboratory had just learned to make liquid helium, so an answer was within reach. It was suggestive, because it told him what to do: cool a very pure metal (mercury, purified by distillation) and measure its resistance. And it was fruitful: the answer was superconductivity, which raised theoretical questions that took nearly half a century to answer.

Note. Precision is not on the list. Discussion 3.2 warns that a question that is too precise at the start can rule out lines of thought that later turn out to be important, as with Einstein's early, vague question about riding along with a light beam.

U3-SG04Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) comparing the criteria for a valid answer in science to criteria for a valid answer in some other area of human activity such as law, literature, art or religion.

Source Discussion 3.2; Discussion 7.2 (jury trials); Derry ch. 9

Discussion 3.2 gives three criteria that an answer must meet to count as scientific. It cannot imply the violation of an established empirical fact, unless it explains why the violating cases have not yet been observed, which yields predictions that can be tested. It must be consistent with existing theories, or give a good reason for changing them. And it cannot involve a logical contradiction. Answers such as "it is obvious," "it just feels right," "it is the will of God" or "it is morally and ethically correct" are inadmissible. Comparing these criteria with those for a valid answer in law shows a shared ancestry and some important differences.

The similarities are real. Discussion 7.2 suggests that science first blossomed in Greek cities such as Miletus partly because legal disputes there were settled by jury: claimants argued their case and the jury debated the merits of each side before voting. That habit of settling disagreement by public argument and reason is also the habit of science. A modern trial applies all three criteria in some form. A verdict must fit the established facts; a proven alibi defeats a charge. It must be consistent with existing law and precedent, unless a higher court gives good reason to change them. And testimony that contradicts itself is rejected, as a self-contradictory theory is. Law also borrows scientific answers directly: Derry (ch. 9) notes that DNA evidence in criminal trials and epidemiology in toxic substance suits bring science into the courtroom.

The differences come from the purpose of each activity. First, law must reach a final decision, by a deadline, about one particular past event, and in a criminal trial guilt must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt. Science answers general questions and can wait for more evidence: Snow's water theory was strongly supported in 1854 but was not given its "definitive final touch" until the cholera bacterium was identified some thirty years later, and scientific answers always stay open to revision. A verdict is meant to be final, and a person who is acquitted generally cannot be tried again for the same offence. Second, law deliberately weighs values such as justice, intent and mercy, so "it is morally and ethically correct" is a legitimate legal argument, though inadmissible in science. Third, legal validity rests partly on authority: a statute is valid because a legislature passed it, while no authority can make a scientific claim true, as Aristotle's "nature abhors a vacuum" learned from Torricelli's mercury column. Fourth, in a trial two sides argue before a judge or jury, while in science the whole community criticizes a conjecture and nature has the final word.

In short, law and science both demand evidence, consistency and freedom from contradiction, and their histories are linked. But science judges an answer by how well it generalizes and survives testing against nature, while law judges it by whether it settles a particular dispute fairly under rules that society has chosen.

U3-SG05Study guide

Identify at least five sorts of questions that can be asked in science.

Source Discussion 3.2

Discussion 3.2 lists seven sorts of questions that can begin scientific work.

1. Is a hypothesis true, consistent with a given theory, or consistent with experiment? Snow questioned the competing hypotheses about how cholera spread and accepted the one that it spread through the water supply.

2. If a theory or hypothesis is true, what are its consequences for further theory and for predictions? Einstein asked what follows if the speed of light is constant, which led to special relativity.

3. What must be assumed as true for a particular result to follow? For example, what must be assumed to explain the motions of the planets. Ptolemy and Copernicus began from the same question but assumed very different things.

4. What is the relation between the elements of a set or collection? Linnaeus asked how different kinds of plants and animals are related, and answered with a species concept based on interbreeding: members of the same species can mate and produce fertile offspring.

5. What is the composition or structure of an entity? Dalton asked how chemical compounds might be composed, and developed the atomic theory of matter.

6. Why is a thing this way and not otherwise? Olbers asked why the night sky is dark: if there are infinitely many stars, every line of sight should end on a star and the whole sky should be bright.

7. What data must be obtained, and how, to test a hypothesis or theory? In 1919 an expedition measured the bending of starlight by the sun, which Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted.

Also asked before any experiment. Discussion 3.2 adds five questions to ask before any investigation: whether the procedure will disturb the system's natural behaviour, whether the system can show the expected behaviour, whether the equipment can detect the expected result, whether the system's initial state is properly prepared, and whether the procedure will destroy the system in a way that invalidates the result.

NoteDiscussion 3.2 places the 1919 expedition in Paraguay. The two 1919 eclipse expeditions actually went to Príncipe, off West Africa, and Sobral, in Brazil. The point about the type of question is unaffected.

U3-SG06Study guide

Describe Roland Omnès's four stages of scientific activity as presented in Discussion 3.2.

Source Discussion 3.2

Roland Omnès describes four stages of scientific activity, which he attributes to Pierre Duhem (1861-1916) (Discussion 3.2).

1. Exploratory stage. It "consists in the observation of facts, the performing of experiments 'to see what happens,' the compiling of a catalogue of data, and, eventually, the discovery of empirical rules." Example: Tycho's catalogue of planetary positions, from which Kepler extracted his three laws, which are empirical rules.

2. Conceptual stage. It consists in "the development and the selection of appropriate concepts permitting a representation of Reality," and the invention of the principle or principles that might govern that representation. Example: Newton's concepts of inertia, force and universal gravitation.

3. Developmental stage. It consists in examining all possible consequences of the principles, although in most cases only certain consequences are considered, mainly those concerning known facts. Example: Newton showed that his laws predict all of Kepler's laws, and Laplace and others used perturbation methods to work out the motions of the known planets.

4. Verification stage. Here "each prediction is systematically subjected to the test of experience." Successful predictions lead to tentative acceptance; failed ones show that the theory is false or at least incomplete and needs clarification. Example: Adams and LeVerrier predicted where an unseen planet perturbing Uranus must be, and Galle found Neptune on his first night of searching in 1846.

5. Relation to the eight-stage model. The Exploratory stage covers stages 1 to 3 (initial interest, delineation of the phenomenon, empirical database); the Conceptual stage is stage 4 (classification and conceptualization); the Developmental stage is stage 5 (generalization and theory construction); and the Verification stage covers stages 6 to 8 (hypothesis testing, analysis and debate, assimilation into existing theory).

6. Not a rigid sequence. In practice, work goes on in all stages at once, with feedback among them, and the process is cyclic: the Uranus discrepancy that verification uncovered became a new object of exploration.

U3-SG07Study guide

Describe three different ways that scientific discoveries have been made, and give an example of each.

Source Derry chs. 2-4 (also ch. 1)

Derry's Chapters 2 to 4 describe three different ways that discoveries have been made.

1. Finding a pattern in existing data (ch. 2). The discovery is an underlying coherence hidden in a mass of facts, like jigsaw pieces falling into place. Example: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869). By about 1850 some sixty elements were known, along with a great deal about their properties. Mendeleev recorded every fact about each element on a card, hung the cards on his wall and rearranged them until a periodic pattern based on atomic weight emerged. The pattern was strong enough for him to correct the accepted atomic weights of indium, uranium, cerium and titanium and to predict missing elements; gallium (1875) and germanium were found with the predicted properties. Wegener's continental drift is a second example, assembled from matching coastlines, rock formations, fossils and past climates.

2. New instrumentation (ch. 3). Instruments extend our senses, or create new conditions, such as extreme cold, in which to observe. Example: Leeuwenhoek's microscope. His hand-ground lenses magnified over 300 times, and in 1674 he looked at pond water and found a whole unsuspected world of microbes; he went on to discover bacteria, spermatozoa and blood capillaries. Kamerlingh Onnes's liquid helium (superconductivity, 1911) and Jansky's radio receiver (radio astronomy, 1930s) are further examples.

3. A discrepancy between expectation and observation (ch. 4). A small result that does not fit can trigger a major discovery. Example: argon. Around 1890 Lord Rayleigh found that nitrogen taken from air was denser, by about one part in a thousand, than nitrogen made from ammonia. Because his measurements were precise and repeated, he knew the difference was real. Removing the nitrogen chemically left a residue, and Rayleigh and Ramsay identified a new, heavy, inert gas, argon (1894), the first of a whole new column of the periodic table. Torricelli's explanation of why suction pumps cannot lift water above 34 feet, and the discovery of Neptune from a tiny discrepancy in the orbit of Uranus, are further examples.

Why it matters. The three routes show that there is no single method of discovery. In each case a prepared investigator had to recognize what was significant, and the result then had to be tested and accepted by the scientific community.

U3-SG08Study guide

What were the major pieces of evidence that led Snow to his discovery of how cholera is transmitted?

Source Discussion 3.4

Discussion 3.4 describes several lines of evidence that together led Snow to conclude that cholera is spread by contaminated water, specifically by the excretions of victims.

1. Cholera is communicable. Snow began with many examples showing that the disease passed from person to person.

2. Evidence against effluvia (air transmission). Everyone in close contact with a victim breathes in the supposed effluvia, yet not everyone in such contact falls ill; and cholera sometimes broke out in new areas where nobody had been exposed to earlier victims.

3. Who caught it, and who did not. People who cared for the sick and washed their clothing and bedclothes had a high chance of getting cholera, while physicians and others who washed their hands, or did not eat food prepared in the sick-room, rarely did. This pointed to ingestion of "morbid material" rather than breathing.

4. The Broad Street pump. During the 1853-54 outbreak in Soho, Snow noticed that many victims came from households that got their water from the pump on Broad Street.

5. Removing the pump handle. He persuaded the parish Board of Guardians to remove the handle, and the incidence of cholera in the area dropped significantly.

6. The workhouse and the brewery. Two groups living near the pump had very few cases, and neither drank from it: the workhouse had its own water supply, and the brewery workers drank their daily allowance of beer instead of water.

7. The two water companies. In one district, houses side by side were supplied either by the Lambeth Company, which had moved its intake upstream above London's sewage, or by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, which drew contaminated water. Snow argued there was no other difference in the condition or occupation of the people supplied, so 300,000 people had been divided into two groups "without their choice."

8. The death rates. In 1853-54, Southwark and Vauxhall houses had 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses, Lambeth houses 37, and the rest of London 59. The contaminated supply carried about 8.5 times the death rate of the clean one.

Why it was convincing. Each line of evidence was independent, the alternatives were refuted, and the conclusion explained all the facts at once. The studies did not prove the theory, but they gave "sufficient reasons" for it; the bacterium itself was identified about 30 years later.

U3-SG09Study guide

Identify the main questions that Snow asked, and describe how he answered them as he carried out his research.

Source Discussion 3.4

Snow's research (Discussion 3.4) can be read as a sequence of questions, each answered by evidence or argument.

1. Is cholera a communicable disease? He answered by gathering many examples of the disease passing from one person to another.

2. Is it spread by effluvia, something breathed out by patients or given off by the dead? No. Not everyone who breathes the same air as a victim falls ill, and outbreaks appear in places with no exposure to earlier victims. Since diseases are known to spread in other ways, there was no need to focus on effluvia.

3. Why do some people in close contact fall ill while others, especially physicians, do not? Those who washed the sick person's linen were often infected, while those who washed their hands and did not eat food prepared in the sick-room rarely were. So the disease seemed to enter by the mouth.

4. Is the failure to see the agent under a microscope an objection? No. In Snow's words, "the matter of small-pox and of chancre can only be recognized by their effects, and not by their physical properties."

5. What carries the morbid material to people far from any patient? The water supply. He tested this locally by mapping cases to the Broad Street pump and having its handle removed, after which cases in the area dropped.

6. Why did some people near the pump escape? The workhouse had its own water and the brewery workers drank beer, so the exceptions confirmed the rule.

7. Does the source of the water change the death rate across a large population? He compared houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company (contaminated intake) with houses supplied by the Lambeth Company (clean intake) in the same streets, and found about 315 versus 37 deaths per 10,000 houses.

8. What should be done? From his conclusions he proposed public health measures that are still used: hand washing, washing or boiling soiled linen, uncontaminated drinking water, good drainage, education and quarantine.

Significance. This is the guided question-and-answer process of Discussion 3.2 in action: each answer narrowed the hypothesis and raised the next question, and the criteria for valid answers (fit the facts, fit theory, no contradiction) were applied at each step.

U3-SG10Study guide

Chapter 5 of What Science Is describes the history of our theories of planetary motion. Apply the eight-stage model of scientific development given in Discussion 3.2 to map out the corresponding stages in this history. Note that you may need to consider more than a single cycle of this process.

Source Derry ch. 5 (pp. 52-65); Discussion 3.2; Discussion 3.3

Derry's Chapter 5 history fits the eight-stage model of Discussion 3.2 best as two full cycles followed by the start of a third, with stages overlapping and feeding back into one another.

Cycle 1: from Babylon to Ptolemy

1. Initial interest. The Babylonians watched the lights in the night sky, which for them was a place of myth and wonder populated by living beings.

2. Delineation of the phenomenon. They recorded the positions of the moon, stars and planets and noticed that the planets wander against the fixed stars.

3. Empirical database. Their careful records, together with mathematical techniques for finding regularities, were passed on to the Greeks.

4. Classification and conceptualization. The Greeks asked about causes, not just predictions. Pythagoras held that the world is based on mathematical relationships, and Plato taught that the circle and sphere are perfect shapes. The planets' odd behaviour was classified as retrograde motion, a deviation that needed explaining.

5. Generalization and theory construction. Pythagorean thinkers built world systems; Aristarchus proposed a sun-centred one; Eudoxus used nested spheres; and Ptolemy accounted for every planet with epicycles moving on larger circles around the earth, 39 circles in all.

6. Hypothesis generation and testing. The rival systems were judged by how well they predicted planetary positions. As the model warns, the data available could not decisively eliminate one of them.

7. Analysis and debate. The earth-centred view won, for reasons no one really knows, and Aristarchus's system was forgotten.

8. Assimilation. Ptolemy's astronomy was combined with Aristotle's physics of crystal spheres, rediscovered by Europe in the twelfth century and absorbed into Christian theology. It dominated European thought, the medieval equivalent of the textbook.

Cycle 2: from Copernicus to Newton

9. New initial interest (stage 1). The Renaissance needed better astronomy for navigation and calendar reform, and Ptolemy's predictions were inaccurate and could only be patched with more epicycles. Accepted theory from cycle 1 thus produced the new problem. Tycho was drawn in when he saw an eclipse occur on time but a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn miss its predicted date by several days.

10. Delineation and database (stages 2 and 3). Regiomontanus built better instruments, and Tycho, with royal support on the island of Ven, recorded the planets with the highest precision possible before the telescope, at many points in each orbit. His observations of the 1572 new star and of comets showed that the heavens change and that the crystal spheres could not exist.

11. Conceptualization and theory (stages 4 and 5). Copernicus worked out the mathematics of a sun-centred system as carefully as Ptolemy had done for the earth-centred one, and reclassified retrograde motion as an illusion caused by the earth's own motion. Tycho offered a hybrid. Kepler, using Tycho's data, found that orbits are ellipses, that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, and that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance. He also proposed a physical cause emanating from the sun.

12. Testing (stage 6). Circular models failed against Tycho's data while ellipses fitted. Copernicus predicted stellar parallax, which could not be seen, so this test was inconclusive. Galileo's telescope showed mountains on the moon, phases of Venus and moons of Jupiter, evidence that favoured Copernicus.

13. Analysis and debate (stage 7). Aristotelian scholars, the Church and Galileo argued over whether the earth moves; the debate ended in Galileo's trial. Meanwhile Galileo's science of motion and Descartes' straight-line inertia replaced Aristotle's physics.

14. Assimilation (stage 8). Newton combined inertia, his second law and universal gravitation, and showed that they predict all of Kepler's laws. Classical mechanics became the accepted theory, taught today as Newton's laws.

Cycle 3 begins. Newtonian mechanics then became the background for new questions. Perturbation calculations matched every known planet until a tiny discrepancy in the orbit of Uranus (stage 1) led to the prediction and discovery of Neptune in 1846 (Derry ch. 4), and parallax was finally measured once instruments became sensitive enough.

Feedback. The stages were not strictly sequential. Tycho's data gathering (stages 2 and 3) was driven by the stage 7 debate between Ptolemy and Copernicus, and Kepler's concepts (stage 4) were shaped by Pythagorean theory carried forward from cycle 1.

Learning objective drills7

U3-OBJ01Objective

Describe some of the factors that motivate people to engage in scientific activity.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 1

Discussion 3.1 and the Unit 3 readings point to several motives for doing science.

1. Wonder and curiosity. Aristotle says people began to philosophize "owing to their wonder," seeking knowledge for its own sake. Newton's Opticks overflows with wondering questions, and Selye says the true scientist never loses the faculty of amazement.

2. The desire to understand. Out of wonder we ask questions, and to understand we seek answers. Sagan calls understanding "a kind of ecstasy," and using our intelligence gives us pleasure, like using a muscle.

3. The desire for truth. To know the truth we test our answers against experience, for internal consistency and against the scrutiny of other scientists.

4. Delight in beauty. Poincaré says the scientist studies nature because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful. Kepler's joy at finding the "signature of God" in his equal-areas law is an example.

5. Fundamental questions about ourselves. Who are we? Where did we come from? Where are we going? Science pursues them under constraints that yield public knowledge that is "as accurate as we can get."

6. Practical need. Navigation and calendar reform pushed Renaissance astronomy forward, and Jansky discovered cosmic radio waves while Bell Laboratories was trying to remove static from transatlantic telephone links.

7. A scientific tradition and good questions. Scientists belong to a historical movement with its own values, and a good question "grabs you right in the gut" and will not let go. Personal ambition also plays a part: Tycho guarded his data, perhaps fearing Kepler would replace him.

U3-OBJ02Objective

Discuss science as a guided process of questions and answers.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 2

Discussion 3.2 presents science as a guided process of questions and answers.

1. Questions come first. Popper called science "conjectures and refutations," but a conjecture must answer a question, and once it is made we ask new questions: does it answer the original question, is it consistent with accepted theory, and does it fit the facts?

2. Questions need a context. Asking "Why?" or "How?" without a context in which the question makes sense produces no useful answer. In a developing theory, questions arise about logical consistency, explaining data, and applications; the answers are conjectures that other scientists criticize, and survivors may be accepted.

3. Kuhn: puzzle solving within a paradigm. A paradigm, the basic assumptions of a discipline, sets the questions and assumes they can be answered within it. Only when central questions stay unanswered for a long time is the paradigm itself questioned, starting a revolution.

4. Toulmin: Ideals of Natural Order. Science asks why nature deviates from its assumed natural behaviour, such as circular orbits for the Greeks or straight-line motion for Newton.

5. Good questions sustain a field. Von Foerster argues that a paradigm dies when it stops generating interesting questions, as a mine is abandoned when the gold runs out. Einstein chose physics because there he could tell important questions from trivial ones.

6. Wheeler's Twenty Questions. In his game the answer is built up during the questioning, with each reply consistent with all earlier ones. The course takes a mild realist view: honest question sequences tend to converge, as Schrödinger's and Heisenberg's formulations of quantum mechanics did, and sometimes reach anomalous questions that force new assumptions.

7. Guidance by criteria. Answers are admissible only if they fit established facts, fit or justify changing existing theory, and contain no contradiction. The Overview traces this method back to the master-apprentice relationship and to Socrates. Snow's cholera work is a model of the process.

U3-OBJ03Objective

State the forms of some of the common questions that are asked in science.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 3

Discussion 3.2 lists common forms of scientific questions.

1. Is hypothesis H true, consistent with theory T, or consistent with experiment? (Snow testing hypotheses about how cholera spreads.)

2. If H is true, what follows for theory and prediction? (Einstein assuming a constant speed of light.)

3. What must be assumed for result R to follow? (What must be assumed to explain the planets' motion.)

4. How are the members of a set related? (Linnaeus and the interbreeding species concept.)

5. What is X composed of, or how is it structured? (Dalton and the atomic theory.)

6. Why is X this way and not otherwise? (Olbers: why is the night sky dark?)

7. What data are needed, and how can they be obtained, to test H? (The 1919 eclipse measurement of starlight bending.)

8. Questions before any experiment. Will the procedure disturb the system? Can the system show the expected behaviour? Can the equipment detect the result? Is the initial state properly prepared? Will the procedure destroy the system in a way that invalidates the result?

U3-OBJ04Objective

List some of the basic criteria for valid answers to scientific questions.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 4

Discussion 3.2 gives three basic criteria for a valid scientific answer.

1. It must not violate an established empirical fact, unless it also explains why the cases where the violation would occur have not yet been observed; in that case it makes predictions that can be tested.

2. It must be consistent with existing theories, or provide a good reason for changing them.

3. It must not involve a logical contradiction.

4. Inadmissible answers. "It is obvious," "it just feels right," "it is the will of God" and "it is morally and ethically correct" may satisfy other areas of life, but not science. It is the criteria for acceptable answers "that give us science."

5. Testing and public scrutiny. Discussion 3.1 adds that answers are tested against experience, for internal consistency and against the scrutiny of other scientists.

6. Example. To explain the discrepancy in Uranus's orbit, abandoning the inverse-square law would violate criterion 2 without good reason, and a passing comet was untestable. An unseen planet fit Newtonian theory and made a testable prediction, which Galle confirmed by finding Neptune (Derry ch. 4).

U3-OBJ05Objective

Describe the stages in the development of a scientific idea, or an entire field of science.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 5

Discussion 3.2 describes the development of a scientific idea or field in stages.

1. Omnès's four stages (from Duhem). Exploratory (observing, experimenting "to see what happens," cataloguing data and finding empirical rules); Conceptual (choosing concepts and inventing principles to represent reality); Developmental (working out the consequences of the principles, mostly for known facts); Verification (testing each prediction against experience).

2. Eight stages, first half. (1) Initial interest, when something odd catches attention; (2) delineation of the phenomenon and choice of tools; (3) building an empirical database by designed observation and experiment; (4) classification and conceptualization, grouping regularities and building a taxonomy.

3. Eight stages, second half. (5) Generalization and theory construction, finding causal regularities; (6) hypothesis generation and testing; (7) analysis and debate within the community; (8) assimilation into existing theory and the textbooks.

4. How they correspond. Exploratory covers 1 to 3, Conceptual is 4, Developmental is 5, and Verification covers 6 to 8.

5. Not linear. Work goes on at every stage at once, with feedback and feedforward links, and the cycle repeats: the accepted theory of stage 8 is the background against which new phenomena arise at stage 1. Choosing tools at stage 2 already requires thinking about the concepts of stage 4.

6. Different questions at different stages. A 17th-century question about how acceleration, velocity, momentum and kinetic energy relate is no longer asked, and questions about caloric have become meaningless since the caloric theory of heat was abandoned.

7. Example. Planetary astronomy went from Babylonian records (stages 1 to 3) through Greek concepts and Ptolemy's epicycles (stages 4 and 5) to a second cycle of Tycho's data, Kepler's laws, the Copernican debate and Newton's synthesis (Derry ch. 5).

U3-OBJ06Objective

Describe some of the different factors that can lead to new scientific discoveries.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 6

The Unit 3 readings show that many different factors can lead to a discovery.

1. Recognizing a pattern in data that has defied understanding: Mendeleev's periodic table and Wegener's drifting continents (Derry ch. 2).

2. New instruments that extend our senses or create new conditions: Leeuwenhoek's lenses revealed microbes, liquid helium let Onnes discover superconductivity, and radio telescopes revealed pulsars and quasars (ch. 3).

3. Noticing a discrepancy instead of dismissing it: argon from a one-part-in-a-thousand density difference, atmospheric pressure from the 34-foot pump limit, Neptune from a 30-arc-second error in Uranus's orbit (ch. 4).

4. Thematic imagination combined with precise measurement: Kepler's Pythagorean search for harmonies, disciplined by Tycho's data, produced his three laws (ch. 5; Discussion 3.3).

5. Technology and work from other fields: wartime radar improved radio astronomy, and sonar, deep-sea core sampling and seismography revealed the ocean floor that confirmed plate tectonics.

6. Collaboration and the social and cultural setting: radio and optical astronomers together found quasars; the Renaissance revival of Greek texts exposed Copernicus to heliocentrism when Ptolemy's system was weakening.

7. A prepared mind and the routes in Derry ch. 1: serendipity, intuition, idealized models, exploration and the hypothetico-deductive method. Herschel's discovery of Uranus combined chance with a high-magnification telescope and an expert eye.

U3-OBJ07Objective

Describe some case histories of scientific discovery in terms of the question-and-answer process.

Source Unit 3 Overview objective 7

Several Unit 3 case histories can be told as a sequence of questions and answers.

1. Torricelli and the barometer (Derry ch. 4). Why can a suction pump lift water only 34 feet? First he needed a prior question: why does suction make water rise at all? "Nature abhors a vacuum" could not explain the limit. His answer was that air has weight, so the pressure of the atmosphere balances a 34-foot water column. That raised a testable question: what height will mercury, 13.6 times denser, reach? The answer, 2.5 feet, confirmed atmospheric pressure, and Pascal's mountain experiment confirmed that pressure falls with altitude.

2. Rayleigh and argon (ch. 4). Why is nitrogen from air denser than nitrogen from ammonia? Is it a heavier form of nitrogen? No, it could not be made any other way. What is left if all the nitrogen is removed from air? A residue of a new, heavy, inert gas, argon.

3. Onnes and superconductivity (ch. 3). What happens to a metal's resistance near absolute zero? Platinum levelled off, perhaps because of impurities, so he asked again with pure mercury. The resistance dropped suddenly to zero. Was that real or a short circuit? Persistent currents in superconducting rings showed it was truly zero.

4. Kepler and Mars (ch. 5; Discussion 3.3). What circular orbit fits Tycho's observations of Mars? None fits closely enough. What shape does? An ellipse with the sun at one focus. Why does the planet speed up near the sun? This led to the equal-areas law and to the question of a physical cause from the sun, which Newton later answered.

5. Snow and cholera (Discussion 3.4). Is cholera communicable? Yes. Is it carried by effluvia? No. What carries it? Water, shown by the Broad Street pump, its exceptions and the comparison of two water companies (315 versus 37 deaths per 10,000 houses).

Lesson. In each case an answer was accepted only after it passed the criteria for valid answers, and each answer generated the next question.

Lists and concept recall9

U3-R01Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Vico's two errors in viewing the past. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Vico's two errors in viewing the past (Discussion 3.1)

1. Conceit of nations. Looking back to a golden age of people of incomparable intellectual and moral genius, the deification of "founding fathers" (Vico, in Discussion 3.1).

2. Conceit of scholars. The opposite error: viewing people of the past as ignorant and primitive, with nothing to teach the present.

3. Example. Footnote 40: young children make the first error when they treat their parents as the source of all wisdom; adolescents make the second when they think their parents hopelessly ignorant. In science, wondering why geologists rejected continental drift for over 40 years, as if they were foolish, is the conceit of scholars; Derry (ch. 2) shows they had good reasons, since Wegener's proposed mechanism was millions of times too weak.

4. Significance for scientific reasoning. Both errors project our point of view onto the past. Avoiding them means recognizing historical continuity: past science, including theories now abandoned, is the foundation of present science, as the Greek search for elementary components of matter is of modern atomic theory.

5. A further lesson. Judging past scientists by the evidence and tools they actually had (Tycho had no way to see stellar parallax) teaches us to judge present theories the same way: by the evidence now available, knowing that later evidence may change the picture.

U3-R02Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Four characteristics of a good question. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Four characteristics of a good question (Discussion 3.2)

1. The four characteristics (Discussion 3.2). A good question has depth (it goes to the heart of a situation), is tantalizing (it seems to hold out the possibility of an answer), is suggestive (it almost tells one how to look for an answer) and is fruitful (its answer will matter to several areas of science).

2. The overall test. A good question grabs the scientist's imagination and demands an answer.

3. Example. Torricelli's question, why a suction pump cannot lift water above 34 feet (Derry ch. 4), had depth (it went to the cause of suction), was tantalizing and suggestive (if air has weight, a denser liquid should rise less, which can be tried), and was fruitful (it produced the concept of atmospheric pressure, the barometer and the ability to make a vacuum).

4. Precision is not required. Asking too precisely too early can eliminate lines of thought that later prove important; Einstein's vague question at 16 about riding a light beam became a precise one only after much study.

5. Significance. Because questions formulated at the start of a project tend to persist and shape it, choosing a good one is a major part of scientific reasoning. Von Foerster argues that a field dies when it stops producing good questions.

U3-R03Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Three criteria for a scientific answer. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Three criteria for a scientific answer (Discussion 3.2)

1. Criterion 1. No answer can imply the violation of an established empirical fact, unless it also explains why the cases where the violation would occur have not yet been observed; then it offers testable predictions (Discussion 3.2).

2. Criterion 2. Every answer must be consistent with existing theories, or provide a good reason for changing them.

3. Criterion 3. No answer can involve a logical contradiction.

4. What is excluded. Answers such as "it is obvious," "it just feels right," "it is the will of God" or "it is morally and ethically correct" are inadmissible in science. The criteria are what "give us science."

5. Example. Faced with the small discrepancy in Uranus's orbit, scientists did not throw out universal gravitation, which would violate criterion 2 without good reason; Derry calls that a last resort. A passing comet was possible but untestable. An unknown planet was consistent with Newtonian theory and made a definite prediction, confirmed when Neptune was found in 1846 (Derry ch. 4).

6. Significance. The criteria let the scientific community compare rival answers in a public, impersonal way, and they explain why science can be progressive: new answers must build on, or explicitly justify replacing, what is already known.

U3-R04Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Seven sorts of questions asked in science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Seven sorts of questions asked in science (Discussion 3.2)

Discussion 3.2 lists seven sorts of questions that begin scientific inquiry.

1. Whether a hypothesis is true, consistent with theory or consistent with experiment. Snow's testing of hypotheses about cholera.

2. What consequences follow if a theory is true, for theory development and prediction. Einstein and the constant speed of light.

3. What must be assumed for a particular result to follow. What must be assumed to explain the planets' motions; Ptolemy and Copernicus answered differently.

4. How the elements of a set are related. Linnaeus's species concept based on interbreeding.

5. What the composition or structure of an entity is. Dalton and the atomic theory.

6. Why something is this way and not otherwise. Olbers's paradox: why is the night sky dark?

7. What data are needed, and how to get them, to test a hypothesis. The 1919 eclipse measurement of the bending of starlight predicted by general relativity.

Significance. Knowing these forms helps a scientist turn vague curiosity into a question that can be investigated, and shows that different questions dominate at different stages of a science.

U3-R05Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Five questions to ask before any experiment. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Five questions to ask before any experiment (Discussion 3.2)

Discussion 3.2 lists five questions to ask before any experiment.

1. Will the procedure disturb the system's natural behaviour so much that the results are unrepresentative? A bird kept in a small cage may behave completely differently, while a small thermometer in a large beaker barely changes the liquid's temperature.

2. Can the system show the expected behaviour? It is useless to test the spelling of infants who cannot yet talk.

3. Can the equipment detect the expected result? The Copernican theory predicted stellar parallax, but it was well over 100 years before instruments could measure it.

4. Is the initial state properly prepared? Rats trained to perform a task for food must be hungry when they are tested.

5. Will the procedure destroy or disable the system, and does that invalidate the experiment? An electrode so large that it kills a nerve cell is useless, but physicists legitimately study nuclei by smashing them and analysing the fragments.

Significance. These questions prevent wasted effort and false conclusions. Ignoring question 3, for example, would turn the absence of observed parallax into a false refutation of the moving earth.

U3-R06Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Omnès's four stages of scientific activity, attributed to Pierre Duhem. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Omnès's four stages of scientific activity, attributed to Pierre Duhem (Discussion 3.2)

Roland Omnès describes four stages, which he attributes to Pierre Duhem (Discussion 3.2).

1. Exploratory. Observing facts, doing experiments "to see what happens," compiling a catalogue of data and eventually discovering empirical rules.

2. Conceptual. Developing and selecting concepts that represent reality, and inventing the principles that might govern that representation.

3. Developmental. Examining the consequences of the principles; in most cases only some are considered, mainly those concerning known facts.

4. Verification. Systematically testing each prediction against experience. Success brings tentative acceptance; failure shows the theory is false or incomplete.

5. Example. For the barometer (Derry ch. 4): pumps were known to lift water only 34 feet (exploratory); Torricelli conceived atmospheric pressure (conceptual); he worked out that mercury should stand at 34/13.6 = 2.5 feet (developmental); and the mercury column and Pascal's mountain experiment confirmed it (verification).

6. Significance. The stages correspond to stages 1-3, 4, 5 and 6-8 of the eight-stage model, and show that observation alone is not science until concepts, consequences and tests are added.

U3-R07Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: The eight-stage model. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source The eight-stage model (Discussion 3.2)

Discussion 3.2 breaks scientific development into eight stages.

1. Initial interest. A phenomenon catches someone's attention: "That's funny, what's going on here?"

2. Delineation of the phenomenon. Researchers describe it more fully, develop a "feel" for it and choose or build tools.

3. Empirical database. Designed observations and experiments build a body of data.

4. Classification and conceptualization. Regularities are grouped into classes and concepts, perhaps a taxonomy, carving nature "where the joint is" (Plato).

5. Generalization and theory construction. Relations among concepts and causal regularities are found and built into theory.

6. Hypothesis generation and testing. Hypotheses make new predictions that are tested; tests alone may not eliminate all rivals.

7. Analysis and debate. The community compares the surviving hypotheses and modifies them toward consensus.

8. Assimilation into existing theory. The best-supported (or, failing that, most elegant) hypothesis becomes part of accepted theory and the textbooks.

Not linear but cyclic. All stages run at once, with feedback; the theory accepted at stage 8 is the background for new interest at stage 1, and the debates of stage 7 raise new questions. Example: Derry's Chapter 5 runs from Babylonian records (stages 1-3) to Newton's synthesis (stage 8), and Newtonian mechanics then set up the Uranus puzzle that began a new cycle.

U3-R08Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Kepler's three laws. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Kepler's three laws (Discussion 3.3; Derry pp. 59-60)

1. First law. Planetary orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus (Discussion 3.3; Derry pp. 59-60).

2. Second law. The line joining a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves faster when it is closer to the sun.

3. Third law. The square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the sun (more exactly, the ratio of the squares of two planets' periods equals the ratio of the cubes of the semi-major axes of their orbits). For example, Mars's orbit is about 1.52 times the size of Earth's, so its period is about 1.52 to the power 1.5, or 1.88 years.

4. How they were found. The first two came from Kepler's years of calculations on Tycho's observations of Mars, whose orbit departs from a circle more than most; the third came about a decade later.

5. Significance. Derry gives three reasons: they were the first correct mathematical description of the planets' motions; Kepler gave up his beloved circles because the data contradicted them, a step toward modern science; and he sought a physical cause from the sun.

6. Later role. About 50 years later Newton showed that his laws of motion and an inverse-square gravitational force predict all three laws, turning empirical rules into consequences of a deeper theory.

U3-R09Recall

State and interpret Snow's comparison of deaths per 10000 houses for the two water suppliers and the rest of London. Why must the denominator be retained?

Source Snow's death rates, 1853-54 epidemic (Discussion 3.4)

1. The figures (Discussion 3.4, Table 3). Southwark and Vauxhall Company: 40,046 houses, 1,263 cholera deaths, 315 deaths per 10,000 houses. Lambeth Company: 26,107 houses, 98 deaths, 37 per 10,000. Rest of London: 256,423 houses, 1,422 deaths, 59 per 10,000.

2. Interpretation. Houses supplied with sewage-contaminated Thames water had about 8.5 times the death rate (315/37) of houses supplied from Lambeth's upstream intake, and over five times the rate for the rest of London. Lambeth houses did better than the London average. This pattern is what the water theory predicts.

3. Why the denominator must be kept. The companies supplied different numbers of houses, so raw death counts mislead. Comparing 1,263 with 98 deaths suggests a ratio of about 13; dividing by the number of houses gives the fair ratio of about 8.5. A larger population will have more deaths even at the same risk.

4. What the denominator is. It is houses, not people. Houses vary in the number of occupants, so these are household rates, not individual risks.

5. Why the comparison is strong. Snow argued that the two companies' pipes ran down the same streets, that each supplied rich and poor alike, and that 300,000 people had been divided into two groups without their choice, so water supply was the main difference.

NoteRecomputing from the table, 1,263/40,046 and 98/26,107 give 315 and 37.5 per 10,000, but 1,422/256,423 gives about 55, not the 59 printed in the table. The conclusions are unaffected.

Key term questions10

U3-T01Term

Define or distinguish Conceit of nations / conceit of scholars. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Vico's two errors in viewing the past (Discussion 3.1). The conceit of nations idealizes a golden age of people of incomparable intellectual and moral genius, deifying "founding fathers." The conceit of scholars sees people of the past as ignorant and primitive, with nothing to teach the present.

2. Distinction. They are opposites: one overrates the past and the other underrates it.

3. Role in this unit. They warn against projecting our own understanding onto the history of science and support the claim that science is progressive, with past science as the foundation of present science.

4. Example of the conceit of scholars. Asking why Tycho rejected Copernicus, as if he were foolish; he rejected it because no stellar parallax could be observed (Discussion 3.3).

5. Example of the conceit of nations. Treating Kepler or Galileo as infallible, when Kepler mixed his laws with number mysticism and Galileo kept circular orbits (Derry ch. 5). Renaissance thinkers, who saw their own age as impoverished beside Greece and Rome, show a similar attitude (footnote 41).

U3-T02Term

Define or distinguish Paradigm. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. In Thomas Kuhn's sense, a paradigm is the basic set of assumptions and beliefs guiding development in a scientific discipline, which therefore provides the context for asking significant questions (Discussion 3.2).

2. Role in this unit. Kuhn describes normal science as "puzzle solving" within a paradigm: its questions of consistency and empirical fit are assumed to be answerable within its assumptions.

3. Revolution. Only when central questions go unanswered for a long time is the paradigm itself questioned; the field of questions widens, a revolution begins, and a new paradigm emerges in which old questions are answered or seen as irrelevant.

4. Example. When the caloric theory (heat as a material fluid) gave way to the kinetic theory (heat as molecular motion), the question of how much caloric a body contains ceased to have meaning (footnote 50). The shift from Aristotle's and Ptolemy's cosmos to Newton's is another example (Derry ch. 5).

5. Distinction. A paradigm is broader than a single theory or hypothesis: it sets which questions make sense. Von Foerster adds that a paradigm dies less from unanswered questions than from failing to generate new interesting ones.

U3-T03Term

Define or distinguish Ideals of Natural Order. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Stephen Toulmin's term (Foresight and Understanding) for assumptions about what is natural: how nature would behave if nothing interfered. Only deviations from this ideal need explaining (Discussion 3.2).

2. Role in this unit. They set the context for scientific questions: science asks why something departed from the natural order.

3. Example: Greek circles. The ancient assumption that planetary orbits are perfect circles was an ideal of natural order; Ptolemy's epicycles were adjustments to explain apparent deviations from "perfect" motion.

4. Example: Newton's first law. Motion in a straight line at constant speed is natural. Rewriting F = ma as a = F/m shows that any acceleration, any deviation from that motion, must be explained by an external force.

5. Changing the ideal changes the questions. For Aristotle, rest was natural on earth and circular motion natural in the heavens, so planetary motion needed no further cause. Once Kepler found ellipses, he felt a physical explanation was needed (Derry ch. 5).

U3-T04Term

Define or distinguish Realism (mild). Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Mild realism is the view that at least some of the theoretical entities science talks about, such as electrons, hydrogen atoms, natural selection and economic forces, actually exist in a reality independent of human thought (Discussion 3.2).

2. Role in this unit. The course adopts it as its working view, and it is the dominant view in science. It answers the anti-realist reading of Wheeler's Twenty Questions game.

3. Realist argument. The analogy is only partial. Honest question sequences may lead to the same place, as Schrödinger's and Heisenberg's different formulations of quantum mechanics turned out to be the same theory. And sequences sometimes reach an anomalous question that cannot be answered consistently, which shows that nature resists our constructions.

4. Example. Neptune was predicted from Uranus's orbit and found on the first night of searching in 1846 (Derry ch. 4). It was there before anyone asked about it, which is what realism expects.

5. Distinction. It is "mild" because it claims only that some theoretical entities are real, not that every current theory is literally true; this fits the course's view that scientific knowledge is relative and revisable.

U3-T05Term

Define or distinguish Anti-realism. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Anti-realism is the position that there is no reality other than the one we create in our own minds, and therefore no standard for comparing different belief systems (Discussion 3.2).

2. Source in this unit. It is sometimes argued from Wheeler's modified Twenty Questions game, in which no object is chosen in advance and the "answer" is built up by the questions asked, so a different sequence might yield a different answer.

3. Role in this unit. It is the view the course rejects in favour of mild realism, while admitting that it has supporters in both science and philosophy.

4. Realist reply. The analogy is pushed too far: different honest question sequences in science tend to converge on the same theory, and they sometimes reach anomalous questions that cannot be answered consistently, requiring new assumptions.

5. Example. An anti-realist might say the periodic table is just one way we chose to organize our data. Against this, Mendeleev's table predicted gallium and germanium with properties no one had yet observed (Derry ch. 2), which suggests it captured something real.

U3-T06Term

Define or distinguish Retrograde motion. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Retrograde motion is the way the planets occasionally appear to stop, move backwards against the stars for a while, and then resume their usual direction (Derry ch. 5).

2. Role in this unit. It was the central problem for anyone who believed planets move in perfect circles around the earth, since such planets should always move the same way at a constant rate.

3. Geocentric solution. Eudoxus used sets of nested spheres; Ptolemy put each planet on a small circle (epicycle) moving on a larger circle around the earth, giving a path that loops backwards.

4. Copernican explanation. Retrograde motion is an optical illusion caused by the earth's own motion. In a year the earth goes all the way around the sun while Jupiter moves only a small part of its orbit, so from the earth Jupiter appears to change direction although it does not.

5. Significance. The simpler Copernican explanation of retrograde motion was a major point in favour of heliocentrism, and it is a good example of an apparent deviation from an Ideal of Natural Order being explained away.

U3-T07Term

Define or distinguish Epicycle. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. An epicycle is a small circle on which a planet moves, while the centre of that circle itself moves on a larger circle around the earth (Derry ch. 5).

2. Role in this unit. Epicycles let Ptolemy reproduce retrograde motion and all the observed motions of the sun, moon and five planets using only circular motion, 39 circles in all, as philosophy required.

3. Copernicus also used them. Because the planets do not really move in circles and some Greek observations were wrong, Copernicus had to reintroduce epicycles, about as many as Ptolemy.

4. Example of patching a theory. By the Renaissance, Ptolemy's inaccurate predictions could only be patched by adding more epicycles, a sign of a "tired and decaying system" (Derry ch. 5). Toulmin calls such details adjustments to explain deviations from an ideal of perfect circular motion.

5. Distinction. An epicycle is a geometric device built from circles; Kepler's ellipse replaced the whole system with a single curve per planet that fitted Tycho's data without epicycles.

U3-T08Term

Define or distinguish Stellar parallax. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Stellar parallax is the slight shift in the positions of stars in the sky when they are observed from different points in the earth's orbit, for example six months apart (Discussions 3.2 and 3.3).

2. Role in this unit. The Copernican theory predicted it, but no instrument of the 16th or 17th century could detect it; it was more than 100 years before sufficiently sensitive instruments were developed.

3. Example: Tycho. Because he could not observe stellar parallax, Tycho, an observational astronomer following the best available data, rejected the Copernican theory and proposed his hybrid system.

4. Lesson. It illustrates the pre-experiment question "Is the available equipment capable of detecting the results expected?" and shows that a theory can be adopted even though a predicted effect is not yet observable, as Snow accepted an invisible cholera agent (Discussion 3.4).

5. Related use. Tycho also used the absence of parallax to show that the 1572 new star was not in the atmosphere but among the fixed stars, so the heavens can change (Discussion 3.3).

NoteParallax was first measured by Friedrich Bessel in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni, at about a third of a second of arc, far below the precision of Tycho's naked-eye instruments.

U3-T09Term

Define or distinguish Effluvia. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Effluvia were, in the theory Snow opposed, something given off in the exhalations of patients or by the bodies of the dead that supposedly caused communicable diseases such as cholera (Discussion 3.4).

2. Role in this unit. The effluvia theory was the main competitor to transmission by microscopic living organisms, a germ theory that was then considered highly speculative.

3. Snow's first argument. Everyone in close contact with a victim breathes the effluvia, yet not everyone in such contact gets sick.

4. Snow's second argument. Cholera sometimes breaks out in new areas where no one has been exposed to earlier victims.

5. Example of reasoning. Snow added that since diseases are known to spread in other ways, there was no need to focus on effluvia, and he showed that ingestion of contaminated water explained what effluvia could not: the Broad Street pump cases and the two water companies' death rates.

U3-T10Term

Define or distinguish Perturbation. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. A perturbation is a small disturbance to a system that is treated as a correction to a solution that can be found exactly. In planetary astronomy, the gravity of the other planets is treated as a small perturbation on an orbit calculated using only the sun (Derry ch. 4).

2. Why it is needed. Newton's laws can be solved exactly for at most two interacting bodies; the equations for three or more cannot be solved directly. The sun's great mass makes the planets' pull small, so the approximation works, and it improves as the perturbation gets smaller.

3. Role in this unit. Laplace and others used perturbation methods to work out all the planets' motions, and the predictions fit the observations, until Uranus.

4. Example. By the 1840s Uranus's observed position differed from the perturbation calculations by about 30 seconds of arc. Adams and LeVerrier worked backwards from that discrepancy to the position of an unknown perturbing planet, and Galle found Neptune in 1846.

5. Distinction. The perturbation is the physical cause (an extra small force); the discrepancy is the observed gap between prediction and observation that revealed it.

Applied cases and reasoning12

U3-A01Applied10 marks

Compare pattern recognition, improved instrumentation and discrepancy detection as routes to discovery. Give an assigned example of each and explain what made the observation scientifically significant.

Source Derry Chapters 2 to 4

Derry's Chapters 2 to 4 describe three routes to discovery.

1. Pattern recognition: what it is. Finding an underlying coherence in data that has so far defied understanding, as jigsaw pieces fall into place once the picture is seen (ch. 2).

2. Pattern recognition: example. Mendeleev gathered every known property of every element on cards, arranged them by atomic weight and found a periodic law (1869).

3. Pattern recognition: why significant. The pattern held so much factual detail that it "had to be real," and it made risky predictions: corrected atomic weights for indium, uranium, cerium and titanium, and missing elements later found as gallium (1875) and germanium.

4. Improved instrumentation: what it is. Using instruments to extend our senses into new ranges or create new conditions, such as extreme cold, in which nature shows unsuspected behaviour (ch. 3).

5. Improved instrumentation: example. Leeuwenhoek's hand-ground lenses magnified more than 300 times, and in 1674 he saw in pond water a swarm of tiny creatures no one had ever seen.

6. Improved instrumentation: why significant. It revealed a whole new world: he went on to discover bacteria, spermatozoa and capillaries. Before then microbes "essentially did not exist" in a conceptual sense, and his work began microbiology.

7. Discrepancy detection: what it is. Noticing that a result differs from what accepted ideas predict, and taking the difference seriously instead of dismissing it (ch. 4).

8. Discrepancy detection: example. Rayleigh found nitrogen from air denser than nitrogen from ammonia by about one part in a thousand; chasing the difference led him and Ramsay to argon (1894).

9. Discrepancy detection: why significant. Because his measurements were precise and repeated, the small difference had to be real. It revealed not just one new gas but a new family of inert gases and a new column of the periodic table.

10. Comparison. The routes differ in where the novelty comes from: patterns reorganize facts already known, instruments supply facts that could not be had before, and discrepancies exploit the gap between theory and precise measurement. They are not exclusive: Rayleigh's discrepancy was visible only because of precise instruments, and argon then fitted Mendeleev's pattern. In all three, significance came from a prepared investigator and from consequences that others could test.

U3-A02Applied5 marks

Explain how Mendeleev's pattern organized known elements and generated expectations about missing ones. Why are successful unforeseen consequences stronger than a rearrangement of known facts alone?

Source Derry Chapter 2

1. The pattern. Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic weight and found that chemical and physical properties recur periodically, so chemically similar elements such as the alkali metals fall into the same column (Derry ch. 2).

2. Organizing the known. His intimate knowledge of thousands of facts let him fit most known elements into one system, which made it far more convincing than earlier partial patterns such as Döbereiner's triads or Newlands's octaves, which many skeptics attributed to coincidence.

3. Expectations about the unknown. Where an element did not fit, he claimed the accepted atomic weight was wrong (indium, uranium, cerium, titanium), and where there was a gap he predicted a missing element with its atomic weight and a detailed list of properties (eka-aluminium and eka-silicon). Gallium (1875) and germanium were found with the predicted properties, and his corrected weights were largely verified.

4. Why successful unforeseen consequences are stronger. Any clever person can arrange known facts into some pattern after the fact, and several people did; such a fit could be coincidence or the result of choosing the arrangement to suit the data. A prediction about something not yet observed could easily have failed, so its success is evidence that the pattern reflects reality. It meets the scientific criterion of offering predictions that can be tested, and it was the predictions that convinced chemists: "few could doubt the correctness of the periodic law after this."

5. An even stronger case. The inert gases, starting with argon, were not predicted at all, yet they filled a whole new column with just the right atomic weights. A pattern that absorbs genuinely unforeseen discoveries without being changed is especially strongly confirmed.

U3-A03Applied5 marks

Using continental drift, explain why an attractive pattern may remain scientifically problematic when its proposed mechanism conflicts with other well-established knowledge.

Source Derry Chapter 2

1. The attractive pattern. Wegener saw that the coastlines (properly, the continental shelves) of Africa and South America fit together, and that the geology, fossils and living plants and animals on both sides matched. He also explained why the continents' past climates were so different (Derry ch. 2).

2. The conflicting mechanism. He proposed that small differences in gravity between the poles and the equator, combined with tidal forces, moved the continents. These forces are millions of times too small. Opponents also argued, from established knowledge, that the lower crust is not fluid enough to let the upper crust move.

3. Why that matters. A scientific answer must be consistent with existing theory or give a good reason for changing it (Discussion 3.2). Drift seemed to require forces physics said did not exist, and a rival explanation, sunken land bridges, accounted for the same similarities. So the pattern could be fitted together in more than one way, and most scientists reasonably waited for decisive proof.

4. Where the critics went wrong. Dismissing the whole theory because the mechanism was wrong ignored the large body of empirical evidence Wegener had gathered; the pattern could be real even if his explanation for it was not. Holmes proposed a plausible mechanism, mantle convection, in 1928, but by then drift had been so thoroughly dismissed that few took notice.

5. Resolution. New empirical pieces came from the ocean floor after World War II: young basaltic sea floor, mid-ocean rifts, Hess's sea-floor spreading (around 1960), paleomagnetism showing the continents had moved as Wegener said, and magnetic stripes matching field reversals. In the mid-1960s, Tuzo Wilson and others combined them into plate tectonics. The lesson is that a pattern becomes accepted science when it is joined to a mechanism and to evidence consistent with the rest of knowledge.

U3-A04Applied5 marks

Choose an instrument from Derry's Chapter 3. Explain what became observable, which new questions it made possible and why an instrument reading still requires interpretation.

Source Derry Chapter 3

I choose the radio telescope (Derry ch. 3 §3).

1. What it is. In 1930 Karl Jansky at Bell Laboratories, tracing static on transatlantic radio telephone links, found a faint hiss coming from the Milky Way. A radio telescope is essentially a large antenna that detects these radio waves, which our eyes cannot see at any magnification.

2. What became observable. A whole "radio universe": enormous radio sources and violent jets at the cores of calm-looking galaxies, supernova remnants that are dim in light but bright in radio, pulsars whose radio intensity varies with clockwork regularity, and quasars.

3. New questions. What causes cosmic radio emission? How can a quasar, a source only a few hundred times bigger than our solar system, give off more energy than 100 galaxies? These questions brought radio astronomers, optical astronomers, astrophysicists and general relativity experts together.

4. Why a reading needs interpretation: position. Early radio telescopes gave only blob-like indications of direction, and astronomers ignored them. Only after wartime radar work, much larger antennas and combinations of widely separated antennas improved positional accuracy could a radio source be matched with a visible object.

5. Why a reading needs interpretation: meaning. The first quasar looked through an optical telescope like an ordinary star. Its distance, 4.5 billion light-years, had to be inferred from spectroscopy, Doppler shifts and the expansion of the universe, and its nature from theory: the current consensus is that quasars are supermassive black holes. The instrument records a signal; theory and other instruments turn it into an observation. Kamerlingh Onnes's zero-resistance reading, first taken to be a short circuit, makes the same point.

U3-A05Applied5 marks

Reconstruct how a small discrepancy in nitrogen density led to the investigation of argon. Distinguish recognizing a discrepancy from dismissing it as experimental noise.

Source Derry Chapter 4

1. The discrepancy. Around 1890 Lord Rayleigh was measuring gas densities only to improve their precision. Nitrogen made from air (by removing oxygen and other reactive gases) was denser than nitrogen made by decomposing ammonia, by about one part in a thousand (Derry ch. 4).

2. Testing the obvious explanation. He first assumed the nitrogen itself differed, for example that some was a heavier triatomic molecule, like ozone. But he could not make heavier nitrogen any other way: only nitrogen from the atmosphere was anomalously dense.

3. Finding argon. He then removed the atmospheric nitrogen by chemical reaction and found a small residue of gas that could not be removed. William Ramsay got the same result. The residue was a new gas, much heavier than any known gas and completely unreactive. Measurements of its density, refractive index, solubility and spectrum convinced a skeptical community, and argon (1894) became the first of a new family of inert gases.

4. Recognizing a discrepancy versus dismissing it as noise. Random experimental error scatters results in both directions and shrinks when measurements are repeated.
