A butterfly, for example, begins as an egg, becomes a caterpillar, enters a cocoon, and eventually emerges, as a butterfly that lays eggs. It was believed that this process could be speeded up by an appropriate application of heat under the appropriate conditions. So, for example, beginning with lead one might produce tin, copper, silver, and eventually, gold.

a. What is the ideal of natural order behind this theory?

b. What are some possible means of explaining deviations from this order?

c. What is the basic pattern of explanation that is used?

d. Is there any field today, scientific or otherwise, where this form of theory might apply? If so, what would be the analogue of heat? Of the closed vessel (or "womb") in which the transformations are to take place?

Source Discussions 3.2 and 4.2 (ideals of natural order); Discussion 2.1 (alchemy)

a. The ideal of natural order. Everything in nature develops through definite stages toward its state of perfection, just as an egg becomes a caterpillar, a cocoon and a butterfly. For metals the natural sequence runs from lead through tin, copper and silver to gold, the perfect metal. Development toward perfection is what nature does by itself, so it needs no explanation.

b. Ways of explaining deviations. What needs explaining is a failure to reach perfection, such as lead that stays lead or an experiment that produces nothing. An alchemist could say that:

1. the process was not complete (not enough time had passed) or was interrupted;

2. the heat was wrong: too much, too little or uneven;

3. the materials were impure, or the vessel was contaminated or not properly sealed;

4. the stages were carried out in the wrong order or at the wrong time, for example under unfavourable astrological conditions;

5. on the spiritual reading of alchemy that Discussion 2.1 attributes to Jung and Burkhardt, the alchemist was not inwardly prepared or pure.

c. The pattern of explanation. It is developmental and teleological: a thing is explained by its place in a sequence of stages leading to a final goal. Change is maturation, and heat in a closed vessel speeds it up, just as warmth in an egg or womb nurtures a growing embryo. Like Newton's framework, it explains deviations from a natural course, but the natural course is growth toward an end rather than motion in a straight line.

d. Fields where this form of theory might apply today.

1. Education and personal development. Learners pass through stages from novice to master. The heat is effort, challenge and practice; the vessel is the school, apprenticeship or mentoring relationship that contains and protects the learner. This matches Jung's reading of alchemy as personal transformation (Discussion 2.1).

2. Psychotherapy. The heat is the emotional intensity of the work; the vessel is the confidential therapeutic relationship, which must be "sealed" for transformation to occur.

3. Embryonic development and incubation. Here the analogy is literal: the heat is body or incubator temperature and the vessel is the womb or egg.

4. Stellar nucleosynthesis. It is a real transmutation of elements: the heat is the enormous temperature and pressure inside a star, the vessel is the star held together by its own gravity, and light elements are built up into heavier ones.

NoteIn each case the analogy only organizes ideas; whether it explains anything must be tested independently. Turning lead into gold by ordinary heating is impossible because heating affects only chemical bonds, not the nucleus. Elements were shown to change only with the discovery of radioactivity around 1900 (Derry ch. 14).

Learning objective drills7

U4-OBJ01Objective

Describe the top-down and bottom-up approaches to science, including some of the ways each approach is used, and some of the difficulties with them.

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 1

Discussion 4.1 says the subjects of science are almost always systems, which can be studied in two complementary ways.

1. Bottom-up approach. Begin with the most basic components and how they interact and fit together, and try to understand the properties of the whole from those interactions.

2. Uses of bottom-up. Chemistry explains the properties of compounds by their molecular and atomic composition; elementary particle physics works this way; and medicine understands many diseases as the malfunction of a particular organ, group of cells or gene.

3. Top-down approach. Assume the system must satisfy certain constraints, from general laws of nature or to maintain its integrity as a system, and ask what conditions those constraints impose on the components and their interactions.

4. Uses of top-down. Symmetry, optimality and conservation principles are applied this way. Human physiology has feedback mechanisms keeping body temperature, heart rate, blood sugar and blood pressure within acceptable ranges, so it is reasonable to assume that the need for survival imposes anatomical and physiological conditions on the body.

5. Difficulties with bottom-up. It is often unclear how systemic properties emerge from the parts: nothing in hydrogen and oxygen tells us water will be wet. It can also leave a mass of data with no unified picture, as when science is studied only through the activities of individual scientists, journals, conferences and instruments.

6. Difficulties with top-down. It is often unclear which principle is appropriate, and a vague principle can impose wrong requirements: if health means no pain we focus on painkillers, if it means looking healthy we focus on cosmetic surgery. Starting from an ideal of what science is for produces a unified system that may bear little resemblance to reality.

7. Together. Neither alone gives a complete picture. Their complementary use is "perhaps the fundamental process involved in scientific reasoning," as in Mendeleev's periodic table, built from thousands of facts and then used as a constraint to correct atomic weights and predict new elements (Derry ch. 2).

U4-OBJ02Objective

State the difference between "formal purpose" and "functional purpose," and identify at least three different functional purposes of science.

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 2

1. Formal purpose. What a thing is for in itself, the end that defines the activity. For science, Discussion 4.1 says the best statement of formal purpose is "to understand the world rationally."

2. Functional purpose. The role the activity serves in a wider context of human activity and development. It depends on the viewpoint from which we evaluate science and invites us to think teleologically.

3. Aristotle's example (footnote 67). For a bow and arrow, the formal purpose is to project the arrow far enough and hard enough to embed it in a target; the functional purpose is our choice of target and why we want to shoot at it.

4. Functional purposes of science (Discussion 4.1 lists nine):

a. to free people from fear (Epicurus; Halley's comet; the eradication of smallpox);

b. to free people from drudgery and repetitive labour;

c. to provide leisure and vehicles for personal self-expression;

d. to provide a vehicle of personal development (Lecomte du Noüy; the athlete analogy);

e. to attain understanding of ourselves and the world;

f. to improve human health and security;

g. to provide a basis for standards of moral and ethical conduct, and social regulation;

h. to foster social cohesion and interaction through a basis of commonly accepted knowledge;

i. to provide means of defining and attaining ideals.

5. The relation. The functional purposes depend on the formal one: technology, health and freedom from fear are by-products of understanding. A corporation funds research for profit, which is a functional view based on social utility, but this does not define what science itself is.

U4-OBJ03Objective

Provide a general definition of "conceptual framework," and describe how conceptual frameworks are related to points of view.

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 3

1. Definition. A conceptual framework is the context within which meaning arises (Discussion 4.2). It is the set of concepts, assumptions and ideals through which we look at and interpret the world. Kuhn calls such frameworks paradigms.

2. What it contains. Assumptions about how to reason and interpret evidence, and ideals of natural order, which say what needs no explanation.

3. What it does. It determines how we go about looking and how we interpret what we see, and which questions are important and which answers are significant.

4. Point of view. Point of view relates to our attitude and to our willingness to look without fear (Discussion 1.1). It concerns whether and how openly we look. Meaning is relative to point of view: the cross means something very different to Christians than it did to the ancient Romans.

5. How they are related. Both shape meaning, but at different levels. Point of view is the attitude with which we approach things; the framework is the conceptual equipment we use once we look. An open, unafraid point of view makes it possible to examine and revise our framework, while a fearful one clings to it.

6. Example. Tycho and Kepler watching the sunrise (Hanson) both looked carefully and honestly, so neither had a fearful point of view, but their frameworks differed: Tycho saw the sun moving around the earth, Kepler saw the earth turning, and so they asked different questions.

U4-OBJ04Objective

Define understanding in science in terms of conceptual frameworks.

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 4

1. Definition. "To understand something means to be able to interpret it within a conceptual framework, and to experience intuitively the validity of the interpretation, to see that it is a good fit" (Discussion 4.2).

2. Two parts. An analytical part (fitting the thing into the framework by rational argument) and an intuitive part (grasping that the fit is right). Without the intuitive part we are only playing with words, as Rota's mathematician who can verify a theorem but asks "What is this good for?" shows.

3. Explanation. To explain something is to show how it fits within a conceptual framework. Explanation and understanding are always relative to a particular framework.

4. Ideals of natural order. A scientific framework rests on ideals of natural order that say what needs no explanation; scientific explanation accounts for deviations from them (Unit 4 Overview).

5. Scientific constraints. In science the framework must be internally consistent (coherence) and allow experimental testing with conclusions that correspond to observation (correspondence).

6. Epistemé. The Greek word for this kind of understanding, from epistanai, "to stand upon": knowledge that stands on a secure conceptual framework.

7. Formal purpose restated. To say that science aims to understand the world rationally is to say it aims to develop conceptual frameworks within which observed aspects of the world can be rationalized.

U4-OBJ05Objective

State the difference between "prediction" and "explanation," or "forecasting" and "understanding."

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 5

1. Prediction (forecasting). Saying what will happen, for example where a planet will be on a given night or when an eclipse will occur. It can be done from regularities in past records without knowing why they hold.

2. Explanation (understanding). Showing why something happens by fitting it into a conceptual framework, and grasping intuitively that the fit is right (Discussion 4.2).

3. Toulmin's example. The Babylonians predicted planetary positions and eclipses excellently but attributed the motions to gods acting for unknown reasons, so they had forecasting without understanding. The early Greeks predicted less accurately but placed the motions in a system of circles around the earth, so they had understanding with weaker forecasting (Discussion 4.1).

4. Which is the goal. Toulmin argues that understanding is the purpose of science and that the predictivist thesis, that the goal of science is accurate prediction, is secondary.

5. How they relate. Good understanding normally yields predictions, and testable predictions are a key way of checking a theory (Derry ch. 14). Laplace notes that Newton's theory let Halley predict his comet's return, turning fear into interest. But prediction can exist without understanding, and an understanding is valuable even before it predicts better, as with early Copernicanism.

U4-OBJ06Objective

Describe the Aristotelian ideals of natural order in dynamics, planetary motion and the theory of matter, and contrast them to the ideals of natural order introduced by Galileo (in dynamics), Newton (in dynamics and planetary motion), and 18th century chemists (in the theory of matter).

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 6

An ideal of natural order defines what needs no explanation; only deviations from it need explaining (Discussion 4.2).

Aristotle

1. Dynamics. On earth the natural state of a body is rest at its natural place; a heavy body left free falls toward it (and a light one rises). Any other ("violent") motion is unnatural and needs a mover acting on the body for as long as it moves (Derry ch. 5).

2. Planetary motion. The celestial bodies are carried by crystal spheres whose uniform circular motion is natural and eternal. The heavens are perfect and changeless and obey different laws from the earth, which sits at rest at the centre.

3. Matter. Everything is made from four elements, earth, water, air and fire, defined by the paired qualities hot or cold and wet or dry (the Greek cross in Discussion 11.2). By changing a quality, one element can turn into another, so transmutation is natural, which made the alchemists' aim of turning lead into gold reasonable within this framework.

The new ideals

4. Galileo (dynamics). Motion does not need a continuing mover: a body once moving keeps moving unless something stops it. Derry notes that he took this natural motion to be circular. He also insisted that the same laws hold on earth and in the heavens.

5. Newton (dynamics). Rest and uniform straight-line motion are natural (the first law). Only a change of speed or direction needs explaining, by a force, a = F/m. Slowing to rest, which Aristotle thought natural, now needs a cause such as friction.

6. Newton (planetary motion). The same laws apply everywhere. A planet's ellipse is not natural; it is a deviation from straight-line motion explained by the sun's inverse-square gravitational force, and these laws give all three of Kepler's laws (Derry ch. 5).

7. 18th-century chemists (matter). Following Lavoisier (1789), an element is a substance that cannot be broken down or changed into anything else (Derry chs. 2 and 14), and matter is conserved in chemical change. Permanence is now natural; what needs explaining is any apparent change, such as the gain in weight when a metal burns, which Lavoisier explained as combination with oxygen rather than loss of phlogiston (Derry ch. 14).

8. The contrast. In every case what Aristotle treated as natural (rest, celestial circles, transmutation) became something to explain, and the new ideals were more abstract: straight-line motion and immutable elements are rarely, if ever, observed directly. The element ideal itself was later overturned when radioactivity showed elements changing into one another around 1900.

NoteDiscussions 3.2 and 4.2 state the Newtonian ideal directly. The Aristotelian and Galilean dynamics come from Derry Chapter 5, the four elements from Discussion 11.2, and the chemists' ideal from Derry Chapters 2 and 14. Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass is standard history of chemistry that the course text does not state in those words.

U4-OBJ07Objective

Describe the distinction between "physiology" and "pathology" in terms of ideals of natural order.

Source Unit 4 Overview objective 7

1. Physiology studies the normal functioning of a living organism. It plays the role of the ideal of natural order: the healthy working of the body is what we expect and needs no special explanation.

2. Example of the ideal. Discussion 4.1 notes that human physiology contains feedback mechanisms that keep body temperature, heart rate, blood sugar and blood pressure within acceptable ranges. Staying within those ranges is the natural order.

3. Pathology studies disease, that is, deviations from the normal physiological state. These are what require explanation.

4. Explaining deviations. Pathology explains a departure from normal function by causes such as infection, the malfunction of a particular organ, group of cells or gene (Discussion 4.1), or injury.

5. The parallel with physics. Just as Newtonian physics treats uniform straight-line motion as natural and explains deviations by forces, medicine treats physiological balance as natural and explains illness by pathological causes.

6. A caution. The ideal must be defined carefully. Deciding what counts as "normal" or "healthy" is a top-down difficulty: if health means only the absence of pain, attention goes to painkillers; if it means appearance, to cosmetic surgery (Discussion 4.1).

NoteThe course readings do not spell out this objective in a separate passage. The answer applies the ideals-of-natural-order idea (Discussions 3.2 and 4.2) to the medical examples in Discussion 4.1.

Lists and concept recall5

U4-R01Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Top-down and bottom-up approaches to systems. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Top-down and bottom-up approaches to systems (Discussion 4.1)

1. Systems. The subjects of science are almost always systems: complex units of diverse parts that exchange molecules, energy or information and are more or less segregated from their surroundings. Changing one part can have unforeseen effects on others and on the whole (Discussion 4.1).

2. Bottom-up. Start from the basic components and how they interact, and explain the properties of the whole from them, as chemistry explains compounds by their atoms.

3. Top-down. Start from constraints the whole must satisfy, from general laws or to keep its integrity, and ask what they require of the parts, as in symmetry, optimality and conservation principles or the body's feedback mechanisms.

4. Example. Mendeleev used both: thousands of facts about individual elements led him to the periodic law, and he then used the law as a constraint to correct atomic weights and predict gallium and germanium. The pattern was later explained bottom-up from atomic structure by Bohr and Pauli (Derry ch. 2).

5. Significance. Each approach has its own blind spot (emergence for bottom-up, choosing the right principle for top-down), so their complementary use is "perhaps the fundamental process involved in scientific reasoning."

U4-R02Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Formal and functional purpose. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Formal and functional purpose (Discussion 4.1)

1. Origin. The distinction between formal and functional purposes was worked out by Aristotle (Discussion 4.1, footnote 67).

2. Formal purpose. What a thing is for in itself. For a bow and arrow, it is to project the arrow with enough force to embed itself in a target. For science, it is "to understand the world rationally."

3. Functional purpose. The role the thing plays in a wider context. For the bow, it is our choice of target and why we want to shoot at it. For science, it is the purposes science serves in human life and cultural evolution, such as freeing people from fear or improving health.

4. Example. Halley's comet: the formal achievement was understanding comets through Newton's gravitation; the functional result, as Laplace said, was that fear of comets as omens gave way to scientific interest.

5. Significance. The distinction shows that the question "what is the purpose of science?" has different answers depending on perspective. Judging science only by functional by-products, such as technology or corporate profit, misses what science itself aims at, while the formal purpose explains why science can serve so many functional ends.

U4-R03Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Nine functional purposes of science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Nine functional purposes of science (Discussion 4.1)

Discussion 4.1 lists these functional purposes of science, saying that what is taken as the purpose of science is relative to the perspective from which we evaluate it:

1. to free people from fear;

2. to free people from drudgery and repetitive labour;

3. to provide leisure and vehicles for personal self-expression;

4. to provide a vehicle of personal development;

5. to attain understanding of ourselves and the world;

6. to improve human health and security;

7. to provide a basis for standards of moral and ethical conduct, and social regulation;

8. to foster social cohesion and interaction through a basis of commonly accepted knowledge;

9. to provide means of defining and attaining ideals.

Example. The eradication of smallpox, announced by the World Health Organization in 1980, served purposes 1 and 6 at once.

Significance. These are functional purposes, distinct from the single formal purpose, "to understand the world rationally," on which they all depend. Listing them reminds us that the value of science is wider than technology; Discussion 4.1 says we are "distracted by the obvious" material benefits and scarcely notice how well science has freed us from fear.

U4-R04Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: The fear chain. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source The fear chain (Discussion 4.1)

1. The chain. Discussion 4.1 states a psychological truism: Ignorance → Fear → Belief.

2. How it works. We fear what we are ignorant of; to control the fear we create a belief; and we attack anyone who questions that belief with a ferocity proportional to the underlying fear. History is full of fanaticism and atrocities in defence of such beliefs.

3. Example. When the great comet of 1682 appeared, Kino read it as a sign of droughts, wars, epidemics and the deaths of prominent people. After Newton and Halley, Laplace could say that knowledge of the laws of the system of the world had dissipated the fears born of ignorance.

4. The remedy. The way out is a cool, detached point of view that suspends judgement on all beliefs, the "inductive" attitude, which lets us admit ignorance and begin to reason. Marie Curie: "Nothing in life is to be feared. It is only to be understood."

5. Significance. Philosophy helps us face ignorance without fear, and science supplies the most effective known method for gaining publicly verifiable knowledge. This explains Epicurus's claim that the purpose of science and philosophy is "to free man from fear," and it is a warning that scientists too react defensively when their own deeply held beliefs are questioned.

U4-R05Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Understanding in science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Understanding in science (Discussion 4.2)

1. Definition. To understand something is to be able to interpret it within a conceptual framework and to experience intuitively that the interpretation is valid, that it is a good fit (Discussion 4.2).

2. Conceptual framework. The context within which meaning arises, Kuhn's paradigm. It determines which questions are important, how we interpret what we see, and through its ideals of natural order what needs no explanation.

3. Scientific standards. The framework must be coherent (internally consistent) and correspond to observation and experiment. Knowledge that stands on such a framework is epistemé, "to stand upon."

4. Example. Tycho and Kepler saw the same sunrise but understood it within different frameworks. It is unfair to say Tycho did not understand the planets; his understanding rested on a framework that later proved wrong, partly because of his own observations.

5. Significance. Explanation is always relative to a framework, so the same data can be explained in rival frameworks and must be judged by further evidence and fertility. Understanding also needs the intuitive part: Rota's mathematician can verify a theorem yet miss its sense, and people who only manipulate words give a false impression of understanding.

Key term questions8

U4-T01Term

Define or distinguish System. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. A system is a complex unit made up of diverse parts that exchange something (molecules, energy, information) and that is more or less segregated from its surroundings (Discussion 4.1).

2. Key property. Changing one of its parts can have consequences, often unforeseen, for other parts and for the system as a whole.

3. Role in this unit. The subjects of science are almost always systems, which is why the unit introduces the bottom-up approach (from components) and the top-down approach (from constraints on the whole).

4. Example. The human body is a system whose feedback mechanisms keep temperature, heart rate, blood sugar and blood pressure within acceptable ranges. The solar system is another: Newton explained it by the interaction of its parts, the sun's gravity acting on each planet.

5. Distinction. A system differs from a mere collection or heap of parts because its parts interact. Poincaré's remark that a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house makes the same point about knowledge (Derry ch. 2).

U4-T02Term

Define or distinguish Bottom-up / top-down. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Bottom-up. Begin with the most basic components of a system and how they interact and fit together, and try to understand the properties of the whole from them (Discussion 4.1).

2. Top-down. Begin with constraints the system must satisfy, from general laws of nature or to maintain its integrity, and ask what conditions they impose on the components.

3. Role in this unit. They are complementary views of systems; their combined use is "perhaps the fundamental process involved in scientific reasoning." The distinction reappears throughout the course.

4. Example. Bottom-up: chemistry explains the properties of compounds by their atoms, and medicine treats a disease as the malfunction of an organ, cells or a gene. Top-down: conservation and symmetry principles, and assuming that survival imposes conditions on the body's anatomy and physiology.

5. Typical weaknesses. Bottom-up struggles with emergence (water's wetness is not obvious from hydrogen and oxygen); top-down may choose the wrong principle (defining health as no pain leads to painkillers).

U4-T03Term

Define or distinguish Formal / functional purpose. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Formal purpose. What a thing is for in itself. For science, "to understand the world rationally" (Discussion 4.1).

2. Functional purpose. The role a thing plays in a wider context of human activity, such as freeing people from fear, improving health or providing a vehicle for personal development.

3. Example. Aristotle's bow and arrow (footnote 67): its formal purpose is to send the arrow into a target with enough force to embed it; its functional purpose is the choice of target and why we shoot.

4. Role in this unit. The distinction lets the unit answer "what is the purpose of science?" at two levels: understanding is the formal aim, while the functional purposes vary with the viewpoint, such as Epicurus's "to free man from fear" or social utility.

5. Distinction in use. Defining science by a functional by-product, such as technology or profit, confuses the two. The functional purposes depend on the formal one, since freedom from fear of comets came from understanding them.

U4-T04Term

Define or distinguish Predictivist thesis. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The predictivist thesis is the view in philosophy of science that the goal of science is to make accurate, successful predictions (Discussion 4.1; Unit 4 Study Question 4).

2. Role in this unit. It is the rival to the course's view that the formal purpose of science is understanding. Toulmin argues it is secondary to the goal of providing a means of understanding the world.

3. Example. Babylonian astronomers predicted planetary positions and eclipses excellently, yet attributed the motions to the gods; the early Greeks predicted less well but understood the motions as circles around the earth. On the predictivist thesis the Babylonians would count as the better scientists, which seems wrong.

4. What it gets right. Predictions matter as tests: falsifiable predictions expose a theory to refutation, and successful predictions of unforeseen results, such as Mendeleev's gallium and germanium, are a criterion of a good theory (Derry chs. 2 and 14).

5. Limitation. A forecasting rule may work without any understanding of why, and a theory may be worth keeping despite a failed prediction (stellar parallax and Copernicus, Derry ch. 14).

U4-T05Term

Define or distinguish Conceptual framework. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. A conceptual framework is the context within which meaning arises. It determines how we go about looking and how we interpret what we see (Discussion 4.2). Kuhn calls it a paradigm.

2. Contents. Assumptions about how to reason and interpret evidence, and ideals of natural order that say what needs no explanation.

3. Role in this unit. Understanding in science is defined in terms of it: to understand is to interpret something within a framework and see intuitively that it fits; to explain is to show how something fits.

4. Example. Tycho and Kepler watching the same sunrise (Hanson): within Tycho's geocentric framework the sun rose; within Kepler's heliocentric framework the earth turned. Their frameworks led to different questions, kinematic circles versus a central force.

5. Distinction. A point of view is our attitude and willingness to look without fear; a framework is the conceptual equipment that determines how we look and interpret.

U4-T06Term

Define or distinguish Ideals of natural order. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

Use a specific example from the Unit 4 readings and explain one limitation or possible misunderstanding of the idea.

1. Definition. Ideals of natural order are assumptions about how nature behaves when nothing interferes. Phenomena that follow them need no explanation; only deviations do (Toulmin, Discussions 3.2 and 4.2).

2. Role in this unit. They are basic elements of a conceptual framework that ground theoretical work by telling us what does not need to be explained (Unit 4 Overview), and so they shape which questions scientists ask.

3. Example from the readings. In Newtonian physics, rest and uniform straight-line motion are natural. A planet's curved orbit is a deviation, explained by the force of gravity. For the Greeks the planets' natural motion was a perfect circle, and Ptolemy's epicycles explained deviations such as retrograde motion (Discussion 3.2, Derry ch. 5).

4. Contrast. Different frameworks have different ideals: Aristotle took rest on earth as natural, so continued motion needed a mover; Newton took uniform motion as natural, so only change of motion needs a force.

5. A limitation or misunderstanding. It is easy to think an ideal of natural order is a fact about nature that must be true. It is an assumption of the framework, and it can be over-extended. Discussion 4.2 warns that the Newtonian ideal of equilibrium disturbed by external forces, carried into social and psychological life, wrongly suggests that systems cannot change from within, so that individuals are not responsible for their actions and institutions can change only by being overthrown from outside. Systems with their own inner dynamics, such as ecosystems, do not fit it.

U4-T07Term

Define or distinguish Epistemé. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Epistemé is the ancient Greek word for understanding: knowledge that stands upon a secure conceptual framework. It comes from epistanai, "to stand upon," and gives us the word epistemology, the study of knowledge (Discussion 4.2).

2. What qualifies. Such knowledge can be supported by rational arguments showing its coherence with the basic assumptions and axioms of a framework. In science the framework itself must also be logically coherent and agree with empirical observation.

3. Role in this unit. It names the kind of understanding science seeks, so the formal purpose "to understand the world rationally" means building frameworks that satisfy both coherence and correspondence.

4. Distinction. Discussion 6.1 contrasts epistemé with tekhné (practical skill, proved by performance) and gnosis (intuitive apprehension of truth). Discussion 4.2 adds that real understanding also needs the intuitive grasp of fit.

5. Example. Newton's explanation of planetary orbits is epistemé: Kepler's laws follow by rational argument from the framework of the laws of motion and gravitation, and the framework agrees with observation.

U4-T08Term

Define or distinguish Teleological. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Teleological explanation explains something by its purpose, goal or end (Greek telos) rather than by prior causes.

2. Role in this unit. Discussion 4.1 says that using "purpose" in the functional sense "invites us to think teleologically," asking what purpose science serves in the wider context of human activity, ultimately the purpose of human life.

3. Example. The alchemists' theory (Study Question 8) is teleological: lead becomes tin, copper, silver and finally gold because all nature strives toward perfection, as an egg develops into a butterfly.

4. Contrast. Newtonian explanation is not teleological: a planet's orbit is explained by inertia and the force of gravity, not by a goal the planet is trying to reach.

5. A caution. Teleology is natural when asking about human purposes, such as why society should support science, but projecting goals onto inanimate nature, as the alchemists did, assumes what needs to be shown.

Applied cases and reasoning12

U4-A01Applied5 marks

A scientist studies a bird by modelling its component tissues; another begins with constraints on flight and whole-body function. Identify the two approaches and explain how each could help or mislead.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Identify. Modelling the bird from its component tissues is the bottom-up approach. Starting from constraints on flight and whole-body function is the top-down approach (Discussion 4.1).

2. How bottom-up helps. It shows how particular structures work, such as how hollow bones, flight muscles and feathers each contribute, and it can locate the cause of a malfunction in a particular tissue, as medicine does with organs, cells or genes.

3. How bottom-up can mislead. Whole-body properties may not be visible in the parts. Just as nothing in hydrogen and oxygen tells us water is wet, a perfect model of muscle and feather tissue need not reveal how the bird balances, steers or migrates, and the details may pile up without a unified picture.

4. How top-down helps. Constraints that any flying body must satisfy, such as producing enough lift to support its weight, keeping weight low and supplying enough power, tell us what the tissues must be like, much as the need for survival imposes conditions on human anatomy and physiology. It explains why features exist.

5. How top-down can mislead, and the remedy. If the scientist picks the wrong governing principle, say flight speed when the bird's survival depends on efficient long-distance gliding or diving, the model imposes inappropriate requirements and may bear little resemblance to the real bird. The best account combines both: constraints guide which tissue details matter, and tissue data check whether the assumed constraints are the real ones.

U4-A02Applied5 marks

Explain how a successful account of a system can combine bottom-up components with top-down constraints rather than requiring an exclusive choice between the two.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. The claim. Discussion 4.1 says neither approach alone gives a complete picture; their complementary use is perhaps the fundamental process of scientific reasoning, so a good account of a system usually contains both.

2. The roles divide naturally. Top-down constraints say what the whole must achieve; bottom-up components say how it is achieved. Each covers the other's typical weakness: constraints supply the unity that a pile of component data lacks, and components check whether an assumed constraint really holds.

3. Physiology example. The body must keep its temperature within a narrow range (a top-down constraint from survival). The account is completed by the components that do it: sensing, sweating, shivering and changes in blood flow, linked in a feedback loop.

4. Planetary example. Kepler's three laws describe the whole system's regular pattern. Newton explained them from the interaction of components, each planet's inertia and the sun's inverse-square gravity, and showed that his laws yield all three of Kepler's laws (Derry ch. 5). Conservation principles used in mechanics are themselves top-down constraints that the component motions must satisfy.

5. Periodic table example. Mendeleev's periodic law acted as a constraint on the whole set of elements, strong enough to correct atomic weights and predict new elements; the components (atomic structure, Bohr and Pauli) later explained why the law holds (Derry ch. 2). The two levels are not rivals but two parts of one explanation.

U4-A03Applied5 marks

Use the development of the periodic table to distinguish organizing data under a whole-system pattern from explaining the pattern through components.

Source Discussion 4.1 and Derry Chapter 2

1. Organizing under a whole-system pattern. Mendeleev arranged all the known elements by atomic weight and found that their properties recur periodically, so families such as the alkali metals and halogens fall into columns. The periodic law is a pattern of the whole set of elements, built from thousands of facts on his cards (Derry ch. 2).

2. What the pattern could do without explanation. Used as a constraint on the whole, it corrected the atomic weights of indium, uranium, cerium and titanium and predicted the properties of undiscovered elements; gallium (1875) and germanium matched. It later absorbed the unforeseen inert gases as a new column.

3. What it could not do. It did not say why the properties recur. Derry is explicit: "Mendeleev was not the first to note these regularities and did not explain them." It is a powerful organization and a source of predictions, but on its own it is closer to a law than to an explanation.

4. Explaining through components. After Mendeleev's death, Bohr, Pauli and others explained the periodicity from the structure of atoms: the arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus determines how an element bonds, so elements with similar outer electron arrangements behave alike. This is a bottom-up explanation of a top-down pattern.

5. The distinction. Organizing tells us what goes together and lets us predict; explaining shows how the pattern arises from the parts and so where its exceptions come from. Atomic theory explained, for example, why tellurium comes before iodine despite its slightly greater atomic weight: the true ordering quantity is atomic number, not weight.

NoteThe tellurium and iodine example and the description of electron shells are standard chemistry from outside the Unit 4 readings; Derry refers only to the explanation by Bohr and Pauli in Chapter 18.

U4-A04Applied5 marks

An accurate forecasting rule gives no account of why events occur. Evaluate whether this alone achieves the formal purpose of science in this course.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. The formal purpose. Discussion 4.1 states the formal purpose of science as "to understand the world rationally," which means interpreting phenomena within a conceptual framework and seeing that the fit is good (Discussion 4.2). A rule that gives no account of why events occur does not do that, so on its own it does not achieve the formal purpose.

2. Historical precedent. The Babylonians had exactly such rules: excellent predictions of planetary positions and eclipses, with the motions attributed to gods acting for unknown reasons. Toulmin uses them to show that prediction is secondary to understanding.

3. Practical weaknesses. Without knowing why the rule works, we cannot tell when conditions have changed enough for it to fail, cannot extend it to new cases and cannot connect it with other knowledge. Ptolemy's epicycles predicted adequately for centuries within a framework that turned out to be wrong.

4. What it does contribute. An accurate rule is valuable. It serves functional purposes such as navigation and calendar reform, and it can be a stepping stone: Kepler's laws were precise regularities that Newton later explained by gravitation (Derry ch. 5). It also supplies testable predictions, which help check any theory proposed to explain it.

5. Evaluation. The forecasting rule is a useful achievement and often a necessary step, but it reaches the formal purpose only when it is placed within a conceptual framework that shows why the events occur.

U4-A05Applied5 marks

Explain why a functional benefit such as improved health does not by itself define the formal purpose of science. Show how the two purposes can nevertheless support one another.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. The distinction. Formal purpose is what science is for in itself, "to understand the world rationally"; improving health is one of its functional purposes, a role it serves in the wider human context (Discussion 4.1).

2. Why health cannot define it. If science were defined by health benefits, any remedy that made people feel better, such as a folk cure or a placebo, would count as science, while research with no medical use, such as astronomy or the periodic table, would not. Health is an outcome that many activities can produce; what makes science distinctive is the rational understanding behind its results.

3. The bow and arrow. The formal purpose of a bow is to send the arrow accurately into a target; which target we choose is functional (footnote 67). Health is one possible target, and the same understanding can serve others, including bad ones, which footnote 69 acknowledges as technological abuse.

4. How understanding supports health. Medicine treats physiology as the normal order and explains disease as deviations caused by a particular organ, cells or gene, which lets it target treatment. The eradication of smallpox, announced in 1980, depended on understanding infection and immunity, not just on hope.

5. How health supports understanding. Health problems raise new questions that drive inquiry. Snow's study of cholera (Unit 3) sought a way to stop deaths and produced new understanding of how the disease spreads. Each purpose feeds the other, but understanding remains the defining one.

U4-A06Applied5 marks

Use the contrasting responses to Halley's comet in Discussion 4.1 to explain how scientific understanding can change the relation between ignorance, fear and belief.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. The fear chain. Discussion 4.1 states the truism Ignorance → Fear → Belief: we fear what we do not understand, invent a belief to control the fear, and defend it fiercely.

2. Before understanding. After the great comet of 1682 appeared, the Jesuit Kino wrote that it threatened droughts, hunger, earthquakes, wars, epidemics and the deaths of prominent people, and that because it was so large and lasted so long its evil would be universal and long-lasting. Ignorance of what comets are produced fear, which was organized into a belief in comets as omens. Laplace notes that the comet of 1456 had "spread terror throughout Europe."

3. After understanding. Laplace explains that knowledge of "the laws of the system of the world," Newton's universal gravitation, dissipated those fears. Halley recognized the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 as one object and predicted its return for late 1758 or early 1759. The learned world awaited it "with impatience" as a confirmation of science.

4. What changed. The fear was not replaced by a new comforting belief but by understanding: the comet became a natural object following the same laws as the planets, so its appearance carried no message about human crimes. The belief lost its function because the ignorance that fed the fear was gone, illustrating Epicurus's "to free man from fear" and Marie Curie's "Nothing in life is to be feared. It is only to be understood."

5. A qualification. A cynic might say science has replaced old fears with new ones, such as pollution or nuclear war. But those fears are more realistic and can themselves be studied and addressed; the cynic forgets the "dustheap of ancient fears" science has removed.

U4-A07Applied5 marks

Two observers agree on what an instrument displays but disagree on what it means. Explain how conceptual frameworks can account for the disagreement and how it might be investigated.

Source Discussion 4.2

1. Same observation, different frameworks. Discussion 4.2 says the framework determines how we look and how we interpret what we see. Two observers can agree on the instrument reading, the observation, and still understand it differently because they read it within different conceptual frameworks.

2. Example. Hanson's Tycho and Kepler see the same sunrise: Tycho interprets it as the sun moving around the earth, Kepler as the earth turning. Similarly, two doctors may agree that a thermometer reads 38.5 °C, and one may interpret it as a fever signalling infection while the other treats it as normal after hard exercise, because they hold different ideals of what is normal for this patient.

3. Why the disagreement persists. The same data can often be explained within two or more frameworks, each with its own ideals of natural order and its own sense of what needs explaining. Neither observer is necessarily making an error in reading the instrument.

4. How to investigate. First make the frameworks explicit, since Bateson notes scientists should know and state their presuppositions (Discussion 4.1). Then find a consequence on which the frameworks differ and test it: in the doctors' case, measure again after rest. For heliocentrism, such tests were the phases of Venus and, much later, stellar parallax (Derry chs. 5 and 14).

5. Further checks. The instrument's own theory may need examining, since the Quine-Duhem thesis notes that instruments operate according to theories (Derry ch. 14). If the data still cannot decide, other factors such as coherence and fertility, which questions each framework opens, help decide, as when Copernicanism won (Discussion 4.2).

U4-A08Applied10 marks

Contrast what needs explanation in Aristotelian terrestrial motion and in Newtonian motion. Explain how a changed ideal of natural order changes the questions scientists ask.

Source Discussion 4.2 and Unit 4 Objective 6

What needs explanation: Aristotle

1. The ideal. On earth the natural state of a body is rest at its natural place; heavy bodies fall toward the centre and light ones rise (Derry ch. 5). Natural motion needs no further explanation.

2. What must be explained. Any other, "violent" motion needs a mover acting on the body for as long as it moves. A cart keeps moving only while it is pushed; when the push stops it comes to rest, which is natural.

3. The question it generates. "What keeps this body moving?" For a thrown stone, which keeps flying after leaving the hand, an Aristotelian had to find a mover, such as the air pushing it along.

What needs explanation: Newton

4. The ideal. Rest and uniform straight-line motion are natural (the first law) and need no explanation (Discussions 3.2 and 4.2).

5. What must be explained. Any change of speed or direction, an acceleration, requires an external force: a = F/m.

6. The question it generates. "What changes this body's motion?" The thrown stone needs no mover to keep going, but its curved path and its eventual stop must be explained, by gravity and air resistance.

How the changed ideal changes the questions

7. Slowing down becomes a problem. For Aristotle, a rolling ball coming to rest is natural; for Newton it is a deviation demanding a cause, so friction and air resistance are recognized as forces to be studied.

8. Falling becomes a problem. For Aristotle, an apple falls because it seeks its natural place, so there is nothing more to ask. For Newton, the fall is an acceleration and requires a force, and asking what that force is led to universal gravitation, the same force that holds the moon and planets.

9. Earth and heavens unite. Aristotle had separate laws for the changeless heavens, where circular motion was natural. Under Newton's ideal a planet's curved orbit is a deviation from straight-line motion, so the question becomes what force bends it, answered by the sun's inverse-square gravity, which gives Kepler's laws (Derry ch. 5).

10. The lesson. Nature did not change; the baseline of what counts as normal changed, and with it what scientists measure (acceleration rather than mere velocity), which causes they look for, and which questions seem worth asking. Newton's ideal is more abstract, since uniform straight-line motion is almost never actually seen, yet it is far more fertile.

U4-A09Applied5 marks

Explain how an ideal of natural order helps distinguish physiology from pathology. Why must the assumed normal condition be examined rather than treated as self-evident?

Source Unit 4 Objectives and Discussion 4.2

1. Physiology as the ideal. Physiology describes the normal functioning of an organism, its natural order. Feedback mechanisms keep temperature, heart rate, blood sugar and blood pressure within acceptable ranges (Discussion 4.1), and that state needs no special explanation.

2. Pathology as deviation. Pathology studies departures from that norm, disease, and these are what need explaining, by causes such as infection or the malfunction of an organ, cells or a gene. The ideal is what makes a deviation stand out as something to investigate, just as Newton's straight-line motion makes a curved orbit demand a force.

3. Why "normal" must be examined. Choosing the ideal is a top-down step, and Discussion 4.1 warns that a vague principle imposes inappropriate requirements. If health means no pain, medicine focuses on painkillers; if it means a healthy appearance, on cosmetic surgery.

4. Normal depends on context. What is normal varies with the person and the situation. A trained endurance athlete may have a resting heart rate far below the usual range without being ill. A fever, an abnormal reading, is often part of the body's defence against infection. Treating the textbook norm as self-evident could label healthy variation as disease, or try to cure a useful response.

5. The general lesson. An ideal of natural order is an assumption of a conceptual framework, not a self-evident fact. If it is wrong, the questions scientists ask and the treatments they choose will be wrong too, so the assumed normal state must itself be tested against evidence.

NoteThe athlete and fever examples are standard physiology from outside the Unit 4 readings.

U4-A10Applied5 marks

A speaker repeats a correct explanation but cannot apply it to an unfamiliar case. Use the course account of intuitive insight to explain what may be missing from the speaker's understanding.

Source Discussion 4.2

1. What understanding requires. Discussion 4.2 defines understanding as interpreting something within a conceptual framework and experiencing intuitively that the interpretation is a good fit. Repeating a correct explanation shows only the first, verbal part.

2. What is missing. The speaker lacks the intuitive grasp of how the explanation fits the framework: why each step holds, which parts are essential, and what follows from them. Without this, Discussion 4.2 says, "we are only playing with words."

3. Rota's example. A mathematician who has checked every step of a proof may still ask "What is this good for?", because verification does not give the sense of a statement, its role in the theory. The speaker has the words of the explanation but not its sense.

4. Why the new case exposes the gap. Applying an idea to an unfamiliar case needs exactly what is missing: seeing which features of the new case matter and how they fit the framework. Discussion 6.1 notes that tekhné is proved by performance, and Discussion 8.1 describes empathetic reasoning as what gives "the real feeling of a fit." Memorized words carry over only to the familiar example.

5. Significance. This is how false understanding is detected. Discussion 4.2 warns that people who manipulate opinion with clever arguments and scientific words gather in the pseudosciences. The test is to ask for application to a new situation, which genuine understanding passes and verbal fluency does not.

U4-A11Applied5 marks

Explain why the Newtonian image of a system disturbed by external forces can become misleading when extended without qualification to social or psychological change.

Source Discussion 4.2

1. The Newtonian image. In Newtonian physics, rest and uniform straight-line motion are natural, and every deviation is explained by an external force. In popular form, if a system is not in equilibrium, some external force must be acting (Discussion 4.2).

2. Its hidden assumption. A basic part of this ideal is that no overall change of a system can come from inside the system itself. That is true of a billiard ball, which this framework describes very productively.

3. Misleading in psychology. Applied without qualification to people, it suggests that individuals are not responsible for their actions, because those actions are controlled by external forces. It leaves no room for a person who changes through their own reflection, learning or choice.

4. Misleading in society. It suggests that social institutions cannot change from within and must be overthrown by outside forces, ignoring reform driven by an institution's own members.

5. Why it fails, and the lesson. When systems can change their state through their own inner dynamics, the ideal of equilibrium disturbed by external forces cannot fully apply, and the very concept of force may need revising. In an ecosystem, species distributions may result from the mutual interactions of all species or from the overall system dynamics, not only from "selective forces." An ideal of natural order belongs to a particular framework, so carrying it into a new domain must be justified, not assumed. The idea has some validity there, but over-application leads to serious error.

U4-A12Applied10 marks

Explain how alchemical development toward perfection provides an ideal of natural order. Give a hypothetical modern developmental analogy and specify where that analogy would cease to justify conclusions.

Source Unit 4 Study Question 8 and Discussion 4.2

The alchemical ideal of natural order

1. The ideal. All of nature develops through definite stages toward perfection, as an egg becomes a butterfly; metals naturally mature from lead through tin, copper and silver to gold (Unit 4 Study Question 8). Development toward perfection needs no explanation.

2. What must be explained. Failure to develop: a metal that stays lead. Deviations are blamed on interrupted or incomplete processes, wrong heat, impurities, a badly sealed vessel or poor timing.

3. The pattern of explanation. It is developmental and teleological: things are explained by their place in a sequence leading to a final goal, and heat in a closed vessel, like warmth in a womb, speeds up the natural maturation.

A hypothetical modern analogy

4. Becoming an expert programmer. Suppose a training program claims that every trainee developer naturally passes through fixed stages, from novice through junior and senior to architect, the "gold." The heat is challenge and practice; the closed vessel is a protected apprenticeship with a mentor, where mistakes are contained. Raising the heat with harder projects is expected to speed up the maturation.

5. What the analogy gets right. Skill does develop in stages, practice does drive it, and a supportive setting does help, so the analogy can organize thinking about training, much as Jung read alchemy as a picture of personal transformation (Discussion 2.1).

Where the analogy stops justifying conclusions

6. No fixed final goal. The analogy assumes every trainee is headed to one predetermined end. People develop in different directions, and not becoming an architect is not a failure of nature; the teleology is assumed, not shown.

7. More heat is not always faster. Too much challenge produces burnout rather than faster growth, as too much heat cracks the vessel. The analogy cannot tell us the right amount; only observation can.

8. Failures can always be explained away. If a trainee does not develop, the theory can blame impure material, insufficient heat or a leaky vessel. A theory that accommodates every outcome this way makes no statement that observation could show to be false, like the invisible substance one of Galileo's opponents imagined filling the moon's craters (Derry ch. 14).

9. Analogy is not evidence. The similarity to a butterfly or to lead becoming gold proves nothing about developers. Claims such as "harder projects speed promotion" must be tested directly, for example by comparing similar trainees given different workloads.

10. The historical warning. The alchemical ideal itself failed when tested: Lavoisier's chemistry treated elements as unchangeable (Derry ch. 2), and the transmutations that do occur, in radioactive decay, are nuclear processes that heat in a vessel cannot produce (Derry ch. 14). An ideal of natural order must earn its place by the explanations it makes possible, not by its appeal.

Multiple choice practice15

U4-MC01Multiple choice2 marks

In the bottom-up approach to a system, we:

  1. A. start from constraints the whole system must satisfy
  2. B. start from the basic components and how they interact
  3. C. start from the purpose of the system
  4. D. ignore the components

B. Start from the basic components and how they interact. Starting from constraints the whole must satisfy (A) is the top-down approach (Discussion 4.1).

U4-MC02Multiple choice2 marks

The point that nothing in the atomic nature of hydrogen and oxygen tells us that water is wet illustrates a difficulty of:

  1. A. the top-down approach
  2. B. the bottom-up approach
  3. C. the predictivist thesis
  4. D. Pyrrhonian skepticism

B. The bottom-up approach. Its difficulty is that it is often unclear how properties of the whole emerge from the components (Discussion 4.1).

U4-MC03Multiple choice2 marks

According to Discussion 4.1, the best statement of the formal purpose of science is:

  1. A. to make accurate predictions
  2. B. to free people from fear
  3. C. to understand the world rationally
  4. D. to produce technology

C. To understand the world rationally. Prediction, freedom from fear and technology are functional purposes or by-products (Discussion 4.1).

U4-MC04Multiple choice2 marks

Epicurus summed up the purpose of science and philosophy as:

  1. A. 'To know the will of the gods'
  2. B. "To free man from fear"
  3. C. 'To predict eclipses'
  4. D. 'To make life comfortable'

B. "To free man from fear." Discussion 4.1 illustrates it with Halley's comet and the eradication of smallpox.

U4-MC05Multiple choice2 marks

Toulmin contrasts Babylonian and Greek astronomy to show that:

  1. A. prediction is the true goal of science
  2. B. understanding is the goal of science and prediction is secondary
  3. C. the Babylonians understood the planets better
  4. D. the Greeks predicted eclipses more accurately

B. Understanding is the goal of science and prediction is secondary. The Babylonians predicted well but attributed the motions to the gods; the Greeks understood the motions as circles even though they predicted less well.

U4-MC06Multiple choice2 marks

The psychological truism given in Discussion 4.1 is:

  1. A. Fear -> Ignorance -> Knowledge
  2. B. Ignorance -> Fear -> Belief
  3. C. Belief -> Doubt -> Truth
  4. D. Evidence -> Theory -> Prediction

B. Ignorance → Fear → Belief. We fear what we do not know and create a belief to control the fear (Discussion 4.1).

U4-MC07Multiple choice2 marks

In Discussion 4.2, the difference between point of view and conceptual framework is that:

  1. A. they are the same thing
  2. B. point of view is our attitude; the framework determines how we look and interpret
  3. C. the framework is an emotion
  4. D. point of view is a scientific theory

B. Point of view is our attitude; the framework determines how we look and interpret. Point of view concerns our willingness to look without fear (Discussion 4.2).

U4-MC08Multiple choice2 marks

In Newtonian physics, which needs NO explanation as an ideal of natural order?

  1. A. A planet's curved orbit
  2. B. A falling apple
  3. C. Uniform straight-line motion
  4. D. A body speeding up

C. Uniform straight-line motion. Rest and uniform straight-line motion are Newton's ideals; the other three are accelerations that require a force.

U4-MC09Multiple choice2 marks

N. R. Hanson's example of Tycho and Kepler watching the sunrise shows that:

  1. A. Tycho was a poor observer
  2. B. the same observation can be understood differently within different conceptual frameworks
  3. C. Kepler could not see the sunrise
  4. D. observation is independent of theory

B. The same observation can be understood differently within different conceptual frameworks. Tycho saw the sun rise around the earth; Kepler saw the earth turn (Discussion 4.2).

U4-MC10Multiple choice2 marks

Rota's mathematician who asks "What is this good for?" about a proved theorem is missing:

  1. A. the logical proof
  2. B. the sense of the statement, its role in the theory
  3. C. the notation
  4. D. the axioms

B. The sense of the statement, its role in the theory. The mathematician has verified the proof; Rota says logical verification alone does not give the sense (Discussion 4.2).

U4-MC11Multiple choice2 marks

The early success of the Copernican theory over the Ptolemaic was based mainly on:

  1. A. a much better fit to the observations
  2. B. the observation of stellar parallax
  3. C. opening up new directions of exploration and new questions
  4. D. being far simpler in its first form

C. Opening up new directions of exploration and new questions. Discussion 4.2: at first Ptolemy often fit the data better, Copernicus was not much simpler, and stellar parallax was not observed.

U4-MC12Multiple choice2 marks

In Aristotle's dynamics, the natural state of a body on earth is:

  1. A. uniform straight-line motion
  2. B. circular motion
  3. C. rest (or falling to its natural place)
  4. D. acceleration

C. Rest (or falling to its natural place). Any other motion needs a mover; Galileo and Newton later made continued motion natural (Derry ch. 5).

U4-MC13Multiple choice2 marks

Which is an example of a top-down constraint?

  1. A. Listing every component without relating them
  2. B. Beginning from a conservation principle that the whole system must satisfy
  3. C. Choosing the most vivid observation
  4. D. Counting publications

B. Beginning from a conservation principle that the whole system must satisfy. Discussion 4.1 names symmetry, optimality and conservation principles as typical top-down constraints.

U4-MC14Multiple choice2 marks

What changes when an ideal of natural order changes?

  1. A. Nature must change to obey the theory.
  2. B. All previous measurements become imaginary.
  3. C. The distinction between expected behavior and what needs explanation changes.
  4. D. Explanation becomes unnecessary.

C. The distinction between expected behavior and what needs explanation changes. Nature does not change; the baseline does, as when motion from Aristotle to Newton went from needing a mover to needing a force only for acceleration.

U4-MC15Multiple choice2 marks

Which statement best fits the course account of understanding?

  1. A. A fluent explanation guarantees insight.
  2. B. Prediction is the only possible goal.
  3. C. Memorizing a definition is always sufficient.
  4. D. A coherent interpretation within a framework also requires an intuitive grasp of its fit.

D. A coherent interpretation within a framework also requires an intuitive grasp of its fit. Discussion 4.2 defines understanding by both parts; fluency or memorization alone is "only playing with words."

People and attributions13

U4-P01Person

Identify Gregory Bateson (1904-1980) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1 epigraph

1. Who. Gregory Bateson (1904-1980) was an anthropologist and systems thinker. Discussion 4.1 opens with an epigraph from his book Mind and Nature: A Necessary Unity.

2. Quotation. "Science, like art, religion, commerce, warfare, and even sleep, is based on presuppositions." It differs from most other human activities because "not only are the pathways of scientific thought determined by the presuppositions of the scientists but their goals are the testing and revision, even abandonment of old presuppositions and the creation of new ones" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Meaning. Science does not begin free of assumptions. What sets it apart is that its own presuppositions are things to be tested, revised or abandoned, so Bateson adds that "it is clearly desirable for a scientist to know consciously and be able to state his or her own presuppositions" (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. The epigraph frames Unit 4's question about the purpose of science: the goals of science include testing and revising its own presuppositions. A scientist who can state their presuppositions can test them when the evidence requires, instead of mistaking them for facts about the world; this is the inductive attitude applied to one's own starting points.

U4-P02Person

Identify E. O. Wilson and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. E. O. Wilson was an American biologist. Discussion 4.1 quotes his book Consilience: The Unity of Knowledge (1998) at the head of the section "Science and Philosophy."

2. Quotation. "Science is the systematic enterprise of gathering knowledge about the world and organizing and condensing that knowledge into testable laws and theories" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Meaning. The definition names three activities: gathering knowledge, organizing it and condensing it. The product is not a pile of facts but laws and theories, and they must be testable, so they stay answerable to observation.

4. Significance. Wilson describes what science does; Unit 4 then asks what it is for. Discussion 4.1 concludes that the best statement of its formal purpose is "to understand the world rationally," and testable laws and theories are the means by which that understanding is condensed and checked (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P03Person

Identify Albert Einstein and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Albert Einstein, the physicist, called himself an "epistemic opportunist" (Discussion 4.1). The course quotes his "Reply to Criticisms" in Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist.

2. Quotation. "Epistemology without contact with science becomes an empty scheme. Science without epistemology is ... primitive and muddled" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Idea. An epistemologist who has fought through to a clear system is inclined to read science in terms of that system "and to reject whatever does not fit." The scientist cannot go that far, because "External conditions, which are set for him by the facts of experience" do not allow him to be restricted by one epistemological system (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. Philosophers of science disagree even on basic points, so the course advises learning a little about each position and asking whether it is useful for doing science, without becoming "a dogmatic adherent" of any one. Formal systems are "tools for thought, not its masters" (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P04Person

Identify Stephen Toulmin and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Stephen Toulmin was a philosopher, the author of the book Foresight and Understanding (Discussion 4.1).

2. Idea. His bottom-up analysis first concludes that science has no single purpose, since individual scientists work for many different reasons. By the end of the book he offers a viable candidate for a "purpose of science": to understand the world. He prefers it to the predictivist thesis, that the goal of science is to make accurate predictions (Discussion 4.1).

3. Example. The Babylonians made excellent predictions of planetary positions and eclipses, but they attributed the movements to the gods and so did not understand what they saw. The Greeks at first predicted less well, but they thought in terms of an overall system, with the Earth at the centre and the planets moving in perfect circles, so they could understand the sky (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. For Toulmin, prediction is secondary to understanding: a forecasting rule can work without explaining anything. This supports Unit 4's answer to the predictivist thesis and its definition of scientific understanding as interpretation within a conceptual framework (Discussion 4.2).

U4-P05Person

Identify Pierre Lecomte du Nouy and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Pierre Lecomte du Nouy is quoted in Discussion 4.1 (from Shirley Jones's anthology The Mind of God) on the purpose science serves for the individual scientist.

2. Quotation. "Our intellectual endeavors, our whole science will be of no avail if they do not lead man to a better comprehension of himself, of the meaning of his life, and of the resources buried in his inner self" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Meaning. Science is of no avail unless it leads us to understand ourselves and the meaning of our lives. For an individual scientist, the discipline of the work trains the mental and moral qualities through which they realize their own purpose, so "any discoveries made are secondary to the personal qualities developed in the process of discovery" (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. This is the functional purpose "to provide a vehicle of personal development," which the course traces back to Aristotle. Like an Olympic athlete, whose training matters more than winning, a scientist gains most from the qualities the work develops, and those qualities are the moral qualities required of a good scientist (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P06Person

Identify Epicurus (341-271 BCE) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Epicurus (341-271 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher; the course cites his "Letter to Herodotus" (Discussion 4.1).

2. Quotation. His remarks can be summed up as saying that the purpose of science and philosophy is "To free man from fear" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Meaning. In ancient Greece, ignorance of the tides, the planets, the source of the sun's light, the seasons, the weather and the causes of disease was a source of fear. Science has removed many such fears: the comet once read as an omen became a predicted return, and smallpox, declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980, no longer frightens anyone. A second reading follows a psychological truism: ignorance leads to fear, and fear to a belief that we then defend against anyone who questions it (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. Freeing people from fear is the first functional purpose of science listed in Discussion 4.1. The remedy is a cool, detached point of view that admits ignorance and suspends judgement, the inductive attitude, out of which "have come both philosophy and science" (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P07Person

Identify Wesley C. Salmon, Eusebio Francisco Kino, Pierre-Simon Laplace and Halley and the ideas or contributions the assigned readings attribute to them. Explain their significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Wesley C. Salmon wrote Scientific Explanation and the Causal Structure of the World, which gives "a striking example of how science has helped to eliminate fear" by contrasting two quotations. Eusebio Francisco Kino was a Jesuit priest, Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749-1827) a French mathematician, and Halley the astronomer whose name the comet now bears (Discussion 4.1).

2. Kino's fear. Writing shortly after the great comet of 1682 appeared, Kino read it as an omen: it "promises, signifies, and threatens many fatalities" and indicates "many calamities for all Europe" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Laplace and Halley. Laplace explained comets by Newton's theory of universal gravitation. Comets had "seemed to oppose the order of nature," but knowledge of "the laws of the system of the world" had "dissipated the fears begotten by the ignorance of the true relationship of man to the universe." Halley recognized the comet as the same one seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 and announced its return for the end of 1758 or the beginning of 1759 (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. Kino's fear versus Laplace's explanation and Halley's prediction: the same comet caused terror under ignorance and became a test of a theory once it was understood, as the learned world "awaited with impatience" a return that would confirm a great discovery. The example supports Epicurus's purpose of science, to free people from fear, and shows that understanding, not mere forecasting, is what removed the fear (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P08Person

Identify Marie Curie (1867-1934) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.1

1. Who. Marie Curie (1867-1934) was a physicist and chemist, quoted in Discussion 4.1 from Shirley Jones's anthology The Mind of God.

2. Quotation. "Nothing in life is to be feared. It is only to be understood" (Discussion 4.1).

3. Context. The course quotes her after a psychological truism: ignorance leads to fear, and fear to belief. We fear what we do not understand, create a belief to control the fear, and then attack anyone who questions it "with a ferocity proportional to the underlying fear" (Discussion 4.1).

4. Significance. Curie's answer to fear is understanding, not a comforting belief. The course draws the same lesson: adopt a cool, detached point of view, suspend judgement and admit ignorance. This inductive attitude is how science serves Epicurus's purpose of freeing people from fear (Discussion 4.1).

U4-P09Person

Identify Alfred North Whitehead (1861-1947) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.2 epigraph

1. Who. Alfred North Whitehead (1861-1947) was an English mathematician and philosopher. Discussion 4.2 opens with an epigraph from his Science and the Modern World (Lowell Lectures, 1925).

2. Quotation. "Familiar things happen, and mankind does not bother about them. It requires a very unusual mind to undertake the analysis of the obvious" (Discussion 4.2).

3. Meaning. What seems obvious is what fits our conceptual framework. Events in accord with its "ideals of natural order" seem to need no explanation; only deviations from those ideals are explained (Discussion 4.2).

4. Significance. Analysing the obvious means examining the framework itself. In Newtonian physics, rest and uniform straight-line motion are the ideals of natural motion, so only changes of motion seem to need a cause; the course warns that extending this ideal to social and psychological systems can lead to serious error (Discussion 4.2). Real understanding starts when the familiar is questioned.

U4-P10Person

Identify N. R. Hanson (1924-1967) and the idea or contribution the assigned readings attribute to this person. Explain its significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.2

1. Who. N. R. Hanson (1924-1967) was a philosopher of science; the course cites his chapter "Observation" (Discussion 4.2).

2. Idea. Hanson imagines Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler standing together on a hillside watching the sunrise. Both see the same phenomenon, but they understand it in completely different ways (Discussion 4.2).

3. Example. Tycho, who accepted a form of geocentric cosmology, would say the sun rose as the solar sphere rotated about the earth from east to west; his questions sought kinematic fits for the orbits in perfect circles. Kepler, who believed the heliocentric theory of Copernicus, would say the sun did not move while the earth rotated from west to east; his questions were dynamic, aimed at a central force (Discussion 4.2).

4. Significance. Seeing is not yet understanding: a conceptual framework decides which questions are asked and how the same data are read. Because the same observations can often be explained within two or more frameworks, choosing between them may need further observations or experiments and even aesthetic factors (Discussion 4.2).

U4-P11Person

Identify Gerald Holton and the ideas the assigned readings attribute to him and to the two astronomers he quotes, Johannes Kepler and Tycho Brahe. Explain their significance in this unit.

Source Discussion 4.2

1. Who. Gerald Holton, a historian of science, wrote Thematic Origins of Scientific Thought: Kepler to Einstein, the course's source for the words of Kepler and Tycho (Discussion 4.2).

2. Kepler's aim. "My aim is to show in this that the celestial machinery is to be likened not to a divine organism but rather to a clockwork ... insofar as nearly all the manifold movements are carried out by means of a single, quite simple magnetic force" (Discussion 4.2).

3. Tycho's letter. In a letter to Kepler of December 9, 1599, defending circular orbits, Tycho wrote that "one must compose the revolutions of celestial objects definitely from circular motions," since otherwise they could not return on the same path eternally, and that other orbits would be "less simple, and irregular, and unsuitable for scientific treatment." The course notes that the argument is circular, because an elliptic orbit also "comes back on the same path" (Discussion 4.2).

4. Significance. The two men worked within different ideals: Kepler sought a central force acting like clockwork, while Tycho held that only circles were scientific. Ironically, Tycho's own observations of Mars gave Kepler the data for his three laws.
