Note Essay length: 442 words.

U7-SG02Study guide

Based on the readings from Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 of What Science Is, and Discussion 7.1, draw up a list of rules for professional conduct for scientists.

Source Derry ch. 11, ch. 10 §3, ch. 15; Discussion 7.1

Honesty and evidence

1. Report results truthfully; never fabricate or falsify data. You cannot do science without assuming that others give you honest information (Derry ch. 11 §1).

2. Be extremely honest about the uncertainties in your knowledge (Derry ch. 11 §4).

3. Substantiate every claim; never ask for a claim to be taken on faith (Discussion 7.1 norms).

4. Change your mind when the evidence goes against you (open-mindedness); "advocate powerfully, but... concede defeat gracefully" (Ziman, Discussion 7.1).

Openness and credit

5. Publish and share results; keep secrecy to the minimum that military or commercial work really requires (Derry ch. 11 §1, the Manhattan Project).

6. Treat knowledge as public, accept no privileged sources, and judge ideas on their intrinsic merit, not on who proposed them. Prestige is not evidence: Eddington's authority wrongly delayed Chandrasekhar's result (Derry ch. 15).

7. Acknowledge all contributing sources; never steal another scientist's ideas.

8. Submit your work to peer review, and referee others' work carefully and fairly, without cronyism or deference to reputation (Derry ch. 10 §3).

Respect and tolerance

9. Tolerate dissent, protect free inquiry and free speech, and respect the dignity of rivals; answer the argument, never silence the person (Discussion 7.1).

10. Share ideas generously and welcome criticism; avoid obsessive secrecy, fear of criticism, greed and lack of humility.

Responsibility to subjects and society

11. Respect ethical limits on research: no harmful experiments on unconsenting or untreated subjects (the Tuskegee syphilis study, 1932-1972), and careful judgement about animal subjects and fetal tissue (Derry ch. 11 §3).

12. Avoid conflicts of interest, such as selling "expert" testimony for large fees (Derry ch. 11 §1).

13. Keep scientific results separate from value-laden or metaphorical interpretations, and do not pass off personal values as science ("humanity has been dethroned" is not science; Derry ch. 15 and ch. 11 on behaviourism and sociobiology).

14. Before criticizing or borrowing from another field, understand it; do not use scientific language you do not understand (the lesson of the Sokal affair, Derry ch. 15).

15. Scrutinize the broader consequences of your work and join public debate as an informed citizen (Derry ch. 11 §4).

Holton's four principles of integrity (Discussion 7.1)

16. Try to get it right at all costs, sparing no effort; be a scientist first and a specialist second; explore and contribute to the role of science in our overall worldview; do your duty as a scientist and as a human being.

U7-SG03Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing Jacob Bronowski's statement, "[Y]ou cannot know what is true unless you behave in certain ways."

Source Discussion 7.1

Bronowski's claim sounds odd at first: surely truth is a matter of how the world is, not of how we behave. But Discussion 7.1 shows that the way we interact with the world decides what we are able to learn about it.

The psychologists Kelley and Stahelski had students play the prisoner's dilemma, a game in which each player chooses to cooperate or compete without being able to communicate. From their views of the game's aim, players were first sorted into "cooperators" and "competitors," and then mixed. Two competitors simply competed and two cooperators cooperated, but when a cooperator met a competitor, the cooperator soon switched to competing to limit losses. So the competitors learned something false, that everybody is a competitor, while the cooperators learned something true, that the world contains both kinds. The competitors' own behaviour produced the evidence that confirmed their mistaken belief.

Science generalizes this lesson: "truth is more likely to be found by open-minded exploration and vigorous debate than by adherence to dogma or authority." That principle limits how we may behave. We may not kill an opponent or even prevent them from being heard; we may only answer their argument, and we must be willing to change our minds if the weight of evidence is against us. Because science is a search carried out by a community, it succeeds only if each member is truthful, which is why Bronowski states the duty "We OUGHT to act in such a way that what IS true can be verified to be so." From that duty follow the social values science needs: free inquiry, free thought, free speech and tolerance, freedoms that "have never been notable in a dogmatic society."

The same holds for individual scientists. Fraud, falsifying data or stealing ideas, means the cheater has "fallen into the illusion of identifying appearance and reality," and a scientist who cannot be trusted is in effect excluded from the community. Obsessive secrecy and fear of criticism cut a scientist off from the discussion that improves ideas, while productive scientists find that the more generously they share ideas, the more good ideas they have. Without humility, learning is difficult if not impossible, and Idries Shah notes that greed, even for knowledge, prevents real learning. The Sufi who refused to debate a scholar who "was only interested in winning the argument, not in discovering the truth" makes the same point.

Bronowski is therefore right. Knowing what is true is not a matter of having facts handed to us; it depends on honesty, openness, humility and tolerance in the way we look and argue. Those who behave as dogmatists, pure competitors or cheats end up, like the competitive players, confirming their own errors.

Note Essay length: 452 words.

U7-SG04Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing Darwin's statement, "[A]ll observation must be for or against some view if it is to be of any service."

Source Discussion 7.2 (Darwin's 1861 letter to Henry Fawcett); Discussion 5.2; Derry chs. 2, 4, 14

In an 1861 letter to his friend Henry Fawcett, Charles Darwin wrote that "all observation must be for or against some view if it is to be of any service" (quoted in Discussion 7.2). The sentence captures the step that, according to Discussion 7.2, turned traditional belief into science.

An observation is useful when it bears on a question. Discussion 7.2 says the key move was realizing "that at least some forms of experience can be taken as evidence": a test of a belief rather than an instance that merely illustrates it. Once observations can count for or against a view, beliefs become working hypotheses. John Snow's observations in London were useful because they bore on two rival views of cholera: the deaths around the Broad Street pump and the healthy brewery workers who drank no pump water counted for the contaminated-water theory and against the rival "effluvia" theory (Unit 3).

Darwin is also rejecting the picture of science as collecting facts first and theorizing later. Poincaré warned that a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house (the epigraph of Derry ch. 2). Torricelli's mercury experiment was designed to test his idea that the weight of the air, not nature's abhorrence of a vacuum, holds up the liquid in a pump (Derry ch. 4), and Le Verrier's calculation told Galle exactly where to point the telescope that found Neptune (Derry ch. 4). Without a view, we would not know what to look at or which details matter.

But the view must be one that the observation could go against. If every observation is read as support, it becomes an instance, not evidence. The Azande treated every oracle answer as confirming the oracle and explained the wrong answers away as bad poison or broken ritual (Discussion 5.2). Derry adds that observations are theory-laden, so the view shapes what we see (ch. 14); that is why science needs controls, replication and rival hypotheses to keep a favoured view honest.

One qualification is needed: observations made for one view can serve another. Lord Rayleigh measured the density of nitrogen only to improve precision, yet a small discrepancy overturned an unstated assumption, that air held no unknown gas, and led to the discovery of argon (Derry ch. 4). Even a surprise is "for or against" some view once we notice that it surprises us.

Understood this way, Darwin's maxim defines the scientific use of observation: we observe in order to test, guided by a hypothesis, and we must be ready for the result to go either way.

Note Outside the readings: the setting of Darwin's remark. In the same letter (18 September 1861) he recalled people saying that geologists ought only to observe and not theorise, so that "a man might as well go into a gravel-pit and count the pebbles and describe the colours."

Note Essay length: 432 words.

U7-SG05Study guide

What are the three basic mythico-magical assumptions about the world?

Source Discussion 7.2

The three mythico-magical assumptions (Discussion 7.2):

1. Nature is capricious; the unknown is unknowable.

2. Everything is determined by external, willful powers.

3. The future can be controlled by magic.

Under these beliefs the important thing was to learn the will of the gods and other supernatural powers, and to placate them through offerings and submission or control them through magic, with the help of a magician, priest, soothsayer, oracle or prophet who gave insight into the future.

In Miletus they were replaced, without anyone saying so, by the three metaphysical assumptions of science (Discussion 6.1): nature is ordered; this order is comprehensible to human reason; and our understanding of it can be communicated without subjective bias.

U7-SG06Study guide

Find three examples of mythico-magical thinking in the world today (e.g., from news stories, television or popular belief systems).

Source Discussion 7.2

1. Disasters blamed on divine anger. After the January 2010 earthquake in Haiti, the American television evangelist Pat Robertson said on his show that Haitians had "swore a pact to the devil" and had been cursed ever since. The earthquake is explained by the will of an external, willful power (assumption 2), not by the movement of tectonic plates, and nature is treated as capricious, punishing whomever it chooses (assumption 1).

2. Rituals to control luck. Many buildings in North America have no floor numbered 13, and in parts of East Asia the number 4 is avoided because it sounds like the word for "death." Sports fans and players keep lucky socks or pre-game rituals, and lottery players choose "lucky" numbers. Each assumes that the future can be controlled by magic (assumption 3), and that the right ritual can turn chance in our favour.

3. Fortune-telling and ancestral offerings. In Vietnam, where I come from, many families ask a fortune-teller to choose an auspicious day for a wedding, a house move or the opening of a business, and burn paper money and paper goods as offerings so that ancestors and spirits will bring good fortune. In Western countries, horoscopes in newspapers and apps tell readers what the stars have planned for them, and "Mercury in retrograde" is blamed for broken phones and quarrels. Events are decided by external powers (assumption 2), and the future can be learned from and influenced by those who read the signs (assumption 3).

Why these count as mythico-magical rather than scientific: in each case a failure is explained away rather than taken as a test. If the auspicious wedding fails, the date was read wrongly; if the team loses despite the socks, something else went wrong. As with the Azande oracle, experiences are treated as instances that confirm the belief, never as evidence that could count against it (Discussion 5.2).

Note Outside the readings: Pat Robertson's remarks were made on The 700 Club in January 2010; the missing 13th floor, the avoidance of 4 and Vietnamese votive-paper offerings are widely documented customs. The Vietnam example describes common practice, not your own family.

U7-SG07Study guide

The physicists Alan Sokal and Jean Bricmont list four common abuses of science that are found in some areas of new age and postmodern discourse:

a. longwinded discussions of scientific theories with little or no understanding of the actual meaning of what is being discussed.

b. taking natural science concepts and using them in the humanities or social sciences with no rational or empirical justification to support the implied analogy.

c. using technical scientific language in a context where it is irrelevant.

d. using scientific sounding language to talk nonsense.

Find examples of each of these abuses in the popular press, on television or in other domains of popular culture.

Source Unit 7 Q7 (Sokal and Bricmont); Discussion 4.2; Derry ch. 15

a. Long-winded discussion without understanding. Deepak Chopra's best-seller Quantum Healing (1989) and the film What the Bleep Do We Know!? (2004) spend chapters and scenes on the uncertainty principle, the observer and entanglement, and conclude that the mind creates reality and can heal the body. In physics, "observation" in quantum mechanics is a physical interaction with a measuring device, not a human intention, so the long discussion rests on a misunderstanding of what the theory says.

b. Importing a natural-science concept into the social world without justification. The "law of attraction" made popular by the book and film The Secret (2006) claims that thoughts attract matching events because "like attracts like," borrowing the language of magnetism and vibration; in magnetism, in fact, opposite poles attract. Other examples are the claim that "relativity proves everything is relative" in morality, and the social Darwinism of the late nineteenth century, which used "survival of the fittest" to justify class inequality (Unit 7 Overview; Derry ch. 11). In each case no rational or empirical argument shows that the analogy holds.

c. Technical language where it is irrelevant. Shampoo and skin-cream advertisements full of "DNA," "molecular," "ionic" and "nano" technology; a well-known L'Oréal hair-care advert of the early 2000s even announced "Here comes the science bit - concentrate." A dishwasher tablet is sold as "Finish Quantum." Business writers call a reorganization a "quantum leap" (in physics a quantum jump is a tiny, discrete change between states, almost the opposite of what is meant) or describe office life with "chaos theory." The terms add prestige, not meaning.

d. Scientific-sounding language to talk nonsense. Wellness products that "raise your vibrational frequency," "balance your energy field" or sell "structured water" whose molecules have been "re-aligned." A 2015 psychology study (Pennycook and colleagues) found that many people rate randomly generated sentences such as "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty" as profound. The Baudrillard paragraph in Study Question 8 is the course's own example.

Why it matters: these abuses borrow the authority of science without its substance, which is the point Sokal made in 1996 when his parody paper on quantum gravity was published by a leading postmodern journal (Derry ch. 15).

Note Outside the readings: all the examples (Chopra, What the Bleep, The Secret, the advertising slogans, the Pennycook study in Judgment and Decision Making, and the name of Sokal's parody, published in Social Text) are from general knowledge, not the course text.

U7-SG08Study guide

Try to give a simple, one-sentence summary of this paragraph by the postmodern French sociologist and philosopher Jean Baudrillard. [It is possible to do so!]

Our complex, metastatic, viral systems, condemned to the exponential dimension alone (be it that of exponential stability or instability), to eccentricity and indefinite fractal scissiparity, can no longer come to an end. Condemned to an intense metabolism, to an intense internal metastasis, they become exhausted within themselves and no longer have any destination, any end, any otherness, any fatality. They are condemned, precisely, to the epidemic, to the endless excrescences of the fractal and not to the reversibility and perfect resolution of the fateful.

Source Unit 7 Q8; Sokal and Bricmont's abuses 3 and 4

One-sentence summary: Our complex modern systems keep growing and multiplying out of control from within, like a cancer or an epidemic, so they have no goal and can never come to a proper end.

How the sentence maps on to the paragraph: "metastatic, viral... epidemic" means spreading like a disease; "exponential... indefinite fractal scissiparity" means multiplying without limit (scissiparity is reproduction by splitting in two); "can no longer come to an end... no longer have any destination, any end" means they have no goal or conclusion.

Comment: the words borrowed from medicine, biology and mathematics have no technical meaning in this context; for example, nothing is measured to be "exponential" or "fractal." The paragraph is an example of Sokal and Bricmont's abuses (c), technical language where it is irrelevant, and (d), scientific-sounding language for a simple (or empty) idea. Sokal and Bricmont quote it for exactly this reason.

U7-SG09Study guide

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the apparent contradiction between the idea that all science is carried out within, and hence is influenced by, a particular cultural context, and the idea that science produces objective knowledge of the world.

Source Derry ch. 15; Unit 7 Overview; Discussions 5.2 and 7.2

Science is plainly a cultural product. Its basic tools, logic, mathematics and repeatable experiment, grew largely out of Greek and European culture, and Derry concedes that science "is indeed the product of a particular culture in a specific set of historical circumstances" (ch. 15). Postmodern critics conclude that science is just one claimant among many, that its results are social constructions negotiated among scientists, and, with Feyerabend, that voodoo is no better or worse than science. Yet science claims objective knowledge of nature. The contradiction is only apparent.

First, culture influences what science studies and how it is funded and described, but in the long run not what it finds. Politics shapes research agendas (military, agricultural and medical research), and social prestige can delay a result: Eddington's authority kept Chandrasekhar's calculation that massive stars collapse from being accepted for about two generations, until new observations and better theory established black holes. Social forces can delay nature's verdict; they cannot overrule it indefinitely.

Second, underdetermination is weaker than the critics claim. Data alone may not fix a theory, but "our data working together with our demand for logical coherence effectively whittles down the possibilities quite dramatically," and it is usually hard to produce even one explanation that fits everything. Good theories also give back more than was put into them, explaining discoveries no one foresaw. That power is hard to understand if theories are arbitrary constructions; it suggests that they mirror reality in some sense.

Third, the critics offer a false choice. The alternative to "science is absolutely superior" is not "all modes of thinking are equally valid"; between them lies a continuum on which judgements can be made and justified. We should also separate two questions that are often blurred: whether science is good, a question of values, and whether it is valid. And we should separate scientific results from the value-laden metaphors attached to them, such as "humanity has been dethroned."

Finally, objectivity is not freedom from culture but the product of a particular culture: the open, self-critical community of Discussion 7.1. Its norms of public knowledge, no privileged sources, substantiated claims and tolerance of dissent are designed to cancel out individual and cultural bias. As the Unit 7 Overview puts it, the tools of science developed through an evolutionary process whose selection criteria are conclusions that satisfy both the coherence and the correspondence theories of truth. Science is cultural in origin but objective in aim and method, and its objectivity is always provisional, which is exactly what makes it trustworthy.

Note Essay length: 422 words.

Learning objective drills9

U7-OBJ01Objective

Discuss both the rules of professional conduct in science, and the more basic values that underlie these rules.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 1

The rules of professional conduct.

1. The five common norms (Discussion 7.1): knowledge is public; there are no privileged sources; ideas are judged on their intrinsic merit, not their source; claims are not taken on faith but must be substantiated; all contributing sources must be acknowledged.

2. Holton's four principles of integrity: get it right at all costs; be a scientist first and a specialist second; contribute to the role of science in our worldview; do your duty as a scientist and as a human being.

3. Practical rules (Derry ch. 10 §3 and ch. 11): publish and share results, submit to peer review, never fabricate or falsify, be honest about uncertainty, respect ethical limits on research subjects (Tuskegee).

The more basic values beneath the rules.

4. Truthfulness. Science is a search for truth carried out by a community, so it succeeds only if each member is truthful. Bronowski: "We OUGHT to act in such a way that what IS true can be verified to be so." Derry: you cannot do science without assuming others give you honest information.

5. Freedom and tolerance. Truthful communication must be free and uninhibited, which requires intellectual freedom, independence, free inquiry, free thought, free speech and tolerance of dissent. Bronowski: "Independence and originality, dissent and freedom and tolerance: such are the first needs of science."

6. Respect for human dignity. Tolerance implies mutual respect among scientists as fellow seekers of truth; a well-fought controversy is "a form of cooperation" (Ziman).

7. Curiosity and open-mindedness. Learning more about nature is a positive good, and a belief must be given up if the evidence goes against it (Derry ch. 11 §1).

8. The link. The rules are the practical form of these values: "knowledge is public" expresses free communication, "no privileged sources" and "judge on merit" express independence and tolerance, and "substantiate claims" and "acknowledge sources" express truthfulness. As Bronowski puts it, there are no technical rules for success in science; the values are what science "of itself... demands and forms."

U7-OBJ02Objective

Describe the sort of activities that are considered to be misconduct in science.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 2

1. Fabricating or falsifying data. Reporting results that were never obtained, or altering real ones. Discussion 7.1 traces it to fear of failure plus an excessive desire for the appearance of success; such people have "fallen into the illusion of identifying appearance and reality."

2. Plagiarism, stealing another scientist's ideas, and failing to acknowledge all contributing sources (a breach of the fifth norm).

3. Misrepresenting results, for example concealing adverse findings, overstating certainty, or passing off value-laden claims as scientific findings (Derry ch. 11 §4 asks for "extreme honesty concerning the uncertainties").

4. Conflicts of interest, such as scientists who act as paid "experts" in legal proceedings, which Derry calls a potentially corrupting influence, or industry "scientists" who will say anything regardless of evidence (tobacco employees claiming heavy smoking does no harm).

5. Unethical treatment of research subjects, such as the Tuskegee study (1932-1972), in which black men with syphilis were deliberately left untreated (Derry ch. 11 §3).

6. Abuse of the review and credit system, such as cronyism or biased refereeing, which damage the community's means of catching errors (Derry ch. 10 §3).

Harmful but not misconduct in itself: obsessive secrecy and refusing to discuss ideas for fear of criticism, which cut a scientist off from the criticism that improves ideas.

Consequence: a scientist whose results cannot be trusted is effectively excluded from the community; their data are not used and their papers are not read (Discussion 7.1).

Note Outside the readings: official definitions. United States federal policy (2000) defines research misconduct as fabrication, falsification or plagiarism; Canada's Tri-Agency Framework: Responsible Conduct of Research also lists destruction of research records, redundant publication, invalid authorship, inadequate acknowledgement and mismanaged conflicts of interest. Well-known cases: Jan Hendrik Schön's fabricated physics data (Bell Labs, 2002) and Andrew Wakefield's 1998 vaccine-autism paper (retracted by The Lancet in 2010).

U7-OBJ03Objective

State Gerald Holton's four principles of integrity in science.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 3

Gerald Holton's four principles of integrity in science (Discussion 7.1):

1. Try to get it right at all costs, sparing no effort.

2. Try to be a scientist first, a specialist second.

3. Try to explore and contribute to the role of science as part of our overall worldview.

4. Try to do your duty as a scientist and as a human being.

The fourth links science to the social and historical nature of human life: Gurdjieff remarked that everything we possess, even our language, results from the efforts and sacrifices of others, and Dunbar describes science as a long-term collective project of patient, careful checking.

U7-OBJ04Objective

Describe the "first crisis of science," and state how Aristotle resolved it.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 4

1. The gap. The early Greek natural philosophers (Thales, Anaximander, Heraclitus, Pythagoras and others) used reason to explain nature, but there were no established criteria for what makes an argument reliable.

2. The crisis. This created the first crisis of science: the need to find out how to carry out a reasoned argument without simply falling into nonsense (Discussion 7.2).

3. The Sophists brought it to a head in the latter part of the 5th century BCE. They taught rhetoric and "virtue" for a fee to the children of the aristocracy, and since political power depended on persuading assemblies, they taught the art of persuasion: in effect a return to the magical idea that truth is whatever the most persuasive speaker says. They were interested only in winning arguments, not in whether the winning argument was true.

4. The threat to science. The Sophist Gorgias argued against the basic metaphysical assumptions of science (that nothing exists, that if it existed it could not be known, and that if known it could not be communicated; Discussion 6.1). Without a way to refute such arguments conclusively, the very possibility of science was in question.

5. Aristotle's resolution. Socrates and then Plato opposed the Sophists, but Aristotle, Plato's student, resolved the crisis by working out the laws of formal logic (the topic of Discussion 9.2).

6. The principle he instituted. Philosophical and scientific conclusions could be accepted only if supported by logically sound arguments. Appeals to personality, authority or the gods were not accepted, and analogy and metaphor could illustrate a point but not demonstrate that it is correct.

U7-OBJ05Objective

Identify some of the cultural factors that contributed to the emergence of modern science in Europe.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 5

Ancient roots (Discussion 7.2).

1. Exposure to alternatives. The Persian Empire, from Cyrus the Great on, practised official religious tolerance, so it was a mosaic of religions and myths. Traders from Miletus met many conflicting myths, and noticing alternatives is the condition for treating experience as evidence rather than instance.

2. Settling disputes by argument. Greek cities decided legal disputes by jury, where each side argued and the jury debated; it was natural to think that differences between myths could also be settled by debate and reason.

3. Natural, criticizable theories and mathematics. Thales's water theory made no reference to the gods and was open to rival theories; Pythagoras added the mathematical form of laws and perhaps the first conscious experiments; Aristotle's formal logic set standards for argument.

Modern Europe (17th century).

4. Wealth and a spirit of exploration following the discovery of the Americas.

5. New intellectual tools: experimental testing of theories, probability and statistics for interpreting results, the clear distinction between instances and evidence, and the formalized hypothetico-deductive method.

6. Social institutions: open communication, impartial peer review and accurate credit; learned societies such as the Royal Society (1662) and the Académie des Sciences (1666) (Derry ch. 10); and, as Bacon's epigraph says, knowledge preserved in "books, traditions, conferences" and in universities, colleges and schools.

7. The Renaissance humanists made Greek learning available again, which exposed Copernicus to heliocentric ideas (Derry ch. 5).

8. A truce with the churches in which science was given the material world (Unit 7 Overview), and a culture whose values then resonated with science and fed the 18th-century Enlightenment. Areas most resistant to the Enlightenment stayed scientifically backward and under church control.

Note Course-text slip: Discussion 7.1 says that "Discussion 2.2 presented two examples of highly advanced cultures where science could not develop fully," and the Overview cites Discussion 2.2 for a "yes and no" answer about science and Western culture. The current Discussion 2.2 ("Is Science Uniquely Human?") contains neither, so these answers do not rely on it.

U7-OBJ06Objective

Describe some of the ways that science has influenced modern Western and world culture.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 6

1. Through technology. Changes from new technology appear continually in everyday life (computers, the germ theory of disease and medicine), often without challenging central values (Unit 7 Overview).

2. Through new ethical dilemmas. Genetic testing for Huntington's disease, life-prolonging medicine, pesticides and fertilizers, nuclear weapons, automation and privacy all force us to confront old values with new powers: science gives "power but not wisdom" (Derry ch. 11 §2).

3. Through changes in worldview and self-image. Heliocentrism removed the Earth, and with it humanity, from the centre of the universe; Darwin's theory removed the barrier between humans and other animals (Derry ch. 11 §2).

4. Through misapplied ideas. Evolution was misused as social Darwinism and eugenics; Newton's mechanics became a "clockwork universe" without free will; quantum indeterminacy was then claimed as room for free will; behaviourism and gene-centred views shaped how people see human nature.

5. Through diffusing metaphors. Scientific ideas spread into the general culture, often losing their precision and sometimes taking the opposite meaning, as with popular uses of quantum theory (Overview).

6. Through values. The values of science (open communication, evidence, tolerance) resonated with European culture and contributed to the 18th-century Enlightenment (Discussion 7.2).

7. As world culture. Western science is becoming world science because it is effective in improving people's quality of life (Discussion 7.1).

8. Through reaction. Its influence provoked opposition: Appleyard calls science "spiritually corrosive," anti-science views blame scientists for the ills of the modern world, and scientism overreached in the other direction (Overview; Discussion 7.2).

U7-OBJ07Objective

Describe and analyse some of the postmodern claims about science.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 7

The claims (Derry ch. 15; Unit 7 Overview).

1. Science is just one culture's product. Its standards (evidence, logic, predictive success) are artifacts of European thought, so science is one claimant among many; Feyerabend said voodoo is no better or worse than science.

2. Results are social constructions (the strong program). Consensus comes from social negotiation, and prestige, friendship and power always permeate and finally determine the outcome.

3. Underdetermination. By the Quine-Duhem thesis, data do not uniquely fix theories, so scientists invent rather than discover results, through a social process.

4. Science serves ideology. Its results merely reflect the political ideologies, economic interests and prejudices of scientists or their employers; in the Marxist-constructivist version science is an instrument of oppression used by the elite.

Analysis.

5. The continuum reply. Science has no absolute superiority, but the alternative is not "all modes of thinking are equally valid"; between the extremes we can make and justify judgements. Derry admits the extreme argument is hard to counter, because any evidence or logic offered against it can be dismissed as cultural, but it has force only if we restrict attention to the most extreme alternatives.

6. Nature constrains. Chandrasekhar's result was rejected because of Eddington's prestige, but new observations established black holes about two generations later. Critics can be right for a period, not forever.

7. Data plus coherence narrow the options. It is hard to find even one theory that fits all the data coherently, and good theories give back more than was put in, which arbitrary constructions would not do.

8. Valid core of the critique. Politics and economics shape the research agenda; gender discrimination exists; and where data are sparse, phenomena complex and values deeply involved (the nature/nurture debate on intelligence), ideology can dominate. Exposing that is "a valuable service."

9. Confusions to avoid. Whether science is good is a separate question from whether it is valid, and scientific results must be separated from value-laden metaphors. Many critics also understand little of science, which the 1996 Sokal hoax exposed.

U7-OBJ08Objective

Discuss the interrelation between science and culture.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 8

1. Science is embedded in culture. It is carried out by people within a culture, so culture influences what science studies, how it is funded and how its results are described (Derry ch. 11 §3: prosperity and military values shape the research agenda).

2. Science needs certain cultural values. It flourishes only where rational knowledge is valued and free inquiry, free speech and tolerance are protected; these freedoms "have never been notable in a dogmatic society" (Bronowski, Discussion 7.1).

3. Culture shaped its origins. Persian religious tolerance, Greek jury trials and trade at Miletus encouraged rational debate about rival myths; in 17th-century Europe, wealth, exploration and new institutions made experimental science possible (Discussion 7.2). Egypt's erasure of Akhenaten shows the opposite: a culture that could not tolerate an alternative.

4. Values can influence content where evidence is weak. In risk assessment and in the study of humans (heredity research tainted by class and ethnic prejudice, behaviourism in mid-century America, ethology in central Europe), values can shape interpretation (Derry ch. 11 §3).

5. Science changes culture. Through technology, through worldview shifts (Copernicus, Darwin, Newton, quantum theory), through ideas that diffuse as metaphors, and through its values feeding the Enlightenment.

6. The relationship is evolutionary. Because science helps survival, cultures with science-friendly values have an advantage, and Western science is becoming world science because it works. It is opposed where cultures conflict with the values science requires, or with Western values wrongly associated with it (Discussion 7.1).

7. But culture does not make science arbitrary. The tools of science evolved under selection for conclusions that satisfy both coherence and correspondence, so in the long run nature, not culture, decides (Overview; Derry ch. 15).

8. Limits. Science cannot explain everything, and possessing science is no guarantee of wisdom (Hallpike); non-scientific cultures can be fully successful in their environments (Discussion 7.2).

U7-OBJ09Objective

State four ways in which scientific language is abused.

Source Unit 7 Overview objective 9

Sokal and Bricmont's four abuses of scientific language (Unit 7 Study Question 7):

1. Long-winded discussions of scientific theories with little or no understanding of what is being discussed (for example, books on "quantum healing").

2. Importing natural-science concepts into the humanities or social sciences with no rational or empirical justification for the implied analogy (for example, social Darwinism, or "relativity shows morality is relative").

3. Using technical scientific language where it is irrelevant (for example, "DNA" and "molecular" technology in shampoo advertisements).

4. Using scientific-sounding language to talk nonsense (for example, the Baudrillard paragraph in Study Question 8).

Lists and concept recall7

U7-R01Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Inherent values of science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Inherent values of science (Derry ch. 11 §1)

1. Free flow of information. Progress depends on sharing results; a result that is not published cannot contribute. It conflicts with military and industrial secrecy, as when General Groves tried to compartmentalize knowledge in the Manhattan Project (Derry ch. 11 §1).

2. Honesty. It has a special place in science: you can make a political deal without trusting the other side, but you cannot do science without assuming others give you honest information, which is why fraud provokes outrage.

3. Curiosity. Learning more about nature is a positive good, although not everyone in our culture agrees ("curiosity killed the cat"), and it can conflict with ethics (curiosity about how much pain a human can bear).

4. Open-mindedness. If accumulating evidence contradicts a belief, however strongly held, we must give it up; anyone who does not share this value is not a scientist.

5. Significance. These shared values, together with the values used in theory choice (accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness), show that "science is value-free" is "utter nonsense" if it refers to the context in which science is done. They are what makes scientific reasoning self-correcting.

U7-R02Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Common norms of acceptable scientific behaviour. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Common norms of acceptable scientific behaviour (Discussion 7.1)

1. Knowledge is public. Results are shared so others can use, check and build on them.

2. There are no privileged sources. No person, office or tradition can declare a claim true.

3. Ideas are judged on their intrinsic merit, not their source.

4. Claims are not taken on faith; they must be substantiated.

5. All contributing sources must be acknowledged. Significance and example: together the norms make error correction possible, because anyone can check anyone's claim. When the young, unknown Chandrasekhar's calculation was rejected because of Eddington's prestige (Derry ch. 15), norms 2 and 3 were broken, and the truth was delayed for about two generations (Discussion 7.1).

U7-R03Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Gerald Holton's four principles of integrity in science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Gerald Holton's four principles of integrity in science (Discussion 7.1)

1. Try to get it right at all costs, sparing no effort: check and double-check, as Dunbar says, because only patience and careful testing avoid mistakes.

2. Try to be a scientist first, a specialist second: keep the shared values and broad view of science above the narrow interests of a speciality.

3. Try to explore and contribute to the role of science as part of our overall worldview: science is not isolated technique but part of how we understand the world.

4. Try to do your duty as a scientist and as a human being: recognize that everything we have, even our language, comes from others' efforts and sacrifices (Gurdjieff).

5. Significance (Discussion 7.1): scientists share human foibles, and community judgements can be influenced by funding and social needs; integrity is what maintains scientific responsibility. Example: a researcher pressed to publish quickly who still repeats an experiment before submitting follows principle 1.

U7-R04Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Bronowski's values that science demands. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Bronowski's values that science demands (Discussion 7.1)

1. Truthfulness. A community searching for truth succeeds only if each member is truthful: "We OUGHT to act in such a way that what IS true can be verified to be so."

2. Free inquiry and free thought. Freedom to follow whatever clues appear in the search for truth.

3. Free speech, dissent and tolerance. Free, uninhibited communication and freedom to dissent open the door to originality and creativity; these freedoms "have never been notable in a dogmatic society."

4. Independence, originality and respect for human dignity. "Independence and originality, dissent and freedom and tolerance: such are the first needs of science"; tolerance implies mutual respect among scientists.

5. Significance. Bronowski says there are no technical rules for success in science; these values are its real conditions, and science "of itself... demands and forms" them. So science is not value-free. Example: the prisoner's dilemma experiment shows that how we behave decides what we can learn.

U7-R05Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Three mythico-magical assumptions. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Three mythico-magical assumptions (Discussion 7.2)

1. Nature is capricious; the unknown is unknowable.

2. Everything is determined by external, willful powers.

3. The future can be controlled by magic.

4. Consequence. What mattered was to learn the will of the gods and to placate or control them through offerings, submission or magic, guided by priests, oracles and prophets (Discussion 7.2).

5. Significance for scientific reasoning. In Miletus these were replaced by the metaphysical assumptions of science (nature is ordered, comprehensible to reason, and communicable without bias). Only then can a failed prediction count as evidence against an explanation instead of as the gods' whim, so explanations can be tested and improved. Example: Thales explained the world as made of water without reference to the gods.

U7-R06Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: The rise of Western science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source The rise of Western science (Discussion 7.2)

1. From instance to evidence. The key step was realizing that experience can test a belief, which requires awareness of alternatives; traditional cultures, and even liberal Egypt, which erased Akhenaten's religion, would not accept alternatives (Discussion 7.2).

2. Miletus. In the tolerant Persian Empire, traders met many myths, and Greek jury trials made debate the way to settle disputes; Thales (the first scientist) proposed water as the basic substance with no reference to the gods, and rivals proposed air, "the unlimited," fire and the four elements.

3. Pythagoras and the first crisis. Pythagoras found that strings with lengths in simple ratios (2:1, 3:2, 4:3) sound harmonious, giving laws in mathematical form; the Sophists then made truth a matter of persuasion, and Aristotle's formal logic resolved the crisis.

4. Hellenistic to modern. The Hellenistic method was speculative-deductive; in 17th-century Europe, experimental testing, probability and statistics, the hypothetico-deductive method, peer review and credit developed, feeding the Enlightenment and later scientism.

5. Significance. Science evolved out of ordinary human reasoning, and attitude (treating beliefs as testable working hypotheses) was the key factor; today we are more modest, since science still struggles with inner conscious experience.

U7-R07Recall

Explain this topic from the assigned readings: Sokal and Bricmont's four abuses of science. Give an example or explain its significance for scientific reasoning.

Source Sokal and Bricmont's four abuses of science (Unit 7 Q7)

1. Long-winded discussions of scientific theories with little or no understanding of what is being discussed.

2. Importing natural-science concepts into the humanities or social sciences with no rational or empirical justification for the analogy.

3. Technical scientific language where it is irrelevant.

4. Scientific-sounding language used to talk nonsense.

5. Significance and example. These abuses borrow the authority of science without its substance, and confuse metaphor with theory (Derry ch. 15). Baudrillard's paragraph in Study Question 8 ("metastatic, viral systems... indefinite fractal scissiparity") illustrates abuses 3 and 4; in 1996 Sokal got a parody of such writing published in a postmodern journal.

Key term questions9

U7-T01Term

Define or distinguish Ethical neutrality of science. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The doctrine that scientists only produce knowledge and tools, and that how they are used is not their concern but society's: "We produce the tools. We stop there" (C. P. Snow's summary, Derry ch. 11 epigraph).

2. Role in this unit. It is the claim the unit tests. Snow says he "can't accept it for an instant," and Discussion 7.1 argues it is false both for science as a social enterprise and for individual scientists.

3. Example. The atomic bomb grew out of curiosity-driven nuclear physics; many scientists who built it later regretted it or withdrew from military work, while others felt justified (Derry ch. 11 §2).

4. Distinction. Einstein's point that science cannot tell us what should be is about the content of scientific conclusions; ethical neutrality goes further and denies scientists any responsibility. Derry rejects it: scientists must be honest about uncertainty and join public debate as informed citizens.

5. Caution. Rejecting neutrality does not mean blaming scientists for all harms (people who hold that view rarely credit them for the benefits, Overview footnote), since technological consequences often cannot be foreseen when research is done.

U7-T02Term

Define or distinguish Risk assessment. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Estimating the risks to society from toxic pollutants, disasters and similar hazards, usually from small amounts of sketchy, indirect data (Derry ch. 11 §3).

2. Role in this unit. It shows values affecting science itself. The idealized view says science measures the risk and values decide whether to accept it; critics reply that with large uncertainties, scientists must make judgements that values can influence.

3. Example. Toxicity studies on animals at high doses must be extrapolated to humans at low doses, and no one knows exactly how. Someone who thinks industry is over-regulated stresses that the substance may be safe; someone worried about environmental toxins stresses that it may be far more dangerous.

4. Distinction. Neither is bad science, unlike ideological zealots or tobacco-industry employees who say anything regardless of evidence, which is not science at all.

5. Caution. The cure is not to pretend to neutrality but to scrutinize risk assessments critically in terms of both science and values.

U7-T03Term

Define or distinguish Social Darwinism / eugenics. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. Social Darwinism was the late-nineteenth-century attempt to use evolution ("survival of the fittest") to justify existing class inequalities; eugenics is the attempt to "breed" better humans by not allowing the "unfit" to reproduce (Derry ch. 11 §2).

2. Role in this unit. They are the main examples of science's impact on values going wrong, through careless interpretation by people drawing value-laden conclusions from scientific results.

3. Example. The eugenics movements of the early twentieth century, and the work on human heredity of that period, which Derry says was tainted by class and ethnic prejudice (§3).

4. Distinction. These consequences "were in no way implied by Darwinian thought"; the theory describes how populations change, not what society ought to do. They are also an example of Sokal and Bricmont's second abuse, carrying a natural-science concept into the social world without justification.

5. Caution. Derry's lesson: good, solid scientific knowledge rarely causes problems; the problems come when highly value-laden implications are drawn from it, so such interpretations must always be scrutinized critically.

U7-T04Term

Define or distinguish Mythico-magical assumptions. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The three implicit assumptions about the world before science: nature is capricious and the unknown unknowable; everything is determined by external, willful powers; the future can be controlled by magic (Discussion 7.2).

2. Role in this unit. They are the starting point of the story of the rise of science: in Miletus they were replaced, without anyone saying so, by the metaphysical assumptions of science.

3. Example. Seeking the will of the gods through oracles and placating them with offerings; today, blaming a natural disaster on divine punishment or wearing a lucky charm.

4. Distinction. The scientific assumptions are their opposites: nature is ordered, the order is comprehensible to reason, and it can be communicated without subjective bias (Discussion 6.1).

5. Caution. Under mythico-magical assumptions a failed expectation is put down to caprice or an offended power, so experience serves as instance, not evidence; the difference lies in attitude, not intelligence.

U7-T05Term

Define or distinguish First crisis of science. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The crisis that arose because early Greek science had no established criteria for a reliable argument: how to reason without simply falling into nonsense (Discussion 7.2).

2. Role in this unit. It explains why logic became part of science's toolkit, a step in the rise of Western science.

3. Example. The Sophists of the late 5th century BCE taught persuasion to win arguments rather than find truth, and Gorgias argued that nothing exists, could be known or could be communicated; without a way to refute him, science itself was in question.

4. Distinction. Its resolution was Aristotle's laws of formal logic and his principle that conclusions are accepted only if supported by logically sound arguments, not by appeals to personality, authority or the gods; analogy and metaphor may illustrate but not prove.

5. Caution. Logic resolved the crisis of argument but not of testing: the speculative-deductive science that followed still lacked systematic experimental refutation, which came only in 17th-century Europe.

U7-T06Term

Define or distinguish Speculative-deductive method. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The scientific method of the Hellenistic world after Aristotle: top-down explanation deduced from abstract metaphysical principles or commonly agreed premises (Discussion 7.2).

2. Role in this unit. It marks the stage between Aristotle's logic and modern experimental science in the evolution of scientific method.

3. Example. Deducing the motions of the heavens from the agreed principle that heavenly bodies are perfect and so move in perfect circles.

4. Distinction. Observation and experiment existed, but using results to refute a theory, and designing experiments to test one, were unknown or unsystematic; the hypothetico-deductive method of 17th-century Europe made testing central.

5. Caution. Deduction was not abandoned; it remains essential, but conclusions are now only as good as premises that are tested against evidence.

Note Outside the readings: the circular-motion example is a standard illustration of Greek astronomy, not one given in Discussion 7.2.

U7-T07Term

Define or distinguish Scientism. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The belief, common in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, that science as it then existed was the final step in human intellectual development and would soon solve every human problem and answer every question (Discussion 7.2).

2. Role in this unit. It is the overconfident extreme of science's cultural success, the opposite of the anti-scientific view in the Overview.

3. Example. "To a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail"; Derry's extreme reductionists, who say "values are just a branch of biology" (ch. 11 §4), and the behaviourist and gene-centred claims about human nature passed off as purely scientific.

4. Distinction. Valuing science as the best way to understand the external world is not scientism; scientism claims science covers everything.

5. Caution. Today we are more modest: science has difficulty with the inner world of conscious experience, where third-person observation fails, and new methods would have to be integrated with existing ones.

U7-T08Term

Define or distinguish Social constructivism (strong program). Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. The "strong program" of social constructivism holds that social factors (prestige, friendship, power, negotiation) always permeate scientific discussion and eventually determine its outcome, so scientific results are social constructions (Derry ch. 15 §1).

2. Role in this unit. It is the central postmodern claim against scientific objectivity, inspired by Kuhn's work on scientific communities.

3. Example. Eddington's prestige led the community to reject Chandrasekhar's correct calculation that massive stars collapse.

4. Distinction. The weak version, that social factors influence science, especially early on when evidence is sparse, is true. The strong version, that they determine results, is answered by nature's constraint: black holes were accepted about two generations later because of new observations and theory.

5. Caution. Constructivists can be right for a historical period when issues are subtle, data are hard to get and theory is lacking; Derry's conclusion is that science is a construction, but not an arbitrary one.

U7-T09Term

Define or distinguish Postmodernism. Explain its role in this unit and give an appropriate example.

1. Definition. As applied to science, the critique that denies the possibility of objectivity and definite knowledge, and favours multiculturalism, relativism and a worldview in which truth does not exist; since science is a Western product, it is just one claimant among many (Derry ch. 15).

2. Role in this unit. Derry's chapter 15 and Study Questions 7-9 analyse its claims: validity criteria as cultural artifacts, the strong program, underdetermination and ideology.

3. Example. Feyerabend's remark that voodoo is no better or worse than science; Sokal's 1996 parody, published in a leading postmodern journal, brought the controversy to public attention.

4. Distinction. It differs from mild relativism and fallibilism, which accept that science is provisional but deny that it is arbitrary; Derry's continuum lies between "absolutely superior" and "all equally valid."

5. Caution. Its extreme claims are wrong, but moderate postmodern analysis does valuable work, exposing political shaping of research agendas, gender discrimination, and ideology in issues like the nature/nurture debate over intelligence.

Applied cases and reasoning12

U7-A01Applied10 marks

Distinguish a value judgment about what society ought to do from values required to conduct reliable inquiry. Explain how Einstein's and Bronowski's claims can be read together.

Source Unit 7 Overview and Discussion 7.1

Two kinds of value.

1. Social value judgements concern ends: what society ought to do with knowledge. Should we build nuclear weapons, test embryos for genetic disease, keep the very old alive at great cost? (Derry ch. 11 §2).

2. Values required for inquiry (epistemic or internal values) are the conditions for finding truth at all: honesty, curiosity, open-mindedness, free flow of information, the five norms, and Bronowski's freedom, dissent and tolerance (Derry ch. 11 §1; Discussion 7.1).

3. The difference. Social value judgements vary between people and cultures and are settled by debate and wisdom; inquiry values follow from the goal of factual understanding pursued by a community, which must have them "at least as ideals" if it is to succeed (Unit 7 Overview).

4. An example of each. Whether to use pesticides that raise yields but poison wildlife is a social judgement; reporting truthfully what the pesticide actually does to wildlife is an inquiry value.

Reading Einstein and Bronowski together.

5. Einstein says science "can only ascertain what is, but not what should be": scientific conclusions cannot settle social value judgements.

6. Bronowski says "you cannot know what is true unless you behave in certain ways," and "We OUGHT to act in such a way that what IS true can be verified to be so": there is an "ought" inside science.

7. No contradiction. Einstein is talking about the outputs of science and social values; Bronowski about the conduct of science and inquiry values. Both can be true at once.

8. The bridge. Bronowski's values are "deeper illuminations" in whose light good and evil, means and ends, are seen sharply. Accurate knowledge informs social choices without making them: science gives "power but not wisdom" (Derry ch. 11 §2).

9. The two can interact. Social values can leak into inquiry when data are sparse, as in risk assessment, and inquiry values (open debate, tolerance) also spread into the wider culture, as in the Enlightenment.

10. Conclusion. Science and values are related but not hierarchically: science supplies empirical information and depth of understanding, the decisions need a sagacity from outside science, and scientists must be honest about uncertainty and join the debate as informed citizens (Derry ch. 11 §4).

U7-A02Applied5 marks

A senior scientist asks colleagues to accept an unsupported result on reputation alone. Apply the norms of public knowledge, no privileged sources and judgment by intrinsic merit.

Source Discussion 7.1

1. Knowledge is public. The result must be published with its data and methods so others can check it; a claim kept inside one person's reputation is not yet scientific knowledge.

2. There are no privileged sources. Seniority, fame or office do not make a claim true. Expertise can guide where to look, but it is not evidence.

3. Ideas are judged on their intrinsic merit, not their source. Colleagues should ask what the data show, whether the method is sound and whether it can be replicated, exactly as they would for a graduate student. The related norm says claims must be substantiated, not taken on faith.

4. Why it matters. Derry's Eddington case shows the danger: Eddington's prestige led the community to reject Chandrasekhar's better argument, delaying the acceptance of black holes by about two generations (Derry ch. 15). Prestige can impose a wrong conclusion for a long time.

5. What the colleagues should do. Politely ask for the evidence, suspend judgement until it is produced and tested, and if it is not, decline to accept the result, attacking the argument, not the person (Discussion 7.1). If the evidence is good, accept it because of the evidence, not the reputation.

U7-A03Applied5 marks

A researcher withholds an adverse result to protect a successful appearance. Explain the consequences for both professional integrity and the community's ability to discover error.

Source Discussion 7.1 and Derry Chapter 11

1. A breach of integrity. Withholding the adverse result misrepresents the evidence and violates Holton's first principle ("get it right at all costs") and the norm that claims be substantiated; it is a step toward fraud, driven by the "excessive desire for the appearance of success" that confuses appearance with reality (Discussion 7.1).

2. Others are misled. Science is a community activity in which each scientist relies on others' results; colleagues will build on, fund or apply a result that the full evidence does not support, wasting effort and possibly harming people (as in risk assessment or medicine).

3. Error cannot be corrected. The community can only correct mistakes it can see. Hiding the adverse result removes the very evidence that would let others find the error, which defeats organized skepticism and replication.

4. The researcher's own learning suffers. A good scientist wants to know quickly if an idea is wrong to avoid wasting time; concealment, like obsessive secrecy, cuts the researcher off from the criticism that improves ideas.

5. Loss of trust. If discovered, the researcher's work will no longer be trusted, used or read, effective exclusion from the community, and public trust in science is damaged too (Derry ch. 11 §1: fraud is met with outrage because honesty is central).

Note Outside the readings: when many researchers leave negative results unpublished, the published record becomes biased toward positive findings, which is known as the "file-drawer problem."

U7-A04Applied5 marks

Explain how tolerating dissent can improve knowledge without requiring scientists to accept every dissenting claim as equally well supported.

Source Discussion 7.1

1. Dissent tests ideas. Truth is "more likely to be found by open-minded exploration and vigorous debate than by adherence to dogma or authority"; dissent is how weak arguments and hidden errors are exposed (Discussion 7.1).

2. Dissent creates originality. Freedom to dissent "opens the door for originality and creativity"; Bronowski lists dissent among the "first needs of science." Chandrasekhar's dissent from Eddington turned out to be right (Derry ch. 15).

3. Tolerance concerns the person, not the claim. Tolerance means we may not silence or harm a dissenter; we must answer the argument. It does not mean every dissenting claim is equally well supported.

4. Claims are still judged on merit. A dissenting claim must be substantiated like any other, and new results that contradict a well-established consensus meet especially severe skepticism (Derry ch. 12, organized skepticism); between "absolutely right" and "all equally valid" lies a continuum of justified judgement (Derry ch. 15).

5. Result. Tolerating dissent keeps the consensus open to correction when contradictory evidence accumulates, while the requirement of evidence keeps out claims that have none, such as perpetual-motion machines. Skepticism thus keeps change possible while fostering conservatism.

U7-A05Applied10 marks

Apply Holton's four principles of integrity to a scientist facing pressure to publish quickly, specialize narrowly and conceal uncertainty.

Source Discussion 7.1

The case. A scientist is pressed to publish quickly, to stay narrowly specialized, and to hide the uncertainty in results.

Principle 1: Try to get it right at all costs, sparing no effort.

1. Speed must not override accuracy: repeat key measurements, check calculations and run controls before publishing. Dunbar: success comes only from "checking and double checking," because "only by patience and careful testing will we avoid mistakes."

2. Concealing uncertainty fails this principle directly: a result is only "right" when reported with its real error bars and limits. Derry asks scientists to show "extreme honesty concerning the uncertainties in our knowledge" (ch. 11 §4).

Principle 2: Try to be a scientist first, a specialist second.

3. Narrow specialization can blind a researcher to the shared values and methods of science; a scientist first keeps the community's standards (open data, peer review) above the habits of a small field.

4. Breadth also helps catch errors: knowing related fields lets the scientist see whether a result coheres with other knowledge, the coherence that makes theories trustworthy.

Principle 3: Try to explore and contribute to the role of science as part of our overall worldview.

5. The scientist should ask what the work means beyond the speciality and explain it honestly to the public, without overstatement that becomes value-laden myth (Derry ch. 15).

6. Hiding uncertainty distorts that worldview: the public and policy makers need to know how firm a result is, as risk assessment shows.

Principle 4: Try to do your duty as a scientist and as a human being.

7. Duty to the community: publish honestly and share data, since others will rely on the work; resisting pressure that would compromise honesty is part of that duty.

8. Duty as a human being: consider who could be harmed by an overconfident result (patients, the environment) and remember that everything we have comes from the efforts of others (Gurdjieff).

Conclusion.

9. The pressures come from personal goals such as fear of failure and desire for recognition, which Discussion 7.1 says can lead to fraud; integrity means letting the values of science, not those pressures, govern conduct.

10. A practical resolution: publish when the result is solid, report the uncertainty openly, collaborate across fields, and accept that a slower honest paper serves both the scientist's reputation and the truth better than a fast misleading one.

U7-A06Applied5 marks

Reconstruct the cooperator and competitor example. Explain how a person's own behavior can create misleading evidence for a belief about other people.

Source Discussion 7.1

1. The game. Kelley and Stahelski's subjects played the prisoner's dilemma without communicating. Both cooperate: each gains a small reward; both compete: each loses a moderate amount; one competes and one cooperates: the competitor gains a large reward and the cooperator loses a large amount (Discussion 7.1).

2. The groups. From their views of the game's aim, subjects were sorted into cooperators (aim: small profit for both each round) and competitors (aim: outguess the other to win the most).

3. What happened. Competitor with competitor: both competed. Cooperator with cooperator: both cooperated. Cooperator with competitor: the cooperator began by cooperating but quickly switched to competing to minimize losses.

4. What each learned. Competitors only ever saw competition, so they learned something false, that everybody is a competitor. Cooperators saw both behaviours, so they learned something true, that the world contains both cooperators and competitors.

5. Self-created evidence. The competitors' own behaviour turned cooperators into competitors, producing the very evidence that confirmed their false belief. "The way that we interact with the world determines how we see the world and what we are able to learn about it"; this is Bronowski's point that "you cannot know what is true unless you behave in certain ways."

U7-A07Applied5 marks

Distinguish spirited scientific disagreement from a contest aimed only at winning. Explain why acknowledging a strong criticism can advance a collective search for truth.

Source Discussion 7.1

1. Spirited disagreement. Scientists may argue hard and feel emotionally engaged, but the aim is truth: as Ziman says, "advocate powerfully, but... concede defeat gracefully, without making a personal issue of it"; a well-fought controversy is "a form of cooperation" (Discussion 7.1).

2. A contest aimed only at winning treats truth as whatever the most persuasive speaker says, the Sophists' attitude that caused the first crisis of science (Discussion 7.2). In the Sufi story the teacher refused to debate the scholar because "he was only interested in winning the argument, not in discovering the truth."

3. The test of the difference is how each side treats evidence against it: the truth-seeker welcomes it and changes their mind; the contestant hides, dismisses or attacks the person.

4. Why acknowledging a strong criticism helps. It removes an error early (a good scientist wants to know quickly if an idea is wrong), points to a better theory, and shows others which parts of the work are reliable. Science is collective, so a correction benefits everyone who builds on the result.

5. It also keeps the community working. Respect and mutual trust are what let scientists rely on each other's results; graceful concession keeps rivals as cooperators in the search for truth instead of enemies.

U7-A08Applied5 marks

Explain the first crisis of science as presented in Discussion 7.2 and the role assigned to Aristotle's formal logic in responding to it.

Source Discussion 7.2

1. The crisis. The early Greek natural philosophers used reason to explain nature, but there were no established criteria for a reliable argument, no way to tell sound reasoning from nonsense (Discussion 7.2).

2. The Sophists of the late 5th century BCE brought it to a head. They taught the art of persuasion for political success, in effect a return to the magical idea that truth is whatever the most persuasive speaker says, and were interested only in winning arguments.

3. The threat. Gorgias argued against the metaphysical assumptions of science; without a way to refute such arguments conclusively, the very possibility of science was in question. Socrates and Plato opposed the Sophists but did not settle the matter.

4. Aristotle's formal logic provided the criteria: laws that determine which conclusions follow validly from premises (Discussion 9.2), so arguments could be judged by their form rather than their persuasiveness.

5. The principle that went with it. Conclusions could be accepted only if supported by logically sound arguments; appeals to personality, authority or the gods were excluded, and analogy and metaphor could illustrate but not demonstrate. This became the basis of the speculative-deductive science that followed.

U7-A09Applied10 marks

Describe two cultural or institutional conditions that the course links to the rise of modern science in Europe. Explain why historical explanation does not establish the intrinsic superiority of a population.

Source Discussion 7.2

Two conditions the course links to the rise of science.

1. Exposure to alternatives under tolerance. The Persian Empire, from Cyrus the Great on, made religious tolerance official policy, so it was a mosaic of religions. Traders from Miletus met many conflicting myths. Awareness of alternatives is what lets experience serve as evidence rather than instance (Discussions 5.2 and 7.2).

2. Settling disputes by public argument. Greek cities decided legal disputes by jury, with each side arguing and the jury debating (Socrates' jury had over 500 members). It became natural to think that differences between myths could be settled by debate and reason, leading to Thales's natural theory of water.

3. (A further condition in modern Europe.) In the 17th century, wealth and the spirit of exploration after the discovery of the Americas, together with institutions for open communication, peer review and credit, let experimental testing flourish.

4. These are conditions, not traits. The explanation points to trade, politics, law and institutions, things a society has, not inborn qualities of a population.

Why historical explanation does not show intrinsic superiority.

5. The same people changed. Egypt, "as liberal as it was in many ways," erased Akhenaten's religion and could not accept an alternative; Egypt's long decline followed (Discussion 7.2). The same is true of Europe: Hellenistic science was speculative-deductive, and modern experimental science came almost two thousand years later. Conditions changed; people did not.

6. Science was borrowed and shared. Thales studied mathematics and astronomy in Babylon and Egypt; the Pythagorean theorem was known in Mesopotamia and Egypt long before Pythagoras. Science is a cumulative human achievement, not the product of one population.

7. Possessing science is not superiority. Hallpike points out that possessing science and analytic rationality is no guarantee of wisdom or of functioning well in the world; every successful culture has its own means of survival in its environment.

8. Thinking is not the difference; attitude is. The Azande reason coherently within their framework; what they lack is the attitude of treating beliefs as testable, which is cultural (Discussion 5.2). The Overview compares science to singing: an ability that shows up in different forms in different groups.

9. Science spreads because it works. Western science is becoming world science "not because of any imperialistic design" but because it improves quality of life (Discussion 7.1). Anyone, from any background, can learn and practise it.

10. The danger of the opposite view. Treating science as proof of racial or cultural superiority produced the "white man's burden" and the abuses of colonization (Discussion 7.2), and the same move from fact to value fed social Darwinism and eugenics (Derry ch. 11). A historical explanation of where something arose says nothing about the worth of the people involved.

U7-A10Applied10 marks

Contrast the three mythico-magical assumptions with the three metaphysical assumptions of science. Explain how these differences affect whether a failed expectation can prompt revision.

Source Discussion 7.2 and Discussion 6.1

The two sets of assumptions.

1. Capricious versus ordered. Mythico-magical: nature is capricious and the unknown is unknowable. Science: nature is ordered.

2. Willful powers versus comprehensible order. Mythico-magical: everything is determined by external, willful powers. Science: the order is comprehensible to human reason.

3. Magic versus communicable understanding. Mythico-magical: the future can be controlled by magic, through specialists who read and influence the powers. Science: our understanding of the order can be communicated without subjective bias, so anyone can check it (Discussions 6.1 and 7.2).

How a failed expectation is handled.

4. Under caprice, a failure needs no explanation: nature simply did something else this time. Nothing is learned.

5. Under willful powers, a failure means a god or spirit was displeased or another person's magic interfered; the response is more offerings or counter-magic, not a new theory.

6. Under magic, a failure means the ritual was done wrongly. The Azande explained wrong oracle answers as bad poison, poor preparation, ritual errors or witchcraft, so failures were explained away and the oracle was never questioned; experiences became instances, not evidence (Discussion 5.2).

7. Under order, a failed prediction is a signal that our account is wrong somewhere, because an ordered nature would not have surprised a correct theory.

8. Under comprehensibility, we can find the error and propose a better explanation. When Uranus strayed from its predicted orbit, astronomers proposed an unseen planet and found Neptune (Derry ch. 4); when Mercury's orbit could not be fixed the same way, the anomaly eventually helped replace Newton's theory with Einstein's.

9. Under communicability, others can repeat the test and check the reasoning, so a failure cannot be quietly blamed on the observer's private state; replication and peer review make revision a community process.

10. Conclusion. The difference is attitude: science treats beliefs as working hypotheses that experience can count "for or against" (Darwin), while the mythico-magical view protects belief from experience. Only under the scientific assumptions can failure prompt revision, which is why the change made in Miletus was the start of science.

Note Outside the readings: the Mercury example (the anomaly in Mercury's orbit, explained by general relativity in 1915).

U7-A11Applied5 marks

A commentator uses quantum terminology as a metaphor for social relationships without giving a model or evidence. Explain which of Sokal and Bricmont's criticisms might apply and what justification is missing.

Source Derry Chapter 15 and Unit 7 Study Question 7

1. Abuse (b), unjustified analogy. The commentator imports a natural-science concept (quantum superposition, entanglement, uncertainty) into the social world with no rational or empirical justification that social relationships behave like quantum systems.

2. Abuse (c), irrelevant technical language. If the quantum terms add nothing that ordinary words would not, they are used for prestige where they are irrelevant.

3. Possibly abuses (a) and (d). If the commentator explains the physics at length while misunderstanding it (for example, treating "observation" as human attention rather than a physical interaction), or the claims, stripped of jargon, mean nothing, the talk becomes long-winded misunderstanding or scientific-sounding nonsense.

4. What is missing. A model stating exactly which features of the physics correspond to which features of relationships, why the mathematics should apply to people, and evidence (observations or data) showing that predictions based on the analogy succeed. In physics, quantum effects belong to the microscopic scale; nothing shows they carry over to people.

5. Fair use of metaphor. A metaphor may illustrate an idea but not demonstrate it (Aristotle's principle, Discussion 7.2); Derry warns against confusing value-laden metaphorical extensions with science (ch. 15). The commentator should present the idea as a metaphor, or supply the model and evidence.

U7-A12Applied10 marks

Using the Chandrasekhar and Eddington case as Derry presents it, explain both the influence of scientific authority and the possibility of correction through reasoning and evidence.

Source Derry Chapter 15

The case (Derry ch. 15 §1).

1. The calculation. As a young, unknown scientist, S. Chandrasekhar made calculations suggesting that massive stars end their lives by gravitational collapse, what we now call black holes.

2. The authority. Sir Arthur Eddington, the foremost astrophysicist of the time, could not accept such an absurd-sounding conclusion and said that something (unspecified) must be wrong with the theory.

3. The community's response. Although Chandrasekhar had the better argument, Eddington's conclusion was almost universally accepted.

Why authority won at first.

4. Conditions favoured prestige. No observational evidence existed, the idea was strange as well as new, and Eddington's prestige was enormous. Derry says social factors prevail longest when issues are subtle and complex, observations are hard to get, and there is no substantial theoretical context.

5. A breach of the norms. Accepting Eddington's view on his say-so violated the norms that there are no privileged sources and that ideas are judged on their intrinsic merit (Discussion 7.1). It supports the postmodern point that prestige and power enter scientific negotiation.

How correction came.
